title: Solar, wind and batteries can deliver firm power at $0.086/kWh, says Ember - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
An analysis by Ember finds that adding wind power to solar PV and battery storage systems reduces the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105/MWh to $86/MWh. The cost could fall further to $52/MWh by 2050, based on the regional cost projections used in the model.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
16 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
A hybrid project developer by Prosolia
Adding wind power to hybrid systems combining photovoltaics and battery storage can reduce the cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand by nearly one-fifth, according to an analysis by UK-based think tank Ember.
The median cost falls from $0.105/kWh (€0.095/kWh) to $0.086/kWh (€0.078/kWh) when wind generation is included, primarily due to reduced storage requirements.
The study examines 10 years of meteorological data, region by region and hour by hour, combining solar and wind generation with battery storage to assess the cost of meeting 80%, 90% and 99% of electricity demand. The model assumes constant baseload demand throughout the year.
Wind power’s main contribution is to reduce periods when solar generation falls short of demand. In Canada, the battery storage capacity required to achieve 90% coverage falls from 24 hours to 10 hours of demand. In the United States and Europe, it declines from 20 hours to 12 hours, while in China it falls from 18 hours to 12 hours. In India, where wind has a smaller impact on storage requirements, the figure remains at 14 hours.
With wind power included, three-quarters of global electricity demand can be met at 90% coverage for less than $0.10/kWh (€0.091/kWh). Without wind generation, that share falls to approximately half.
The analysis estimates that, under conservative assumptions, global wind energy potential is at least 19 times total global electricity demand. Regions accounting for 93% of global electricity consumption have at least 1 GW of developable wind potential within their territories and coastal zones, while regions representing 82% of demand have at least 10 GW.
The model applies a uniform cost of capital of 7% to compare resources and technologies across regions. When regional costs of capital are applied, the median cost of achieving 90% coverage rises from $0.099/kWh (€0.090/kWh) to $0.104/kWh (€0.094/kWh) in Europe, and from $0.076/kWh (€0.069/kWh) to $0.126/kWh (€0.114/kWh) in Africa.
Seasonal complementarity
The complementary generation profiles of solar and wind power are particularly significant at higher latitudes. Solar output becomes more seasonal farther from the equator, while wind generation tends to be stronger during months when solar output is lower.
In Europe, for example, wind power produces 44% of its annual output between November and February, compared with just 12% for solar. Combining the two technologies results in a more even distribution of electricity generation throughout the year.
Percentage of annual generation by month and technology (%), 2023–2025
North of 45° latitude, adding wind power reduces the median cost of achieving 90% coverage by 40%, from $0.164/kWh (€0.149/kWh) to $0.099/kWh (€0.090/kWh).
In Chile and Argentina, south of 40°S, the reduction is approximately one-third, with costs falling from $0.094/kWh (€0.085/kWh) to $0.063/kWh (€0.057/kWh).
Periods of low generation
Ember also examines how frequently solar and wind power experience prolonged periods of low generation simultaneously. The study defines a “low-generation week” as seven consecutive days during which output from a given technology remains below half its average over the 10-year period analysed.
Globally, when weighted by electricity demand, a week of low solar generation occurs approximately four times a year, compared with eight times for wind. However, low-generation weeks for both technologies coincide, on average, only once every four years.
This complementarity is also evident during extreme weather conditions. In Germany, the worst combined solar and wind generation week of the decade produces a deficit equivalent to approximately five days of average electricity demand, compared with six days when either technology is used alone.
Reduced need for backup generation
Combining solar, wind and battery storage also reduces the need for backup generation during periods of insufficient renewable output.
According to the model, a solar-plus-storage system that meets 90% of electricity demand has an average cost of $0.105/kWh (€0.095/kWh).
At $0.098/kWh (€0.089/kWh), a system incorporating wind power can achieve 95% coverage, halving the amount of demand that must be met by backup generation.
For 90% coverage, the demand-weighted average cost of a solar-and-wind system with backup generation is $0.093/kWh (€0.084/kWh), compared with $0.140/kWh (€0.127/kWh) for a system relying solely on solar and batteries. With wind included, the average cost is $0.089/kWh (€0.081/kWh).
Replacing planned coal and gas capacity
Ember’s analysis identifies 845 GW of coal- and gas-fired power generation capacity currently in the planning stage. With wind power included, renewable energy systems combining solar, wind and battery storage could provide an alternative to 90% of this planned capacity at a cost below $0.100/kWh (€0.091/kWh), compared with 71% for systems without wind.
Of the planned capacity, 706 GW – approximately five-sixths of the total – is located in regions where solar, wind and battery storage could deliver firm power at less than $0.100/kWh (€0.091/kWh). Without wind power, that figure falls to 520 GW.
Outlook to 2050
Ember estimates that the cost of firm power generation from solar and wind, supported by battery storage, could fall from $0.089/kWh (€0.081/kWh) today to $0.052/kWh (€0.047/kWh) by 2050, based on the regional cost projections used in its model.

title: Around 60% of home battery installs rated ‘substandard’ by Australian regulator - pv magazine Global
content:
More than 60% of batteries and about 23% of solar systems installed under the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme (SRES) during the 2025–26 financial year were rated as “substandard” while less than 1% of both were deemed “unsafe,” according to a new report from the Clean Energy Regulator (CER).
The CER has published its
annual inspection report
for the 2025–26 financial identifying installation trends, risks and common areas of non-compliance.
Across the reporting period, the CER completed a record 6,554 inspections, including 3,425 solar battery systems and 3,129 solar inspections.
Just 23.11% of the inspected solar systems were rated as substandard – that is, the installation contains faults that need to be rectified – and 0.93%, or 29 of the 3,129 inspected installs were found to be unsafe – not safe to remain in operation as is.
Of the battery energy storage systems (BESS) inspected, 61.19% were found to be substandard while 0.95% were rated as unsafe.
Critically, the report reveals the common areas of non-compliance identified are almost entirely the result of poor workmanship rather than faulty products.
Solar PV inspections outcomes by installation year
The most common issues leading to a solar system being rated substandard included incorrectly sized or fitted cabling and conduits, improper bonding or earthing of solar panel frames and other equipment, incompatible or incorrectly installed DC connectors, and improperly fitted mounting structures.
Out of the 29 solar systems deemed unsafe under the 2025–26 inspection program, 16 were due to unsafe installation work, 12 were due to a third-party incident such as weather damaging the system, and one was attributed to a product recall.
The main causes for a battery system being rated substandard included missing or incorrect labelling, incorrectly configured or missing wiring, insufficient rated circuit protection, and inadequate physical protection for cables and the battery.
Solar battery inspection outcomes by installation month

title: Coal plant failure, not solar PV, triggered Sri Lanka’s latest blackout - pv magazine Global
content:
The cause of
Sri Lanka’s nationwide black occurred on Oct. 17
was the the loss of 187 MW of electricity from a coal power plant and not the high solar PV penetration as initially thought.
This emerges from a
preliminary investigation report
submitted by the National System Operator (NSO) to the Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka (PUCSL), which explicitly identifies the sudden loss of generation from Lakvijaya Coal Power Plant Unit 1 (LVPP Unit 01) as the initiating event of the blackout.
“LVPP Unit 01 rapidly de-loaded from the unit net generation of 187 MW to 5 MW within 450 ms,” the authors of the report state, noting that grid frequency fell from 49.906 Hz to 48.75 Hz within two seconds.
The unit has a capacity of 300 MW and is located at the 900 MW Norochcholai Power Station in Puttalam, in the country’s North Western Province.
The report does not fully explain why the coal unit lost output or whether distributed PV behaviour contributed to the cascading failure.
Following the blackout, the NSO instructed all PV system owners to disconnect their installations from the grid. The decision appeared to have been informed by a previous nationwide blackout on Feb. 9, 2025, when the Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) identified high solar PV penetration as a major contributing factor.
According to a CEB investigation published in April 2025, the blackout was triggered at noon by a fault at the Panadura grid substation. At the time, solar PV accounted for more than 50% of electricity demand, leaving the grid with insufficient system inertia to withstand the disturbance. The resulting voltage drop and cascading disconnections led to a nationwide blackout.
At the time, the authorities also instructed rooftop solar system owners to disconnect their installations from the grid during restoration efforts.
Sri Lanka’s rooftop PV capacity reached
1.94 GW by the end of 2025
, following rapid growth in installations and generation.
Sri Lanka’s daily electricity demand stood at approximately 58 GWh to 60 GWh in March 2026, equivalent to an average continuous power requirement of around 2,400 MW to 2,500 MW.

title: Dutch watchdog urges solar owners to check energy contracts - pv magazine Global
content:
The Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets (ACM) is advising households with solar installations to check if their current energy contract is still the most suitable ahead of the
end of net-metering
on Jan. 1, 2027.
The end of net metering will mean households can no longer offset electricity exported to the grid against electricity imported from it. ACM’s latest update explains that from the start of next year, households will pay the full retail electricity rate, including energy taxes, for power drawn from the grid, while receiving a separate feed-in payment for surplus electricity.
The regulator adds that the feed-in payment is generally lower than the retail electricity rate. Under Dutch legislation, suppliers must pay at least 50% of the basic electricity supply rate, excluding taxes, for exported electricity until Dec. 31, 2029.
ACM is expecting feed-in charges to decline after the scheme ends, as suppliers will no longer incur costs associated with net metering, but adds that suppliers will continue to face other costs related to solar customers, including expenses associated with balancing the electricity grid when solar generation fluctuates unexpectedly.
ACM, which is responsible for supervising the tariffs of energy suppliers, says it will now include contracts with feed-in charges for solar panels in its monthly overview, known as Energiemonitor. Its most recent monitor says a number of suppliers are charging significantly higher rates for their standard contracts as opposed to dynamic contracts.
The discontinuation of net metering may make home batteries more attractive for some households, ACM added.
The number of home batteries is
growing significantly
in the Netherlands. Figures from ACM state approximately 89,000 home batteries belonging to households and small businesses were registered with grid operators by the end of October but add that as small plug-in battery systems are not always registered, the total is likely even higher. Total installed home battery capacity amounted to 1.1 GW by the end of October, compared to 0.3 GW at the end of October 2025.
ACM says consumers considering a home battery should carefully check what best suits their individual situation.
“Whether a home battery is worthwhile depends, among other things, on the home, energy consumption, and the energy contract,” the regulator said. “Before purchasing a home battery, it is therefore wise to first determine how much energy you use, where you can save, and what suits your home.”
It also warned against unreliable sellers taking advantage of the uncertainty surrounding the end of the net metering scheme.
“They are luring consumers into expensive purchases with misleading sales pitches, sometimes home batteries costing more than €20,000 [$22,035],” ACM said.
ACM’s latest update also reveals that negative electricity prices in the Netherlands currently stand at just over 400 in 2026, lower than in the same period of 2025 and 2024. The regulator says a possible explanation for this is the increase in the number of installed batteries.

title: Global solar installations face first annual decline in eight years - pv magazine Global
content:
London-based analytics firm GlobalData said annual global solar PV additions will decline in 2026 for the first time since 2018, after rising 17.5% to a record in 2025. It attributed the slowdown to market reforms in China, policy changes in the United States and a slowdown in Pakistan.
“The 2026 dip reflects policy shifts in a few large markets rather than a weakening of solar’s fundamentals, with China’s move to market-based tariffs accounting for most of the decline,” said Attaurrahman Ojindaram Saibasan, a power analyst at GlobalData.
The company said it expects global cumulative PV capacity to grow at a compound annual rate of 12.5% from 2025 to 2035, more than doubling solar’s share of global electricity.
China accounted for more than half of 2025 additions, followed by the United States and India. India’s additions rose 87.2%, and Pakistan’s grew 34.3% as rooftop and off-grid demand made it the fourth-largest market. Additions in the Middle East and Africa nearly tripled, while Europe’s rose 2.6% and North America’s fell 3.6%, said GlobalData.
The company said the long decline in module prices has stalled, as higher silver and cell costs, China’s export tax rebate adjustment in April and Beijing’s “anti-involution” campaign pushed prices up in early 2026. Saibasan said grid constraints are now the main barrier to growth, pointing to curtailment in China, negative power prices in Europe and connection queues in the United States, India and Brazil.
“Falling battery costs are the main counterweight to grid congestion, curtailment, and negative power prices. Solar-plus-storage is now competitive for firm supply in high-resource regions, allowing solar to move beyond daytime generation and compete for round-the-clock supply,” he said. “Developers and investors that pair solar with storage and secure grid access early will be best placed to capture the recovery from 2027.”
The forecast follows GlobalData’s March projection that
global solar capacity will reach 6 TW by 2031
. The International Energy Agency’s Photovoltaic Power Systems Programme has estimated that
global solar additions hit 690 GW in 2025
, and in October the International Energy Agency forecast an 11% fall in global renewable capacity additions in 2026, mainly because of slower solar deployment in China.

title: Japan sees increase in corporate solar PPAs - pv magazine Global
content:
The number of corporate solar power purchase agreements (PPAs) signed in Japan is increasing, according to analysis from infrastructure intelligence platform Global Infrastructure Sherpa.
Roberto Krell, founder of Global Infrastructure Sherpa, told
pv magazine
the company logged around 30% more corporate solar PPAs in Japan from January to October this year than across the first ten months of 2025.
Notable examples of agreements signed this year include two solar PPAs between Microsoft and pan-Asian renewable energy platform Blueleaf Energy, announced late last month, with Microsoft acting as the sole offtaker for two solar projects due online mid next year. In May, Spanish developer EDP Renewables commissioned a 44 MW solar project in Fukushima for Amazon under a long-term corporate PPA.
Global Infrastructure Sherpa says that while large-scale players, such as Microsoft and Amazon continue to attract attention, Japan’s corporate PPA market is moving beyond the hyperscalers with manufacturers, logistics companies and advertising groups also entering into long-term solar agreements.
Examples include a 15-year virtual PPA involving a 54 MW solar plant and approximately 130 MWh of battery storage between Japanese manufacturer NSK and Tokyo-based developer Eneos Renewable Energy and a 20-year solar PPA in Hyogo and Kyoto between Nippon Electric Glass and Japanese utility Kansai Electric that is expected to begin delivery in March next year.
Krell told
pv magazine
climate targets are driving corporate solar PPAs in Japan, with some companies looking to solar deals to meet carbon-neutrality targets.
He cited virtual PPAs as another factor, noting that many of this year’s corporate solar PPAs are virtual. “The company buys the green certificates from a new solar plant at a fixed price and keeps its existing electricity supplier,” Krell explained. “That makes a deal much easier to sign, and it’s bringing in buyers that wouldn’t have signed a few years ago, such as railways, retailers and mid-sized manufacturers.”
Krell looked to data centres as another driver. “Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Equinix and At Tokyo have all signed solar PPAs in Japan, and theirs tend to be the large ones,” he said. “[Data center company] Equinix’s 121 MW deal in February is the biggest corporate solar PPA we’ve seen in Japan this year, followed by
Tokyu Railway’s 98 MW
Krell predicted that the upward trend in corporate solar PPAs in Japan is likely to continue in the coming years.
“The data centre build-out around Tokyo and Osaka hasn’t peaked yet, and every new campus is another potential buyer. More companies also have climate targets to meet, and virtual PPAs make it easy for them to sign,” he told
pv magazine
.  “What could slow things down may be challenges like finding good sites without local opposition, and getting grid connections in time.”
Analysis published last year by data platform Japanese Energy Hub said that, since the first corporate PPA in Japan was signed in 2021, the number of disclosed deals has grown to over 500, totaling over 2.5 GW in installed and planned capacity.
Japan’s cumulative solar capacity is estimated at around 100 GW after adding approximately
5.8 GW of solar
last year.

title: Mitsubishi Electric unveils ‘The Little One’ heat pump - pv magazine Global
content:
Japanese electronics and electrical equipment manufacturing company
Mitsubishi Electric
has unveiled a new residential air-to-water heat pump designed for new-build homes in the United Kingdom.
The new system, called The Little One, is part of the manufacturer’s
Ecodan product range
and will be commercially available in 2027.
The company said it developed the unit to address space constraints, installation flexibility and costs for housebuilders preparing for the UK’s Future Homes Standard, which is a building regulation framework designed to ensure new homes are highly energy-efficient and produce significantly lower carbon emissions, primarily through low-carbon heating and improved insulation.
The heat pump uses propane (R290) as its refrigerant and is available in two versions with heating capacities of 4 kW and 6 kW. Both models have an A+++ energy efficiency rating.
The 4 kW model achieves a seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) of 4.77 at a water flow temperature of 35 C, while the 6 kW version reaches 4.65 under the same conditions, according to the manufacturer.
The unit measures 970 mm × 713 mm × 400 mm and weighs 58 kg. According to Mitsubishi Electric, it is 47% smaller and 40% lighter than a comparable model in its existing product range.
The system incorporates the company’s patented Bossless Fan technology, which is designed to reduce weight and operating noise by eliminating the conventional central fan hub. The 4 kW model has a sound power level of 49 dB(A), compared with 51 dB(A) for the 6 kW version.
Mitsubishi Electric said the heat pump also features patented refrigerant technology that incorporates an odorant into the R290 circuit. According to the manufacturer, this eliminates the need for a protective zone around the outdoor unit, allowing greater flexibility in installation locations.
The company said the new range is designed to be more cost-effective than its existing R32 and R290 heat pump offerings, although it did not disclose pricing information.
“By making the unit considerably smaller and lighter, reducing noise, removing the need for an R290 protective zone and delivering excellent efficiency at a more competitive cost, we believe we have created a product that makes specifying and installing heat pumps easier for housebuilders,” said Joanna Crown, product marketing manager at Mitsubishi Electric.
No further technical details about the heat pump technology have been disclosed.

title: Silver prices find $50 floor as solar industry seeks to accelerate shift toward copper - pv magazine Global
content:
Silver prices appear to have stabilized around $50 per ounce following an exceptionally volatile year, but the photovoltaic industry should not expect a return to the much lower prices of previous decades, according to Philip Newman, managing director of
Metals Focus
“I think the price, the floor seems quite strong, but I think you’re still going to see more volatility,” Newman told
pv magazine
. “Could prices dip below 50? Of course they can. But I think the 50 still seems like a decent floor.”
His comments follow the publication of new silver market estimates by the Silver Institute and Metals Focus on November 13. The organizations expect the global silver market to record its sixth consecutive annual deficit in 2026, with demand exceeding supply by 35 million ounces.
Silver reached an
all-time high of $121.65 per ounce on January 26
, driven by strong investment demand and tight physical liquidity in London. It subsequently retreated to approximately $52 by November 4, as shifting US interest rate expectations, a stronger dollar and rising bond yields weighed on precious metals.
Despite the correction, prices remain exceptionally high. The annual average was approximately $40 in 2025, while Newman suggested the 2026 average could exceed $70 per ounce.
Thrifting
The impact of elevated prices is particularly apparent in photovoltaics, where manufacturers are accelerating efforts to reduce silver consumption.
According to
Metals Focus
, global industrial silver demand is expected to decline by 3% to 640 million ounces in 2026. Industrial consumption outside photovoltaics is forecast to grow by 4.5% to 492 million ounces, but this will be more than offset by weaker demand from solar cells.
The consultancy attributes the decline to slower-than-expected PV installations, particularly in China, and accelerated silver thrifting and substitution.
Newman said the industry’s response to higher prices has evolved significantly over the past year. When silver first exceeded $50 in late 2025, manufacturers focused on extending silver-coated copper metallization, already used in heterojunction (HJT) cells, to tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) technology.
Replacing silver entirely with copper was still regarded as a longer-term objective because of potential performance trade-offs. However, January’s price surge changed the discussion.
“Let’s move to copper and we can think about the trade-off afterwards and improve the efficiency,” Newman said, describing the industry’s initial reaction.
Since then, the transition has become more measured, with manufacturers considering not only conversion efficiency but also long-term reliability.
“I think the move to copper has now become more measured,” Newman said, pointing to growing attention to “the shelf life, the longevity of these cells.”
Manufacturers and buyers have different priorities
According to Newman, the transition is also shaped by diverging interests among manufacturers and module buyers.
For manufacturers facing overcapacity and intense price competition, reducing silver consumption represents an opportunity to lower costs. Developers and installers, however, may hesitate to adopt new metallization technologies without sufficient evidence of long-term reliability.
“From the panel manufacturer, to your point about overcapacity and the pressure on costs, they would really like to move to copper quite quickly,” Newman said. “On the other side, the companies that are buying those panels and installing them, I think there’s a lot more hesitancy, more reticence, more cautiousness about doing so.”
This divergence could encourage manufacturers to offer conventional high-silver modules alongside alternatives with reduced silver content or potentially silver-free metallization.
Although research into copper metallization has intensified, fully copper-based solutions have yet to become mainstream in commercial TOPCon products. Intermediate approaches involving silver-coated copper or lower silver loadings appear more realistic in the near term.
The economic incentive remains substantial even after the recent price correction.
Newman estimated that at $60 per ounce, silver accounts for approximately 17% of TOPCon module costs. At $50, the proportion falls to around 14%, compared with roughly 11% when silver traded at $40.
Metals Focus
expects global PV installations to decline modestly in 2026 before returning to growth in 2027. Nevertheless, Newman expects silver thrifting to continue, even if prices stabilize.
Silver shortages unlikely
Despite the sixth consecutive annual market deficit, Newman does not anticipate a physical shortage that would materially disrupt photovoltaic manufacturing.
“No, not really,” he said when asked about potential supply problems.
He pointed to China’s substantial silver imports in 2026, continued availability of silver powder from Japan, and gradually recovering inventories in London.
The Silver Institute expects total silver supply to decline by 3% to approximately 1.045 billion ounces in 2026. Mine production should remain broadly stable at 834 million ounces, while recycling is forecast to increase by 6% to 210 million ounces.
The overall deficit is expected to narrow from 54 million ounces in 2025 to 35 million ounces in 2026, bringing the cumulative shortfall since 2021 to approximately 746 million ounces.
Newman acknowledged that sudden increases in investment demand could generate temporary physical market tightness.
“I don’t think you would ever say never, but I think it’s unlikely,” he said when asked about a repetition of the severe market tightness experienced in October 2025.
He added that metal could be transported from CME inventories to London to relieve pressure, even if renewed investment demand temporarily pushed silver lease rates higher.
The role of interest rates
Looking beyond photovoltaics, Newman believes monetary policy and investor expectations will remain major influences on silver prices.
Geopolitical tensions can support precious metals through safe-haven demand, but rising energy prices can also reinforce inflation concerns and expectations of higher US interest rates.
“I think you’re going to look at each on a case-by-case basis,” Newman said, referring to the impact of geopolitical crises such as the war in Iran.
Silver’s outlook also remains closely linked to gold, which Newman expects to face continued pressure until Federal Reserve policy becomes clearer.
“I think gold will remain under pressure until we have clarity from the Fed,” he said, although he believes the $4,000-per-ounce level could hold.
Metals Focus
‘ central scenario assumes tensions surrounding Iran will gradually de-escalate sufficiently to ease inflation expectations and limit further US interest rate increases. Under those conditions, investment demand for precious metals could strengthen again in 2027.
“Maybe it doesn’t happen that early next year. But maybe by the summer, prices for gold and silver are considerably higher than we see today,” Newman said.
For the photovoltaic industry, such a scenario would reinforce the case for reducing silver consumption, even if the recent price correction has eased immediate cost pressures. The central challenge remains balancing the savings offered by copper-based metallization against the efficiency and long-term reliability requirements of commercial solar modules.

title: Solar recycling 2.0 - pv magazine Global
content:
A number of companies in the United States are vying to leverage capital, experience, and new technology ahead of a wave of end-of-life solar panels expected in the coming years.
According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), the annual volume of end-of-life crystalline silicon modules in the US is expected to hit 87,000 metric tons (MT) by 2030 and skyrocket to 820,000 MT by 2050.
With that volume comes economic opportunity. In 2023, analysts at Rystad Energy estimated the global value of recycled solar materials would hit $2.7 billion in 2030, rising to $80 billion by 2050. Assuming a 15-year panel lifespan, Rystad’s research estimated end-of-life solar modules in North America would be worth $1.4 billion in 2037 – about 15% of the global total.
Special Edition RE+ 26
This article appears in a special edition of pv magazine, produced for RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas. Scan or
Click for free access to the full 54-page magazine
, packed with the latest from the US solar and energy storage industries.
DOWNLOAD FOR FREE
DOWNLOAD FOR FREE
Material values
Most of the material in a solar module is glass, which typically accounts for between 70% and 76% of a module’s weight. The second-largest portion is the aluminum frame, accounting for between 8% and 13%. But the most valuable material inside most solar modules is silver.
Silver now represents an important strategic asset to the United States. Along with silicon, ­silver was added to the US Critical Minerals List in November 2025.
In solar manufacturing, paste formed with the precious metal is screen printed in thin lines onto the surface of a silicon solar cell to collect and transport electrical current. It accounts for around 60% of the cost of those cells, and 10% of the total cost of a solar module.
According to the IEA, solar silver consumption was around 10 mg/W in 2024, down from 16 mg/W in 2020. While this equates to only about 0.05% of a panel’s total weight, the concentration of silver in a solar module rivals that found in many silver ores currently being mined.
That number was even higher for modules produced further in the past, meaning the coming wave of end-of-life modules will be rich in their most valuable component. The trouble is, once the cells are sealed inside layers of encapsulant, the metal contents have proven very difficult to recover without a high-temperature smelting process.
It is common practice for PV recycling companies to separate the glass and frame on the outside of a module, while the laminated components on the inside are shredded and sent to other recyclers often overseas, or even to landfill.
“The industry as a whole up to now has been on a 1.0 system, if you will,” said Adam Saghei, CEO of We Recycle Solar (WRS), in an interview with pv magazine USA. “It’s about shredding. It is heavily dependent on a mechanical process.”
When that shredded material is exported, the valuable silver, silicon, copper, and other trace metals trapped in the encapsulant are exported, too.
In addition, the recovered glass often contains impurities that make it unsuitable for use in high-temperature, closed-loop remanufacturing, such as new solar glass, instead of being used in “down-cycled” applications such as road base, concrete aggregate, and sandblasting media. All of that is changing now.
Latest technology
A number of US companies have developed alternative technologies to capture a much greater proportion of valuable solar materials and sell them domestically.
In September, WRS announced that it planned to open what it called “the nation’s first end-to-end critical materials recovery facility for retired solar panels” on a 10-acre site in Dallas, Texas, by the third quarter of 2027. The company says its “recycling 2.0” process allows it to recover up to 96% of the silver, copper, silicon, aluminum, and glass from end-of-life solar panels.
“Our approach is a little bit different,” said Saghei. “It’s on a very small footprint with regenerative solvents.” He added that the process results in glass with less than 10 parts per million of impurities. “That is essentially pure enough for you to drink out of. It’s as pure as glass comes.”
Meanwhile, OnePlanet Solar has been operating its commercial demonstration plant in Florida since early 2024. The plant is capable of processing 480,000 end-of-life solar modules in a year, equal to around 19,000 tons of material. According to the company, 100% of the outputs of this facility have been sold and consumed within the United States.
In August 2026, OnePlanet unveiled its new “PRISM” process (short for “Photovoltaic Recycling through Integrated Systems and Mechanics”). The company says PRISM results in 99% pure glass before any size reduction step, for both single side and bifacial modules, and also yields a concentrated silicon product with 95% purity that contains 1% silver.
Recycling of end-of-life modules using the PRISM process is expected to begin in 2027, and OnePlanet’s next goal is to refine its own metallurgical-grade silicon (MGS) while capturing the silver as a secondary finished product.
Another US company building out its recycling capabilities is Comstock Metals, which is now in the beginning stages of operating a solar recycling facility in Silver Springs, Nevada. The facility was first commissioned and tested in August 2026, and the company is working to ramp the plant up to 25% of its rated output capacity of 100,000 tons per year.
Comstock is also practicing a new, proprietary process at the Silver Spring site, designed to completely decompose adhesives, encapsulant, and plastic materials before the remaining components of the panel are sorted and separated for additional processing. Judd Merrill, the company’s chief financial officer, explained that the company’s current strategy is to retain the metal-rich material for its own proprietary metals recovery process.
Comstock’s plans for that metal recovery process start with a pilot-scale metals recovery operation, also planned for Silver Springs. “We are developing proprietary extraction and recovery technologies specifically designed to process the concentrated material generated by our solar recycling system. That material contains multiple valuable metals and other recoverable materials, and our objective is to recover those materials into marketable products for domestic reuse without conventional smelting,” said Merrill.
Comstock’s goal is to have a pilot-scale metal recovery line “operating continuously and reliably” by the end of 2026.
Building relationships
A key step in the success of any business is the development of ongoing relationships with partners. For solar recyclers, those relationships are made with entities on both sides of the recycling process.
On the supply side, this means contracting with manufacturers, EPCs, and re-powering companies. Comstock, for example, has minted deals with RWE for decommissioning aged solar panels as well as agreeing to take manufacturing byproducts from solar manufacturer Illuminate USA.
Similarly, leading recycler Solarcycle has partnered with Silfab, Canadian Solar, and Qcells to recycle factory defects and has inked agreements with major developers including Sunrun, EDP Renewables, AES, Orsted, and Greenbacker. The company has also announced public offtake agreements for the outputs of its recycling process. It has signed agreements with Silfab and Illuminate USA for new solar glass made from recycled modules.
Solarcycle is currently in the process of building a 1.1 million square foot glass plant next to its existing recycling facility in Cedartown, Georgia. With glass production at the facility slated to begin in 2028, the company is targeting enough glass production to support up to 6 GW of domestic panel assembly annually.
Regulation and certification
As of 2025, the NC Clean Energy Technology Center tracked 23 states with mandatory statewide decommissioning policies. Despite the widespread nature of those policies, laws in just four states (California, Maine, New Jersey, and New York) effectively prohibit the disposal of solar panels in landfills and dumps.
Outside those states, and in the absence of federal regulation, entities seeking to responsibly offload those products usually engage recyclers based on their own corporate ESG goals.
Obtaining quality and traceability certifications has become a key way recyclers set themselves apart from their competitors. Recyclers often pursue certification under ISO standards 9001 (Quality Management Systems), 14001 (Environmental Management Systems), and 45001 (Occupational Health and Safety).
In addition to obtaining those certifications, many companies seek listing under the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) National PV Recycling Program, which requires a facility audit and analysis of a company’s operations. SEIA currently lists 16 companies as partners under the program.
Recyclers seeking to go one step further obtain a certification from Sustainable Electronics Recycling International (SERI), which certifies PV recyclers under Appendix G of the third version of its Responsible Recycling (R2v3) standard. R2v3 requires annual surveillance audits by accredited certification bodies and complete chain of custody documentation for all materials. It also enforces safe handling procedures for panels, solar glass processing standards, and silicon wafer recovery protocols.
At the time of writing, SERI lists 30 facilities with active R2v3 certifications in North America, including the Comstock and OnePlanet facilities.
“Our view of certifications is pretty straightforward,” Connor Hogan, CFO of OnePlanet, told pv magazine USA. “If you can get a certification, you should just get a certification rather than say that you can attest to it.”
Other companies aren’t as keen on R2v3. “One issue with R2 certification is that it’s kind of open source, and when you spend years cultivating a relationship with a downstream partner, you don’t want to just give that up so everyone knows who you’re selling material to,” said Saghei, adding that “certifications are like a driver’s license – just because everyone has one doesn’t mean they’re a good driver.”
In the coming years, solar recyclers will find many ways to differentiate themselves based on the effectiveness and economics of their logistics and recovery processes, as well as the adaptability of those processes and how quickly they can scale operations.
The relationships recyclers build with manufacturers, developers, downstream offtakers, and policymakers will also be essential. They will face questions from those stakeholders about their certifications and material tracing practices and will likely be presented with new challenges as state governments take action to ensure solar module waste is recycled properly.

title: Why silicon won the solar race and what emerging PV technologies can learn from thin film - pv magazine Global
content:
Crystalline silicon has dominated the global photovoltaic market for decades, while alternative technologies, including thin-film solar cells, have struggled to secure a comparable market share. This dominance is often attributed to technological performance, cost competitiveness and efficiency improvements. However, research from City St George’s, University of London, challenges this explanation, suggesting that the commercial success of solar technologies depends on more than their technical characteristics.
The study, “
Technology (Non)Emergence: How System Interdependencies Among Activities by Heterogeneous Actors Shaped Alternative Solar Technology Trajectories
,” published in
Organization Science
, examines how manufacturing capabilities, accumulated industrial knowledge, investment patterns and policy support influence competition between PV technologies.
“We can think of competition as competition between manufacturing ecosystems, rather than competition in terms of technological characteristics such as efficiency, cost or other design elements,” lead researcher Mara Guerra told
pv magazine
. “This does not mean that technological characteristics are not important, but that competition depends on how manufacturing ecosystems evolve with respect to market requirements.”
According to Guerra, even technologies with promising performance characteristics may struggle commercially without the manufacturing infrastructure, industrial expertise and market support needed to scale production.
“Not even the best-performing tech can succeed if the system of activities around it fails to support its interface with evolving requirements of the market,” she said.
Thin film’s missed opportunity
The researchers found that thin-film PV technologies could have achieved greater commercial success if industrial investments and policy interventions had followed a different path.
“Hindsight is amazing, but thin film could have had greater success with a different pattern of investment across the ecosystem,” Guerra said.
She explained that thin-film technologies struggled to compete in mainstream PV markets, which benefited from policy support and increasingly established manufacturing capabilities. At the same time, some of their characteristics made them suitable for emerging applications, such as building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV), which received comparatively limited policy attention.
“Its characteristics made it ideal for niches such as building-integrated PV which did not receive as much support. Bold policy interventions in these more transformative markets may have helped thin film achieve a larger market share,” Guerra said.
The study also identified shortcomings in investment strategies across the thin-film industry. Rather than prioritizing shared manufacturing knowledge, compatibility with existing industrial processes or expertise from related sectors, investments often focused on the technological uniqueness of individual approaches.
While this differentiation helped attract investors, it did not necessarily support manufacturing scalability.
“Higher investments that rewarded reusing existing manufacturing knowledge or focusing on manufacturing compatibilities could have contributed to more rapid scaling of the technology and larger market share in the mainstream markets,” Guerra said.
The findings suggest that commercial success depends not only on technological breakthroughs, but also on the ability to develop manufacturing processes and industrial knowledge that can be replicated and deployed at scale.
Lessons for perovskites and tandem
The researchers said the historical development of thin-film PV offers important lessons for emerging technologies, including perovskite solar cells and silicon-perovskite tandems, which are attracting significant investment but still face commercialization challenges.
According to Guerra, developers should focus on two priorities: demonstrating reproducible technological performance and balancing innovation with manufacturing standardization.
“Firstly, entrants must move beyond technological records to achieve credible and replicable performance earlier on,” she said. “Technological breakthroughs are useful to build expectations, but in the end commercialization requires demonstrating that these breakthroughs can be consistently reproduced.”
Laboratory efficiency records can generate investor interest and strengthen expectations surrounding emerging PV technologies. However, they may also introduce uncertainty if the reported performance cannot be consistently reproduced.
“Performance records attract investment and generate enthusiasm but may also create unrealistic expectations. When performance records cannot be verified or replicated, they can create more uncertainty than they resolve,” Guerra said.
The second lesson concerns the relationship between technological differentiation and industrial standardization. According to the researcher, thin-film manufacturers frequently emphasized proprietary technological approaches and distinct manufacturing ecosystems, limiting opportunities to benefit from established industrial knowledge and common production practices.
“Thin film overemphasized uniqueness across technology and ecosystems. This helped with attracting investment but undermined scalability,” Guerra said. “Those who combined innovation and uniqueness in their technology with standardization in manufacturing or leveraging existing knowledge from related industries did better when commercializing their technology.”
Can industrial policy reshape PV competition?
The findings also have implications for governments seeking to develop domestic PV manufacturing capabilities and compete with established production ecosystems.
According to Guerra, mature industrial ecosystems benefit from accumulated manufacturing expertise, supplier networks and industrial knowledge that reinforce their competitive advantages. Although these advantages become increasingly difficult to challenge over time, they do not necessarily prevent new manufacturing ecosystems from emerging.
“While challenging an established advantage is increasingly difficult, especially when it is based on existing manufacturing ecosystems that have accumulated capabilities and knowledge that positively reinforce each other, this does not obstruct the creation of new successful and competitive manufacturing ecosystems,” she said.
Guerra argued that the effectiveness of public support depends on how emerging industrial ecosystems position themselves relative to established competitors.
Rather than attempting to replicate existing manufacturing structures or directly displace dominant producers, policymakers could support complementary technologies, specialized manufacturing activities and new market segments.
“The effectiveness of public support in creating competitive manufacturing ecosystems depends on how new ecosystems position themselves relative to others,” Guerra said. “Rather than trying to replicate or dislodge an existing ecosystem, focusing on support or complementary technologies and activities can contribute to the creation of a new and localized industrial advantage.”

title: Exclusive: Three Veterans of Tesla’s Autopilot Team Got a $1 Billion Valuation for a Simulation Startup
content: For two years, Ian Glow managed Tesla’s computer simulation unit, leading a team of gamers who created the ultradetailed equivalent of high-end videogames to help train the automaker’s core new products—self-driving cars and humanoid robots. But in 2022, Glow left the company, wanting to “move faster than was possible” at Tesla to develop virtual modeling tools that he thought were essential to any effort to safely commercialize either technology. Today, Glow is CEO of simulation software startup Zeromatter, which he said has developed a model that reliably replicates aspects of the real world, such as dangerous driving conditions and the use of tools in a factory. Glow, speaking for the first time publicly about Zeromatter, said he is selling such software to companies making self-driving cars, drones and robots. He declined to disclose the startup’s revenue, but last year he raised $110 million in a Series B round that valued Zeromatter at $1.1 billion. In all, Zeromatter has raised $160 million, including two prior rounds. The emergence of the startup reflects a spillover of technology developed in the electric vehicle industry, and specifically at Tesla. Industry veterans say Tesla’s arrival in China drove the development of that country’s EV, materials and robotics supply chains, which today dominate the global EV, battery and robotics industries. In the West, Tesla, with its Optimus robot, has driven a boom in the development of humanoids. Glow co-founded Zeromatter in 2023 with two former senior managers on Tesla’s simulation team—Axel Gneiting, now chief engineer at Zeromatter, and Michael Hosticka, the startup’s head of content strategy. Today the company has a staff of more than 130 people, including some 40 other Tesla veterans. Beyond the Tesla veterans, Glow said he has recruited roughly 10 people from General Motors’ former self-driving division, Cruise, and others from Amazon’s autonomous ride-hailing unit, Zoox, as well as Boeing, Airbus and Lockheed Martin. All three co-founders were videogame developers before working for Tesla. Glow said he was drawn to Tesla because his prior job working on Minecraft in Microsoft’s Mojang Studios was too slow. He said building a simulated world to develop a self-driving car is basically the same as creating one in which humans pretend they are fighting intergalactic aliens. “The idea that you can leverage your game background to actually make robots and drones and planes and a lot of things better was really exciting to me,” Glow said. “You just make a virtual world, and instead of having a human play it, you have an AI play it, or you have some kind of controlled algorithm play it.” Still, what he was doing at Tesla was small potatoes compared with the potential. The idea for Zeromatter centers on safety and reliability: Before a company ever deploys a moving product, that product can be tried out literally a million different ways through a simulator so there is no glitch in actual use. If it’s done right, simulation software, he said, “can accelerate every self-driving car company, every aerospace company, every drone company, anyone who’s building a sensor—anyone, I mean, even in robotics.” There is a term for reaching a real-world approximation of a situation: the sim-to-real ratio. The closer you get to the real side, the more street cred your simulation model has. To get there, you need to check it against the real world, which means comparing the simulation with high-quality data for the actions of a real robot or an actual driving situation. Zeromatter has its own EVs, robots, labs and AI computing power. For example, to ensure the company’s simulation of a camera is realistic, Glow said he buys a real camera, sets it up in a lab, and uses it in a bunch of different shots with various settings, including any defects or miscalibration that can happen. Then his team reproduces all of those scenarios within a simulation tool. “We make sure that it behaves exactly like it would in the real world,” he said. Humanoids are among the toughest challenges. Glow thinks robot developers have solved locomotion—the ability to walk, dance, run and so on. Simulation can help robots get their hands working right—a trickier proposition. “You have to continue to push the physical fidelity into manipulation,” he said. “When you make all that training data, it’s going to roughly represent what's happening in the real world,” he said. “There’s [otherwise] no easy way to test to make sure [that] ‘Yeah, does my self-driving car stop at a stop sign?’ or ‘Can my robot arm actually install this part in this vehicle?’” ------ Noteworthy A U.S. ban on Chinese components is making it far more expensive for drone makers outside China to power their aircraft—about four times as expensive. That’s according to Qichao Hu, CEO of U.S. drone battery maker SES AI, who told me Chinese drone batteries cost about 70 cents per ampere-hour, compared with around $3 for drone batteries made outside China. Hu said China’s cheaper materials largely account for the cost difference. But U.S. government purchasing rules mean this wide pricing gulf doesn’t hurt business for SES and other non-Chinese battery makers, he suggested. Those rules exclude Chinese components, including batteries, in drones purchased by the Pentagon. Enovix showed last week that the drone boom goes only so far in terms of reviving the fortunes of struggling U.S. next-generation battery startups. Last month, we reported that Enovix had landed its first commercial revenue in a big drone battery sale. Last Thursday, Enovix highlighted that news in its third-quarter earnings call, saying it was doubling down on drones by turning its near-term focus largely to making batteries for the aircraft and the significant revenue that business generates. While that announcement was well and good, several analysts on the call had questions about another disclosure, which was that Enovix was putting its prior main ambition—making lucrative smartphone batteries—on the back burner. Investors had been counting on that smartphone revenue. title: How a Chinese Energy Company Is Outpacing the U.S. on AI Power Technology
content: Ulanqab, a city in China’s Inner Mongolia region, used to be known for its potatoes. Now it’s where a Chinese renewable energy firm is trying out a new way to plug in AI chips that shows China’s edge in the power systems that data centers need. Envision Energy has started using an 800-volt direct-current system to power computing workloads at its data center there, the Shanghai-based company said earlier this month. The setup, which wastes less electricity between the grid and the chips, is widely expected to become the standard way to power increasingly energy-hungry AI servers, and Envision says it is the first to run it in a functioning data center. Nvidia and its partners are still preparing the same kind of system for their next generation of AI hardware, due next year. While small, the Envision trial reflects a part of the AI race in which China moves faster than the U.S. The U.S. has the most powerful AI chips. China is quick at building the power system for the chips. Why are power systems such a big deal now? AI chips keep getting more powerful, and more powerful chips use more electricity. Nvidia’s Blackwell graphics processing units, the current mainstay in advanced AI data centers, require around 140 kilowatts per server rack. Its Vera Rubin NVL72 racks, using the latest generation of GPUs, require up to 227 kilowatts per rack. Nvidia has said that its next-generation Kyber racks, expected to start delivery in 2027, will draw about 600 kilowatts per rack. Developing high-voltage systems to power these high-density racks has been the industry’s way of avoiding using higher amounts of electrical current, which typically requires heavy cabling and equipment that take up space. The 800-volt DC systems are designed so that less electricity is lost on the way from the grid to the chips—a vital consideration in AI data centers, where power is a huge cost and access to it is a major constraint on building more capacity. At a conventional data center, power from the electrical grid is converted several times between alternating current and direct current before any electricity reaches the servers. Each conversion wastes energy. The next-generation systems that players such as Envision and Nvidia are developing cut the number of conversions, reducing electrical loss. At Envision’s Galaxy data center in Ulanqab, solid-state transformers—advanced power conversion devices—convert 10,000-volt alternating current from the grid straight to 800-volt DC for the racks. That increases the conversion efficiency to 98.5% from the typical 94% to 95%, Kevin Huang, Envision’s senior vice president, said in an interview. China’s technology for AI rack systems is slightly different from that of U.S.-designed racks, said Eddie Yang, co-general manager of the AI data center product line under Envision AESC, the company’s battery technology affiliate. Traditional AI server racks in China typically have lower power density than those in the U.S. when they host the same amount of chips because American export rules prevent the most powerful AI semiconductors from being sold to China. But Chinese companies now make “super racks”—larger racks that can accommodate more chips and can require up to 400 or 500 kilowatts per rack. Chinese chips individually do less computing than Nvidia’s best, so Chinese companies link more of them together to work as a single machine. Chinese tech giant ByteDance, for instance, showcased a new AI rack system in July that would require up to 500 kilowatts per rack. That’s more than twice the power of Nvidia’s racks on sale today. The Chinese racks still need 800-volt DC supply to work efficiently. “So these different markets have different rack systems driving different types of demand. But the trend is common,” said Yang. Customer adoption Envision’s first commercial deployment in Ulanqab is for a 5-megawatt pilot, relatively small in an age of data centers that can be as big as 1 gigawatt or more. The company is anticipating the wide-scale deployment of Nvidia’s VR200 rack systems in the next six to nine months. Those chips can’t be sold to China under U.S. export controls, but Nvidia can help set the direction for the AI infrastructure industry, and Envision expects more power-hungry racks to push data centers toward 800-volt systems. By then Envision will also have more operational data to validate its technology for customers. Huang expects there to be two power architectures—one for China and another that follows Nvidia’s international architecture, similar to the split in chips. He thinks Envision can set the standard for China’s system. As for the overseas market, Envision is already discussing potential pilots of its 800-volt system with customers in Europe, the Middle East and Asia-Pacific. Envision expects around two years for larger scale adoption of its 800-volt systems. Data center operators don’t want to risk downtime with costly AI chips, so systems using new technology like solid-state transformers would have to prove they won’t cause outages. That may change once the chips get cheaper or depreciate and cost savings from new power systems matter more, according to Ricky Zheng, who leads Envision’s AI data center business. Envision’s power system costs 10% to 15% more up front than conventional designs, but the company expects this to change. “If you talk about solid-state transformers, many of the components we use today are not yet at massive scale,” said Yang. “But as we roll out in the next 18 months, many of the components will quickly go down the path of scaling law, so the component cost will go down easily 20% to 25%.” Envision says its 800-volt DC system architecture is not far from the approach Nvidia outlined in 2025 for its Kyber racks, but Envision’s edge in the market is its ability to integrate everything from power generation to energy storage systems, bypassing the need to coordinate systems between different providers. Envision pairs its solid-state transformers with a battery energy storage system of its own design. The company’s control system coordinates the transformers and batteries in real time to absorb sudden GPU load swings, a frequent occurrence with AI training workloads. Envision typically builds to flexible technical specifications provided by customers rather than around specific types of chips. Because of supply chain bottlenecks, customers don’t always know what chips they can get their hands on. Early this year, customers had excess chips waiting for space in data centers. “But for now, it’s more of data centers waiting for chips,” Zheng said. U.S. and allied export controls restrict China’s access to equipment its companies need to manufacture advanced AI chips. That, coupled with global component shortages, has affected chip supply. But China has leaned heavily on its supply chain strength in other areas. Generator sets—critical backup power systems—now have lead times of six to nine months, exacerbated by U.S. hyperscalers snapping up orders, said Zheng. Envision replaced some of the generator sets with its own battery systems, which took just a few months. Envision also designs renewable energy sources that can be used to power AI data centers. As a wind-turbine maker, it has installed more than 100 gigawatts of wind capacity worldwide to date. Its Ulanqab campus, which began operations in August and has a planned capacity of 3 gigawatts, has a dedicated power line to two wind farms built by the company. Those wind farms could supply more than 60% of the data center’s 240-megawatt load in its first two phases. One project that Envision’s been working on is to better integrate power and cooling systems within its facility. These systems have long been designed by separate industries, but denser AI racks now force them to be optimized to work together. That’s because the more power that goes into a single rack, the more heat it gives off. Keeping those racks powered and cool takes people, too. In Ulanqab, Envision now hires the sons and daughters of potato farmers and trains them as engineers and technicians to work in the data centers, Zheng said.

title: Nvidia’s Earnings on Deck; Anthropic’s Public Debut
content: If life was simple, the biggest question this week for people in tech would be where Anthropic shares open when the AI firm goes public. (Above $150 a share? See below.) Instead, we can’t rule out that more news breaks in the Nvidia drama and overwhelms Anthropic’s week in the sun. That news could be anything from reports of other women who had affairs with the now-departed CEO, Jensen Huang to developments in the campaign to bring him back. Huang, meanwhile, has agreed to testify before Congress, which could happen this week. Of course, even without such developments, Nvidia will be in the news. The AI chip designer on Tuesday is scheduled to report earnings for its third fiscal quarter, ending in late October. Those earnings will remind us all of why it is such a star company: It has projected revenue growth of around 89%, continuing a reacceleration of growth this fiscal year from last year’s “slowdown” (when revenue grew 66%). What we’ll be focused on more than the numbers will be comments from Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress. While as finance chief she’s a fixture on these calls, on Tuesday she makes her first public appearance in charge of the company since Huang’s exit. She’s likely to address the upheaval in some way, in an effort to reassure anxious investors as best she can. Nvidia stock closed Friday at $162.85, down 13% for the week and off 32% since early October. As we’ve written , there are lots of questions about what impact Huang’s exit will have on Nvidia’s business. Those unknowns make investors uneasy. HSBC downgraded the stock to a “hold” on Friday, citing the increase in “long-term uncertainty.” You have to wonder how Nvidia’s revenue will be affected if, as seems likely, the company has to clamp down harder on smuggling of its chips to China. Huang’s ties to alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang fueled billions of dollars in sales of those chips to China, as we reported . (We’d love to be a fly on the wall when President Donald Trump and China’s leader, Xi Jinping, meet this week at their summit , by the way: Will the topic of chip smuggling come up?) Then there’s a question about all the investments Nvidia made under Huang’s oversight in neoclouds and other firms, to ensure demand for its chips remained robust. What is the real level of demand for Nvidia’s chips, assuming the smuggling-into-China route has been closed off properly and assuming Nvidia wasn’t juicing demand by investing in buyers? Answering that question is key to understanding what the company’s future growth looks like. Anthropic's Big Day Anthropic’s public debut is the other big story of the week. By all accounts, demand is intense for the offering, suggesting the IPO will price above the preliminary range of $70 to $78 a share, which represents a valuation of $1.26 trillion to $1.4 trillion. A valuation of $1.5 trillion seems more likely. To get there, Anthropic would price at $84 to $85 a share. Let’s assume that happens. It still leaves plenty of room for enthusiastic traders to bid the stock up. In fact, we’d bet it opens trading at well above $100 a share, possibly above $150. Of course, what really matters is where it trades over the next few weeks. There are some who believe Anthropic will quickly become the most valuable company in the world. Right now, Apple holds that position with a market capitalization of around $5.2 trillion. For Anthropic to pass that number, its shares would have to rise to above $288 a piece. Will it get there and if so, how quickly? (Here are details of Anthropic’s marketing event on Friday at JP Morgan Chase’s headquarters.) title: OpenAI Explored $5 Billion–Plus Acquisition of Startup That Decodes How AI ‘Thinks’
content: As OpenAI staff this summer scrambled to understand how its AI caused security breaches inside and outside the company, leaders including CEO Sam Altman spoke multiple times with Goodfire, an Anthropic-backed startup whose technology aims to figure out why AI models behave the way they do and how to prevent them from going rogue. At one point, a senior OpenAI executive floated the idea of buying the two-year-old startup for more than $5 billion or forming another kind of business partnership, according to two people familiar with the proposal. That price would have represented a steep premium to Goodfire’s private valuation of $1.25 billion in a financing it announced in February. No deal to buy the startup was struck, but the conversations, which haven’t previously been reported, show how a once-obscure corner of the industry is getting newfound attention as AI-powered security breaches skyrocket and staff at Anthropic and OpenAI fret about their companies’ ability to control the technology they’re creating. One reason deal talks fizzled: Executives at Goodfire believe the company will be more valuable than that figure if it remains independent, as it could sell technology to multiple AI developers, according to one of the people. Goodfire says its software is becoming particularly useful as leaders at OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have acknowledged that traditional forms of monitoring AI behavior are becoming less reliable. Its approach differs from the conventional method used by developers such as OpenAI: reading their AI models’ chains of thought—the text that models produce as they reason through problems—and closely watching the actions the AI actually takes. (Watch an interview with the Goodfire CEO below.) Advances in AI such as loop transformers could be contributing to that monitorability issue by reducing the amount of information models write in their chains of thought. Developing stronger safeguards has become critical to OpenAI and other model developers in recent months, in the wake of AI-related security incidents including the infamous Hugging Face breach, which OpenAI’s technology caused. (The technology also breached and took over some of OpenAI’s own systems.) OpenAI, Anthropic and others must now guard against the possibility of large legal liabilities or prosecution if their technology breaks into corporate or government systems and causes economic losses. Goodfire’s specialty is mechanistic interpretability, often referred to as mech interp. Unlike chain-of-thought monitoring, software from Goodfire and rivals like Martian looks at the mathematical computations running inside a model. The approach is not yet as advanced as the chain-of-thought approach, Goodfire admits. And some AI researchers view it as less scientifically rigorous than other forms of machine-learning research. But Goodfire co-founder and chief scientist Tom McGrath said on The Information’s AI Deep Dive that the startup expects its methods to improve rapidly and be far cheaper than chain-of-thought monitoring, which requires an AI developer to run a large language model to read another model’s chain of thought. He said he expects interpretability-based monitoring to catch up to chain-of-thought monitoring within the next six months. The San Francisco startup sells annual subscription licenses to businesses and charges for use of a product called Silico, which provides AI agents that can autonomously carry out research experiments such as finding a way to detect whether a model might be trying to perform a cyberattack. Its customers have included Rakuten and AI neuroscience company Prima Mente. Goodfire has been generating revenue, though it’s not clear how much. Because mechanistic interpretability often requires extensive access to the numbers, or weights, that make up an AI model and model developers guard this information carefully, some of Goodfire’s employees work at customers’ offices. During OpenAI’s discussions with Goodfire, Altman was especially interested in the work of Goodfire researcher Nick Cammarata, according to one of the people. Cammarata, who previously worked at OpenAI, published a viral essay last month, “ Neural Networks Are Already Clean ,” which argued that mech interp has made it easier to understand the billions of so-called neurons, the mathematical functions that make up an AI model, than researchers in the field previously thought. This understanding could help developers build better models, some researchers believe. Several of the major model developers employ researchers who focus on mech interp, although Anthropic, which helped pioneer the mech interp field, has been particularly vocal about the topic. Chris Olah, who is often credited with starting the field of mech interp, co-founded Anthropic after leaving OpenAI in 2020 and now leads interpretability work at the Claude maker. Last year, it invested $1 million in Goodfire , Anthropic’s first ever direct stake in another startup. CEO Dario Amodei said in a statement at the time that the move “reflects our belief that mechanistic interpretability is among the best bets to help us transform black-box neural networks into understandable, steerable systems.” OpenAI is hiring interpretability researchers , according to its job posts, and earlier this year it began using interpretability techniques as part of its safety processes to detect misbehavior, such as AI models responding to potentially harmful requests regarding cyberattacks or biological weapons. OpenAI researchers are becoming more enthusiastic about working on interpretability, according to someone close to the company.

title: The Controversial AI Interpretability Research that Caught Sam Altman’s Eye
content: During OpenAI’s talks in recent months with AI startup Goodfire over a possible acquisition or partnership—discussions my colleagues and I reported this morning—OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was particularly interested in the work of Nick Cammarata , a onetime OpenAI researcher now at Goodfire who has made waves recently with new claims about how AI thinks. Cammarata published an essay last month and a follow-up report last week that have caused quite a stir among AI researchers—with some applauding it as a potential breakthrough in our ability to understand AI models and others dismissing it as hype. The reaction goes to show that some areas of AI research are still so immature that scientists don’t even agree on what counts as good research—a fact that hasn’t prevented billion-dollar valuations for startups based on unproven AI technology. Goodfire’s research specialty is known as mechanistic interpretability , or mech interp for short, which seeks to understand the inner workings of AI models rather than just their outward behavior. AI models are made of trillions of numbers, making them “black boxes” that a person can’t understand the way a programmer can simply read the lines of code in traditional software. As a result, it’s tricky to know how an AI model will act in new situations and to understand mistakes when they occur. Cammarata’s essay, titled Neural Networks Are Already Clean , argued that the artificial “neurons” in AI models—mathematical functions built on those trillions of numbers—could actually be easier to understand than researchers had previously thought. As a result, his argument goes, the outlook for startups like Goodfire that aim to explain how AI models work is more promising. For example, back in 2017 mech interp researchers found a neuron inside an AI image model that seemed to light up when the model was looking at an image of a car or a cat. Most neurons seemed to perform multiple unrelated jobs like this, confounding the researchers who tried to study them. In fact, in 2023, when Cammarata was working at OpenAI, he tried using OpenAI’s GPT-4 model to make sense of the neurons in a GPT-2 model, and found that it could only explain 1.7% of the neurons—at most. But thanks to improvements in training models and techniques to interpret them, the picture is no longer hopeless, Cammarata argues. About 90% of the neurons in Alibaba’s Qwen3-32B have just one job, making them possible to understand. And when Cammarata revisited the car-and-cat neuron, he realized that cat faces and the corner of a car share a similar V-shape, which is what the neuron was actually picking up on. “The story of interpretability, as I see it, has largely been one of finding out that what was under the microscope was better than we thought,” he wrote. “The microscope just wasn’t tuned right, and what needed tuning was often pretty subtle.” Several prominent mech interp researchers were not as convinced by Cammarata’s essay. They commented that his research direction was promising but he was exaggerating the significance of the results. Neel Nanda , who leads Google DeepMind’s work on mech interp, wrote on social media that Cammarata’s essay “is interesting work, but I don‘t think it’s a significant update to the big picture of interpretability.” The essay overestimates how much neurons are understood, Nanda wrote, and even if every neuron was understood, a lot of questions about how a model works would remain unanswered. OpenAI researcher Leo Gao also weighed in, writing a rebuttal to Cammarata titled “ Neural networks are not already clean ” in which he countered that Cammarata’s essay is “nowhere near a sufficient argument that we understand most of what neurons are doing, and these results do not show that interpretability is solved, or even that it is vastly easier than previously anticipated.” Liv Gorton , who previously worked at Goodfire and now works at Anthropic , tried to replicate some of Cammarata’s experiments and found different results. She also pointed out that cats’ faces are not all that V-shaped, and the neuron in question does not respond to plenty of more V-shaped images, such as bird beaks. Cammarata acknowledged the wide variety of reactions to his essay but offered a note of unity. When it comes to interpreting AI models, he wrote , “I think the problem is solvable, whether the simple thing works, it mostly works but we need some new things, or we need big new ideas. I think we can figure it out.” Here’s what else is going on… People on the Move Confidantes of Jensen Huang are informally seeking to reinstate him as Nvidia’s CEO and encouraging him to fight to reclaim his old job. title: 宁德时代与悉尼新南威尔士大学签署合作谅解备忘录--中国能源新闻网
content:
宁德时代与悉尼新南威尔士大学签署合作谅解备忘录--中国能源新闻网
中国能源传媒集团有限公司主办
能源中国IOS版
宁德时代与悉尼新南威尔士大学签署合作谅解备忘录
近日，2026年澳大利亚国际能源展在墨尔本举行。作为南半球规模最大、最具影响力的清洁能源盛会，该展既是高效的知识共享平台，也是链接澳大利亚及亚太地区行业资源的重要桥梁。展会期间，宁德时代与悉尼新南威尔士大学（UNSW Sydney）签署了合作谅解备忘录，正式建立战略伙伴关系。双方意在共同提升澳大利亚清洁能源转型所需的专业技能与产业能力，使创新成果、技术红利与产业机遇惠及更广泛群体。
新南威尔士州是澳大利亚可再生能源与储能基础设施建设的前沿地区。随着相关产业加速扩张，当地专业人才需求快速增长。为此，双方将围绕储能电池人才培养、技术示范验证、联合科研攻关三大方向协同发力，同时依托悉尼新南威尔士大学五十余载的可再生能源创新积淀，将校方长期积累的科研储备转化为产业实用技能，在推动技术突破与迭代的同时，创造本地就业机会、夯实本土产能根基，让能源转型成果惠及更多青年学子，惠及社区民生与区域经济。
未来，双方还将开展战略协同，共建综合可再生能源培训与创新中心（CIRETI）。该中心坐落于澳大利亚新南威尔士州西悉尼地区，充分融合悉尼新南威尔士大学在科研与教育领域的领先实力，以及宁德时代在先进电池技术、能源系统领域的全球产业优势，打通科研、人才培养与产业链，搭建能够适配产业节奏的灵活培训体系，强化学生实操就业能力，推动毕业生与行业岗位的精准对接，以教育赋能驱动包容、公平的发展。
宁德时代澳大利亚总经理周欢表示：“宁德时代非常高兴能够携手悉尼新南威尔士大学，推动澳大利亚在全球能源转型中发挥更大作用。澳大利亚新一代清洁能源从业者的核心能力将聚焦电池系统集成，依靠电池技术保障电网供电可靠性与系统安全。悉尼新南威尔士大学是我们的理想合作伙伴，在能源研究与工程领域享誉全球。我们将汇聚世界级专业力量，为澳大利亚乃至亚太地区培育能源产业人才、筑牢产业发展根基，让绿色转型带来的机遇触达更多人。”
立足全球碳中和发展大势，此次谅解备忘录的签署，是产学研跨国协同的又一生动实践。悉尼新南威尔士大学产业与创新协理副校长 Stephen Rodda教授称：“净零转型是我们这个时代最重要的挑战之一。实现净零目标不能只依靠新技术，还需要专业人才、科研创新与合作网络，才能把创新成果规模化地转化为现实生产力。Progress for All是悉尼新南威尔士大学的核心战略，依托本次合作，我们将与宁德时代打通教育、联合科研和产业资源，携手人才梯队共建，推动储能技术和电网融合技术进步，为本校学生和毕业生创造更多机遇，并最终助力澳大利亚拥有稳定且可靠的清洁能源未来。”
如今，悉尼新南威尔士大学携手全球领先的新能源科技龙头企业宁德时代，共同打造净零转型亟需的专业人才队伍，使这一合作成为开放包容的产学研国际合作典范。双方未来还将继续依托技术互通与资源共享，以创新中心为载体持续深化协同，支撑澳大利亚储能项目长期稳定运行，让绿色科研成果惠及全球。

推进氢能产业高质量发展！侯启军出席并致辞
11月14日，由中国石化主办的氢能应用现代产业链共链行动大会暨氢能产业高质量发展推进会在北京市房山区举行。会议以“氢领未来，绿燃新篇”为主题，聚焦氢能产业高质量发展关键议题，汇聚行业力量，共商发展路径。会上，中国石化宣布乌兰察布绿氢及输氢管道项目全面启动。集团公司党组书记、董事长侯启军出席并致辞。
集团公司总经理、党组副书记赵东作氢能应用现代产业链建设情况报告。集团公司党组成员、副总经理牛栓文、田宏斌出席。工业和信息化部、国家能源局、北京市经济和信息化局相关负责人出席并致辞。会前，侯启军和与会嘉宾共同参观氢能产业链链上企业成果展廊。
11月14日，侯启军在氢能应用现代产业链共链行动大会暨氢能产业高质量发展推进会上致辞。
侯启军表示，近年来，在国家“双碳”目标指引和产业政策引导下，产业链各方同向发力、协同攻坚，推动我国氢能产业从示范探索稳步迈向规模化、商业化发展新阶段。中国石化立足自身资源禀赋、产业基础和网络优势，坚持科技创新引领、产业场景先行、生态协同共建，在氢能领域持续深耕，关键技术攻坚多点突破，产业发展示范作用有效发挥，推动融通发展生态加快成型、标准体系不断完善。新征程上，中国石化愿与产业链各方一道，共聚创新合力、共拓应用场景、共筑融通生态、共促标准完善，持续深化共链行动，加快推动氢能产业高质量发展，为建设能源强国、推动经济社会绿色低碳转型贡献更大力量。
会上，中国石化宣布乌兰察布绿氢及输氢管道项目全面启动，项目建成后将成为国内首个跨省（区、市）、大规模、长距离纯氢输送的“制—储—输—用”全链条工程，推动我国氢能产业首次在制备、储存输送、工业消纳环节形成完整闭环。同步发布氢能供需对接清单，并与中国一汽、东风汽车、东方电气、北汽福田、上海重塑等共同发起氢能交通“百站万辆”行动倡议，助力氢能产业加速迈向规模化、商业化发展新阶段。
当天，侯启军还赴燕山石化现场调研，先后前往高性能膜产业基地，化工一部氢能源装置、新型碱性电解槽生产线，了解科产融创项目进展、新能源新材料产业化攻关等情况，看望慰问一线干部员工；走进安全生产指挥中心，听取安全环保、生产运行、“一企三地”管理等情况汇报；和内蒙古大路煤化一体化项目、天津南港新材料项目视频连线，勉励大家从企业辉煌发展历程中汲取力量，以强烈的政治担当守牢安全环保底线，严把工程安全质量关，加快向新、向绿转型升级，以二次创业的昂扬姿态奋进新征程，齐心协力打造新时代高质量发展“新燕化”，为公司构建“一基两翼三链四新”产业新格局作出更大贡献。

哈工大破解热电器件“长寿”难题助力废热“变宝”
工厂排出的工业余热、生产生活中的各种废热，未来有望转化为清洁电力。记者从哈尔滨工业大学获悉，该校材料科学与工程学院隋解和教授、郭逢凯教授团队开发出一种新型超稳定磷化物阻挡层，有效解决了热电发电器件长期服役过程中的界面稳定性难题，让生产生活中的热能加速“变废为宝”。
热电发电技术就像是在冷热两端之间搭起一座“微型桥梁”，利用温度差就能直接把热能转化为电能。无论是工业生产中的余热回收，还是为深空探测设备、物联网传感器提供电力，这项技术都能发挥重要作用。
然而，如何让热电器件长期稳定工作，一直是困扰业界的难题。热电器件通常由热电材料与金属电极焊接而成，在长期高温运行中，两侧材料里的元素容易互相“串门”（发生扩散），导致器件性能大幅下降甚至失效。这就需要在两者之间加装一层“防火墙”。碲化铋是目前商业化应用最成熟的热电材料，但多年来一直缺乏可靠的阻挡层，制约了温差发电技术的广泛应用。
新型阻挡层磷化镍相关研究图示（新华社发哈工大供图）
针对这一难题，哈工大研究团队优选出磷化镍（Ni2P）作为新型阻挡层。测试结果显示，该阻挡层与碲化铋之间的界面不仅接触电阻低、结合强度高，在约250摄氏度的高温条件下老化90天后仍保持稳定。在同等高温下，基于该阻挡层制备的器件连续运行360小时，输出性能依然稳定。
“在实际应用中，热电器件不仅要能发电，更要能长期可靠。”隋解和表示，随着全球能源需求增长和绿色低碳转型推进，提高能源利用效率愈发重要。这项成果有望推动碲化铋热电发电器件商业化应用，为推动工业余热回收与节能减排提供新选择。这一研究成果15日发表于国际学术期刊《先进材料》。（

title: 中油测井与中国石油大学（北京）克拉玛依校区联合培养
content:
11月10日，中油测井与中国石油大学（北京）克拉玛依校区联合培养的6名学生，依托“在校3年、在企1年”的“3+1”培养模式，正式开启专项实操技能培训，在该公司测井、仪修、解释评价等岗位轮训锻炼。
近10年，中油测井整合企业资源，与高校探索卓越工程师联合培养等方式，选派经验丰富的企业导师驻场教学，推动理论教学与实操训练深度融合，累计为行业输送300余名高素质青年人才；其中20余人入职中油测井，8人成长为作业队长，为公司实现高质量发展储备了坚实的后备力量。（刘海明 陈仁杰 摄 杨倩 文）
