title: Why Immersion Cooling Still Hasn't Gone Mainstream
content:
There is a great deal for data center operators to love about immersion cooling, a technique that keeps IT equipment cool by immersing it in liquid. It is highly efficient from an energy perspective. It requires no water. And because it eliminates many of the moving parts and airflow dependencies associated with traditional cooling, it can reduce certain operational risks.
And yet, very few data centers are actually using immersion cooling or appear to be planning a large-scale shift to it. Other
liquid cooling methods
– such as direct-to-chip cooling, which circulates coolant through pipes placed adjacent to processors rather than immersing entire servers – are
projected to grow rapidly
. Immersion cooling, by contrast,
remains a niche
That raises an obvious question: If immersion cooling is so effective and sustainable, why aren’t more data centers using it? And what technical, financial, or operational changes would the industry need to make for immersion cooling to take off?
Related:
Liquid Cooling Retrofits: Hard, but Sometimes Worth It
To answer that, it is worth taking a closer look at the current state of immersion cooling, the barriers holding it back, and the odds that it becomes more mainstream in the years ahead.
Why Immersion Is Still a Niche
Immersion cooling technology has been around for decades. As of 2026, however, it still has not become a mainstream production cooling strategy among major data center operators. Most of the headlines on immersion cooling in recent years have focused on pilots, demonstrations, and proofs of concept, such as Microsoft’s well-known
experiment
earlier this decade.
Some of the large AI data centers under construction may be planning to deploy immersion cooling. In some respects, the technology is a natural fit for facilities designed for extremely
high power densities
and significant heat loads. But if large operators were preparing to embrace immersion cooling at scale, you might expect them to say so loudly. So far, few have.
What’s Holding Immersion Back
Why aren’t more data centers taking advantage of immersion cooling, given that it is a proven and reliable way to dissipate heat? Two factors likely explain much of the hesitation.
1. The Economics Are Hard to Ignore
First, immersion cooling systems are significantly more expensive to install than most alternatives. Estimates vary, but immersion generally carries materially higher upfront costs than direct-to-chip cooling and vastly higher capital costs than conventional
evaporative or air-based approaches
. According to one
, it costs about $1 million per MW of IT load to implement an immersion cooling system, compared to $650,000 using direct-to-chip. From a CapEx standpoint, it is hard to make immersion look attractive, especially for operators under pressure to bring new capacity online quickly and cost-effectively.
Related:
RDHx: A Simple, Affordable Path to Lower Data Center Energy Use
To be sure, immersion cooling can deliver savings over time through lower operating costs. It can reduce energy required for cooling, improve thermal efficiency, and shrink the physical footprint needed to support a given amount of compute. Adam Silva Consulting
estimates
that “cooling a 64-rack AI cluster over 10 years costs $42M with advanced air, $31M with direct-to-chip liquid, and $28M with single-phase immersion.”
But those long-term benefits do not automatically outweigh the short-term economics. Data center operators may still be too focused on near-term financial targets to invest in systems whose payoff could take years to materialize. It may also be that, when compared to direct-to-chip cooling in particular, immersion’s operational savings are not compelling enough to justify the extra upfront expense.
2. The Industry Doesn’t Change Easily
Cost, however, is probably not the only factor. Part of the issue may also be cultural.
The data center industry is accustomed to designing and operating facilities in ways that have remained fundamentally consistent for decades. Those norms include placing servers in conventional racks, arranging hardware in familiar floor layouts, and relying on established approaches to maintenance, monitoring, and serviceability.
Related:
Can Evaporative Cooling in Data Centers Still Make Sense?
Immersion cooling upends much of that model. With immersion systems, airflow is no longer a primary design constraint, which means data center architecture and white-space layouts can and arguably should change in more fundamental ways. Maintenance procedures change, too, because servers are no longer housed in traditional cabinets and are not accessed in the same way. Monitoring practices, service workflows, and technician training all have to evolve.
Direct-to-chip cooling also requires changes to data center design and operations, but overall, those changes are less disruptive than those immersion cooling demands. Direct-to-chip allows operators to preserve more of the conventional server-and-rack paradigm, making incremental adoption easier.
The cultural barriers to immersion cooling can be overcome. But doing so would require architects, operators, and technicians to rethink not just how they cool IT equipment, but what a data center should look like and how it should function.
Adoption Will Depend on Future Pressures
Whether that rethinking happens, and whether operators decide to make the financial commitments that immersion cooling requires, will largely depend on how data center cooling demands evolve in the coming years.
If power-hungry, heat-intensive workloads such as AI training and inference continue to expand, immersion cooling could become increasingly attractive. The denser and hotter the compute environment becomes, the stronger the case for cooling technologies that can efficiently handle extreme thermal loads. But if the AI boom plateaus before immersion gains real momentum, the technology may remain largely experimental in the data center market.
Another factor is the level of pressure operators face to reduce water and energy use. Public and regulatory concern about
data center water consumption
does not seem quite as intense as it did a year or two ago, which may reduce the urgency around solutions such as immersion cooling that use no water at all.
At the same time, concerns over data centers’ impact on power grids and electricity prices have helped drive
moratoriums
and tighter scrutiny in some markets. That could encourage more operators to seriously consider immersion cooling to
improve power usage effectiveness (PUE)
and reduce cooling overhead. That said, cooling is only one part of the energy equation. The main driver of data center power consumption is the electricity required to run IT equipment itself, with cooling systems playing a secondary role. For that reason, immersion cooling alone is unlikely to become a silver bullet for the industry’s broader power challenges.
Immersion cooling may yet find its moment. For now, even its technical advantages have not been enough to overcome the combined weight of higher upfront costs, operational disruption, and industry inertia.

title: EnBW plans 46 MW/170 MWh battery at German pumped-storage site - Energy Storage
content: EnBW Energie Baden-Württemberg has taken the final investment decision for a 46 MW battery energy storage system (BESS) with 170 MWh of capacity at its Forbach power station in the German state of Baden-Württemberg. Construction is scheduled to begin in 2028, with commercial operation planned for 2029. The four-hour battery will complement a new pumped-storage hydropower plant that EnBW is currently building at the site. The company said the project could qualify for Germany’s grid fee exemption for large-scale battery storage, provided it enters operation by early August 2029. EnBW plans to expand an existing terraced area at the power station to accommodate the battery. It will also reuse infrastructure from the former Murgwerk facility, including cable routes, the transformer area and the switchgear building. “When wind and solar are unavailable for several days, hydrogen-capable gas-fired power plants are needed. All three technologies complement one another. Forbach is a special site for us because it will combine two forms of dispatchable capacity in the future,” said Peter Heydecker, EnBW board member for sustainable generation infrastructure. EnBW currently operates 20 battery storage systems in Germany with a combined capacity of more than 100 MWh, according to the company. It has a further 3,000 MWh of projects under development. At its former nuclear power plant site in Philippsburg, EnBW is building a battery system with 400 MW of power and approximately 1,000 MWh of capacity, which the company describes as one of the largest in Germany. EnBW also routinely combines new solar power plants with battery storage. title: Flower plans 500 MW/2 GWh battery project in eastern Germany - Energy Storage
content: Sweden’s Flower plans to build a 500 MW/2,000 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) at the Ragow substation in Lübbenau, in Germany’s Spreewald region. Commercial operation is scheduled for 2029. Flower acquired the project last year and is developing it with German project developer dces, the company said on Monday. Dces is leading project development, while Flower will handle financing, technical planning, procurement, construction, operation and energy marketing. Planning applications have been submitted. Flower expects the project to reach construction readiness by the end of this year. Dces has been developing projects in Germany for 12 years and has a nationwide pipeline of 3 GW, according to the companies. Its responsibilities include planning and developing large-scale battery systems and coordinating with local stakeholders. Flower entered the German market last year and is expanding its project pipeline. Earlier this year, it acquired a portfolio of battery projects totaling 112 MW from Chint Solar, as well as another project in Saxony-Anhalt with 63 MW of power and 257 MWh of capacity. The company is also developing its own projects, including a 100 MW/400 MWh battery system in Hamburg-Bergedorf. Beyond project acquisitions, Flower has signed a virtual flexibility purchase agreement (FPA) with Engie in Germany. The agreement provides financing support for battery systems with a combined capacity of 126 MW. Flower also plans to introduce a proprietary asset optimization algorithm in the German market next year. The software is intended to enable coordinated control of energy assets. title: Pace Digitek wins 600 MW/1,800 MWh BESS contract in India - Energy Storage
content: Pace Digitek has secured an INR 26.91 billion ($287.3 million) contract from NTPC Green Energy Ltd for the engineering, procurement and construction of a 600 MW/1,800 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) at the NTPC Renewable Energy Ltd (NTPC REL) Khavda solar plant in Gujarat, India. The contract also includes 15 years of operations and maintenance. The award covers two 300 MW/900 MWh blocks under Cluster 1 of the wider 3,300 MWh BESS project at the Khavda site. The company described it as the largest BESS order it has secured to date. The scope includes BESS supply, system integration, installation, testing, commissioning and civil works, alongside long-term operations and maintenance. Following the award, Pace Digitek’s cumulative order inflows for fiscal year 2027 have reached INR 51.29 billion, while its total executable order book stands at INR 134.27 billion. The company said its consolidated BESS project portfolio now totals 6.62 GWh across engineering, procurement and construction (EPC), build-own-operate (BOO) and build-own-operate-transfer (BOOT) models. Pace Digitek said its qualification as a Class-I local supplier, requiring at least 50% local content by value across goods, services and works, was an important factor in securing the contract. It added that investments in localization, including 5 GWh of operational domestic BESS manufacturing capacity and an in-house container fabrication facility, strengthened its bid. The company has 5 GWh of installed BESS manufacturing capacity and plans to increase this to 10 GWh by the third quarter of fiscal year 2027. title: Sonnedix switches on 125 MWh co-located battery storage project in Japan - Energy Storage
content: Global renewable energy producer Sonnedix has commenced commercial operations at a co-located 125 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in Oita prefecture, marking its first storage asset in Japan. The facility is co-located alongside an existing 39 MW solar PV plant in Kyushu, allowing the developer to time-shift solar output and dispatch power in response to grid demand rather than curtailing excess generation. Kyushu has historically suffered some of Japan’s highest solar curtailment rates for a range of reasons, mostly grid bottlenecks. Construction on the Oita project began in October 2025, hitting commercial operation in roughly 13 months. Toshiba Energy Systems & Solutions Corporation acted as the engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contractor, deploying Tesla Megapack units. Photos reviewed by ESS News indicate the cabinet layout suggests Tesla Megapack 2XL. An exact MW power output figure wasn’t provided by Sonnedix, and as a co-located asset, may utilize the same 39 MW output as the solar plant. Trading and market interaction for the asset are being handled by Japanese utility major Osaka Gas. To back the development, Sonnedix secured a JPY 21.4 billion ($139 million) non-recourse refinancing facility arranged by MUFG Bank. The Oita commissioning is part of Sonnedix’s retrofit storage effort across its 570 MW Japanese solar portfolio and wider global fleet. “By adding storage to our existing solar plant, we can now shift generation to the times it is most valuable and respond more effectively to market conditions, supporting a more stable and resilient power system,” said Tomomichi Kageyama, managing director of Sonnedix Japan. The project joins a rapidly accelerating wave of utility-scale battery deployments across Japan, following recent grid connections and portfolio launches from Sunpin Japan and Orix . title: Tesla needs wireless charging fast, or its $30,000 Cybercab can't charge at home
content:
Tesla Robotaxi
Tesla Cybercab
Fred Lambert
| Nov 17 2026 - 6:19 am PT
Tesla is now taking orders for the $29,990 Cybercab, with the first deliveries expected in Austin next month. But there’s a problem buyers should know about: they won’t be able to charge it at home.
The Cybercab has no onboard charger, so it only takes DC fast charging. And the wireless home charging pad Tesla has been teasing since 2023 still isn’t something you can buy.
A DC-only car
When Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in 2024, Elon Musk said it wouldn’t even have a plug. “It just goes over the inductive charger and charges,” he said on stage.
That plan didn’t survive production, or at least the current version in production. Cybercabs have a NACS charge port behind a panel in the rear bumper, and Tesla has been plugging Cybercabs into regular Superchargers in Austin since they joined the fleet.
The bigger issue is what sits behind that port. Tesla confirmed to attendees at Tesla’s Austin launch event in September that Cybercab has no onboard charger, the box that turns the AC power coming out of your wall into DC power the battery can store.
No onboard charger means no Wall Connector. No Mobile Connector on a 120V outlet, and no Level 2 station at the mall either. If it isn’t a DC fast charger, the Cybercab can’t use it.
For a robotaxi, deleting the onboard charger makes sense. It’s one less part to buy, cool, and carry around, and a fleet car spends its downtime at a depot, not in someone’s garage. Those little things help make the car more economical and efficient.
But Tesla is now selling the Cybercab to individuals.
The fine print makes it worse
As we reported last week,
Tesla’s Cybercab autonomy agreement
requires a $299 monthly subscription for the car to move at all. The same document puts charging squarely on the buyer: “You are responsible for registration, insurance, parking, charging, general cleaning and all other costs.”
It also tells owners to “keep the vehicle charged and connected so over-the-air updates can install.” Connected to what, it doesn’t say.
The Cybercab Order Agreement limits the car to NACS DC fast charging, Superchargers included. It also says only the registered owner can use the Cybercab, and only while physically present in it for the entire trip.
subscription agreement
carves out one exception: when service is due, the Cybercab “will travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center.” Nothing similar exists for charging.
So you can’t send your Cybercab to a Supercharger at 2 a.m. while you sleep, which is the one thing a self-driving car should be great at. You’d have to ride along, sit in a two-seater at a Supercharger while it charges, and ride back home.
Tesla has been teasing the fix for years
The obvious answer is the wireless home charger Tesla keeps promising.
Tesla first showed what looked like
a wireless home charging station
during its Investor Day in March 2023. Later that year, chief designer Franz von Holzhausen confirmed the project on Jay Leno’s Garage, saying owners would “just drive over the pad in your garage” to start charging.
Tesla then
filed patents for the charging pad
and, after the Cybercab unveiling,
released a video of it charging the robotaxi
at 25 kW, claiming efficiency “well above 90%.” In February, the FCC granted Tesla a waiver to use ultra-wideband radios to guide the Cybercab onto the pad.
And that’s where it stops. Tesla has never sold the pad, never priced it, and never given it a launch date. It even
gave up on wireless charging for the Cybertruck
last year, even though the truck shipped with the connectors for it.
With deliveries estimated for December, Tesla has about six weeks to launch a home pad if it wants the first owners to charge in their own garage.
The other options aren’t great
Tesla’s own plans for Cybercab charging revolve around fleet depots. In Austin, it filed plans for a hub on St. Elmo Road with 48 V4 Supercharger stalls in a first phase and cabinets to support 80 wireless chargers in a second.
Tesla could, in theory, let private owners use it. But with the owner-presence rule, that means riding to a depot across town and waiting there. That’s a Supercharger visit with extra steps.
The other route is a home DC charger, and those exist. We covered
Sigenergy’s 25 kW bidirectional DC charging module
last year, which bypasses a car’s onboard charger the same way a Supercharger does. Lunar Energy also announced a 25 kW home DC charger this year, but it’s not expected until mid-2027.
Neither is a plug-and-play answer. Sigenergy’s module is built to sit inside its SigenStor home battery system, which isn’t cheap, and Tesla would have to support third-party DC charging on a car it controls this tightly. Tesla could also build its own small DC wall unit. It hasn’t announced one, but CEO Elon Musk talked about integrating one into the Powerwall for years.
Electrek’s Take
This is what happens when you take a vehicle designed for a fleet and sell it to consumers to hit a deadline. And let’s be honest, charging is probably not even in the top 5 of problems with selling the Cybercab to personal owners in its current state.
Musk promised a Cybercab would be sold to a customer for under $30,000 before 2027. Technically, he’s going to make it. But on the Q3 earnings call, he also said “the vast majority” of Cybercabs will stay Tesla-owned and run as transport-as-a-service. The car was clearly engineered around that, and deleting the onboard charger is the best example.
That saved Tesla money on every unit. The cost now lands on the few people buying one.
If you live in Austin next to a Supercharger, you’ll manage. But think about what Tesla is actually selling here: a self-driving car that can’t drive itself to charge, can’t charge in your garage, and needs you sitting in it at a Supercharger. That’s worse than owning a Model 3 with a Wall Connector, and it costs $299 a month on top.
The fix exists in Tesla’s labs. It has the pad, the patents, and the FCC approval. It needs to ship it as a product, ideally bundled with the car, or change the contract to let the Cybercab go charge on its own.
Will the first Cybercab owners get a wireless pad in December, or will they spend their evenings at Superchargers? And if it launches, how much will it cost? The rare few home wireless chargers that have been sold to date have been quite expensive, and the value proposition of the Cybercab, which is currently basically a $300 a month lease with a $30,000 down payment, is already pretty awful.
If you’re buying an EV, how you charge it at home matters as much as the car itself, and pairing it with rooftop solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero. title: Volkswagen is cooking up a 'spicy' new electric hot hatch
content:
Volkswagen
Peter Johnson
| Nov 17 2026 - 7:01 am PT
Volkswagen
will reveal the new GTI hot hatch on Friday, promising it will be “something really spicy.”
Volkswagen is launching a spicy new EV hot hatch
To celebrate the GTI’s 50th anniversary, Volkswagen is “starting a new chapter,” with its first all-electric model to bear the iconic performance badge.
The ID. Polo GTI “brings the legendary GTI driving pleasure into the electric future,” VW said after
opening pre-orders
last month.
Volkswagen previewed a mysterious new hot hatch draped under a cloth that appears to be a souped-up version of the ID. Polo GTI. Despite its attempt to “hide” it, you can see the massive rear wing and wide wheel arches under the cloth.
The company promised that “something really spicy” will be served this Friday, November 20, with the tags #Volkswagen, #GTI, and #GTI50.
Although no other details were revealed, the new hot hatch is thought to be the more powerful “Clubsport” variant.
View this post on Instagram
A post shared by Volkswagen (@volkswagen)
Volkswagen’s head of driving dynamics, Florian Umbach, told
earlier this year that the company is planning to launch the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport, a more powerful variant that will deliver close to 300 hp, up from 223 hp in the standard model.
Umbach said that Volkswagen is developing “a similar kind of paddleshift power delivery that the Hyundai N cars have” for the upcoming electric hot hatch.
Volkswagen ID. Polo GTI (Source: Volkswagen)
Hyundai’s performance EVs, the IONIQ 5 N and IONIQ 6 N, feature a simulated gear-shifting system called N e-Shift that uses paddle shifters on the steering wheel to replicate the feel of an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission. It works with the N Active Sound+ system to make it feel like you’re in a traditional gas-powered sports car.
It has yet to be confirmed whether the hot hatch debuting on Friday is, in fact, the new ID. Polo Clubsport, but the design clues give us a good idea of what’s coming.
Volkswagen previews new “really spicy” GTI hot hatch (Source: Volkswagen)
Check back on Friday for the full details.
Volkswagen opened pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI last month, starting at 39,995 euros (about $45,000).
Like the first Golf GTI from 1976, the electric ID. Polo GTI uses a front-wheel-drive powertrain. The front-mounted electric motor delivers 223 hp (166 kW) and 213 lb-ft (290 Nm) of instant torque, enabling it to sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 6.8 seconds.
In early 2027, Volkswagen will open orders for the
ID.3 GTI
, the second EV to wear the badge, and its first rear-wheel-drive (RWD) GTI.

title: 中创新航/华电新能源/万华化学分别成立新公司
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，近期，华电新能源、万华化学、中创新航持续拓展新能源业务，分别成立绿色能源、新能源材料及储能相关公司，业务涉及风电、光伏发电、储能技术、电池制造及新能源材料等领域。
华电新能成立宣城绿色能源公司
11月10日，华电（宣城市宣州区）绿色能源有限公司成立。企查查股权结构信息显示，该新公司由华电新能源集团股份有限公司全资持股。
新公司注册资本450万元，法定代表人为贾晖辉，注册地址位于安徽省宣城市宣州区。
该新公司经营范围包括发电业务、输电业务、供（配）电业务、储能技术服务、风力发电技术服务、太阳能发电技术服务、技术服务与开发、工程技术服务、工程管理服务等。
万华化学成立宜昌新能源材料公司
11月9日，万华（宜昌）新能源材料科技有限公司成立。新公司注册资本8亿元，法定代表人为王晓星，注册地址位于湖北省宜昌市当阳市坝陵化工园万华大道1号。
股权结构方面，企查查显示，该新公司由万华化学（烟台）电池产业有限公司全资持股。
经营范围包括电子专用材料研发制造与销售、专用化学产品制造销售、化工产品销售、风力发电技术服务、太阳能发电技术服务、发电业务、输电业务、供（配）电业务等。
中创新航参股成立江门凯博绿动科技
11月4日，凯博绿动科技（江门）有限公司成立。
企查查股东信息显示，该公司由魏桥新能源船舶储能换电科技运营（深圳）有限公司、中创新航科技集团股份有限公司、成都凯鑫隆商贸有限公司共同持股，持股比例分别为40%、40%、20%。
新公司法定代表人为李硕，注册资本为2000万元，经营范围包含储能技术服务、电池制造、电池销售、信息系统集成服务、蓄电池租赁、船用配套设备制造、船舶租赁等。

title: 宁德时代、海辰储能等6企储能订单密集落地
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，近期，储能行业多笔订单及合作相继公布。
宁德时代中标储能电芯采购项目，海辰储能签约罗马尼亚储能系统供货项目，三星SDI获得美国16GWh储能电池订单；果下科技、赢科数能分别涉及储能设备采购和移动储能项目，巡鹰集团则与创明智能电池达成3GWh电池采购合作。
宁德时代中标国能信控储能电芯采购项目
11月13日，国能信控技术股份有限公司发布2026年国能信控本部承揽设备类储能用电芯框架公开招标中标结果公告，宁德时代新能源科技股份有限公司成功中标，中标金额为7600万元，折合单价约0.38元/Wh。
此外，近期宁德时代旗下独立后市场品牌宁家服务与罗尔斯·罗伊斯动力系统（Rolls-Royce Power Systems AG）签署战略合作协议，双方将整合服务资源与渠道网络，完善全球售后服务体系。
海辰储能签约罗马尼亚181.25MWh储能订单
近日，海辰储能与罗马尼亚可再生能源工程企业Simtel达成合作，将为罗马尼亚塞贝什大型光储混合能源项目提供直流侧储能系统及长期运维服务，项目配套储能规模为181.25MWh。
据悉，该项目由Windin Capital和El-Mor Group通过项目公司HEPA Energy共同开发，规划建设67.46MWp光伏电站，并配套181.25MWh储能系统。项目建成后，所发绿色电力将接入罗马尼亚国家电网。
根据合作协议，海辰储能将为项目提供29套6.25MWh长时储能系统，并与Simtel共同开展储能系统运维服务，为项目长期运行提供支持。
果下科技获5.04亿元储能设备采购订单
11月13日，神雾节能发布公告称，公司控股子公司武汉联合立本能源科技有限公司与果下科技股份有限公司签订《储能设备采购合同》，合同含税金额为5.04亿元，相关设备将用于新疆喀什地区疏附县20万千瓦/80万千瓦时构网型电化学独立储能电站项目。
根据公告，此次采购内容包括储能电池系统、PCS及升压变系统、储能单元内线缆及电缆终端、储能二次系统，以及相关抽检材料和调试试验等。
赢科数能签约新疆50.145MWh移动储能项目
近日，赢科数能成功签约新疆油气田压裂移动储能供电项目，将投入15台3.343MWh移动电源车，总规模达50.145MWh，为当地油气田压裂作业提供移动储能供电解决方案。
据悉，该项目主要面向油气田压裂作业中的移动供电需求。针对部分井场远离公共电网、井位滚动迁移以及压裂设备负荷波动较大等情况，项目采用移动储能供电方案，以储能系统替代部分传统柴油发电设备，提供离网供电及多机并联支持。
巡鹰集团与创明智能达成3GWh电池采购合作
近日，巡鹰集团与绵阳创明智能电池有限责任公司签署战略合作框架协议，双方将围绕磷酸铁锂大圆柱电池在动力电池及储能领域的应用展开合作，协议明确以年框架采购规模3GWh为基础，推进电池供应与下游应用协同。
根据协议，双方将发挥各自在电池制造、动力电池应用及储能系统集成等领域的业务优势，开展电池采购、产品开发及产能协同。其中，巡鹰集团将结合下游应用场景推动创明智能电池产品落地，双方还计划针对市场需求联合开发定制化产品。
三星SDI获美国16GWh储能电池订单
11月16日，三星SDI宣布，其美国子公司三星SDI美洲公司（SDIA）与美国储能开发商及运营商Jupiter Power签署电池供货协议，将为其美国大型储能项目供应16GWh磷酸铁锂电池，合同价值预计达50亿人民币。
根据协议，三星SDI将于2029年至2031年向Jupiter Power供应上述电池。叠加此前双方签订的供货协议，三星SDI对Jupiter Power的累计供货规模约达27GWh。

title: 近1.4GW！天合光能/通威/正泰接连获组件订单
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，近期，光伏组件市场订单及项目交付持续推进。通威股份、正泰新能拿下罗马尼亚1.36GW组件订单，天合光能签约广东7.2MW分布式光伏项目，正泰新能供货的江苏如东24MW渔光互补项目实现全容量并网。
通威、正泰获罗马尼亚1.36GW组件订单
近日，由Rezolv Energy开发的罗马尼亚1.36GWp Dama Solar光伏项目正式敲定组件供货订单，通威股份与正泰新能分别获得846MW和474MW的份额。
根据双方签署的协议，通威股份将为该项目供应846MW的TNC 3.0光伏组件，目前首车组件已由通威太阳能南通基地正式发车进入履约阶段。
同时，正泰新能源作为EPC总包商承建该项目装机量为474MWp的B期电站，其建设所需的对应光伏组件、逆变器及相关配套设备将由正泰新能与正泰电源提供。
天合光能获广东物流园区7.2MW组件订单
11月，天合光能正式签约广东省一物流园区7.2MW工商业分布式光伏项目。
根据项目规划，该物流园区将利用闲置仓库屋顶建设分布式光伏电站，并选用天合光能基于N型i-TOPCon技术的至尊3代650W中版型组件。
项目建成后，光伏发电时段将与园区白天的高峰用电负荷相匹配，以提高绿电自发自用比例，降低园区综合用能成本，同时为入驻企业的碳足迹核算及ESG披露提供支持。
正泰新能供货24MW渔光互补项目并网
近日，由正泰新能供应组件的江苏如东马塘渔光互补光伏项目实现全容量并网，项目总装机容量24MW，共安装46,197片ASTRO N系列组件。
据悉，该项目位于江苏省南通市如东县马塘镇王渡村，覆盖当地69处鱼塘，采用渔光互补模式，在水面上方建设光伏发电设施，水下保留养殖功能。项目于9月17日正式并网，采用全额平价上网模式，预计年均发电量约3,348.26万KWh。

title: 龙蟠科技：上调对宁德时代2026年销售上限至90亿元
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，11月16日，龙蟠科技发布公告，对与宁德时代关联集团采购框架协议中的持续关联交易年度上限作出修订，将2026年境内交易上限由70亿元上调至90亿元。
根据公告，这份框架协议的交易产品以磷酸铁锂正极材料为主。2026年1月1日至公告发布当日，宁德时代关联集团在该框架下已经完成采购61.04亿元，距离原先70亿元的年度上限已经比较接近。
龙蟠科技在公告中说明，上调额度主要是因为宁德时代关联集团对相关产品的需求有所增加，再加上碳酸锂价格存在波动，原有的额度预计不足以承接后续新增订单。
该笔交易属于港交所规则下的持续关联交易。形成关联关系的原因是，宁德时代间接全资子公司宜春时代持有龙蟠科技旗下子公司龙蟠时代30%股权，宁德时代及其附属公司、其30%受控主体（不含龙蟠时代）属于龙蟠科技子公司层面的关联人士。
本次修订已经通过董事会和独立非执行董事审议。按照上市相关规则，本次事项豁免通函、独立财务意见以及股东表决，后续仍需要按要求完成申报、年度审阅和信息披露工作。
从过往交易情况来看，2023至2025年，宁德时代关联集团在该框架下的年度采购额分别约35.01亿元、31.11亿元、30.51亿元，连续三年稳定在30亿元上下。本次上调后的年度上限，相比前三年有明显提升。
公告同时提到，本次调整的额度只适用于境内采购框架，和公司新加坡子公司与宁德时代签订的海外采购协议相互独立，二者额度不互通。
公告也作出提示，本次只是调整交易金额上限，并不代表保底采购承诺；交易金额同时受出货量、碳酸锂价格波动影响，额度上调，不意味着出货量会同步等比例增长。

title: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
content:
AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways
The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.
The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.
“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.
Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.
Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys
“I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”
Optics to inference’s rescue?
Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.
Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.
VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION
The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once.
The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.
Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.
But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.
McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”
It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.
“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”
With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.
Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.
Bridging the gap in free space
The startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.
Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.
To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory.
Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics
Chris Philpot
The Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector.
Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.
The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.
“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”
Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.
Neurophos
Bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.
Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”
The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is currently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.
Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”
Bridging the gap on-chip
Free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.
“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”
Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.
“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”
Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics
Chris Philpot
One way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.
In Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.
Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the company announced a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.
The energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main issue is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch says, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”
Beyond matrix-vector multiplication
Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.
“A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”
Even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the company believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch says.
The Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” says Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the company’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.
LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.
LightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to quickly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver
Once a particular problem is encoded into the modulator, the gain medium is stimulated to emit random photons. They bounce back and forth, increasing in intensity when passing through the gain medium again, experiencing preprogrammed changes through the modulator and interacting with one another until they reach a steady state—the solution. Then, a simple camera takes a picture of the steady-state result. Using emulation, the LightSolver team recently showed that their LPU can solve differential equations 40 to 80,000 times as fast as a GPU, depending on the workflow. They are now working on explicitly benchmarking the energy improvements.LightSolver’s team is currently working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the company’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi says. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.
Computing in transit
Yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick New, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.
The key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” New says. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”
“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick New, Optalysis
Instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.
Some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.
New says that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”
The likely future of optical computing
How likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he says. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”
However, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Says Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”
Whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”

title: BYD Is Winning Over Japan With A Very Japanese Kind Of EV
content:
The tiny Racco electric kei car is drawing new customers as BYD passes 10,000 cumulative sales in Japan.
Photo by:
Motor1.com Deutschland
7:55am ET
BYD has passed 10,000 cumulative sales in Japan, reaching its second 5,000 much faster than its first.
The Racco recorded 607 sales in October, versus 878 for the Nissan Sakura.
BYD offers more range for a lower sticker price, but subsidies can make the Sakura cheaper.
BYD’s latest milestone in Japan would barely register on its sales charts back home in China. But selling 10,000 cars in a country dominated by domestic brands is progress, especially when part of that momentum comes from selling a vehicle tailored to what Japanese buyers actually want: a small, practical box on wheels, which also happens to be electric.
The Chinese automaker announced that its cumulative Japanese passenger-car sales had passed 10,000. Its first 5,000 took roughly two and a half years after deliveries began in January 2023. The next 5,000 took about 15 months. That includes its entire lineup, rather than just its newest and arguably most interesting addition: the Racco electric kei car.
It was bold to
challenge Japan’s homegrown manufacturers
with something designed specifically for their market and to create the world’s first kei car from a non-Japanese automaker. The Racco’s tall body, tiny footprint, and sliding rear doors follow the familiar Japanese formula for such vehicles. BYD didn’t need to reinvent anything, but its entry needed to be convincing.
Japanese buyers’ initial response to
the Racco
was encouraging. Launched on July 28, it attracted 1,002 orders in two weeks, the fastest order intake of any BYD model in Japan. By the end of August, that had grown to around 1,500. Roughly 80% of buyers chose the range-topping 300 Premium, clearly showing that the cheapest version was less attractive.
BYD credited the Racco with helping deliver record monthly orders across its Japanese lineup in August. Potential buyers who came to see the little EV ended up discovering its other models, too.
offers six passenger-car models in Japan, and every one has a charging port. Five are fully electric: the Racco kei car, Dolphin hatchback,
Seal sedan
, Atto 3 crossover, and Sealion 7 SUV. The sixth, the Sealion 6 SUV, is a plug-in hybrid combining a gasoline engine with electric propulsion. That makes the entire lineup electrified, with no gasoline-only cars or conventional, non-plug-in hybrids on offer.
Stay informed with our newsletter every weekday
What’s more interesting is comparing the Racco’s sales performance to its main rival, the Nissan Sakura EV, which is also Japan’s best-selling electric car. In October,
the Sakura EV
sold 878 units, while the Racco sold 607. That’s almost 70% of the volume, marking a 37% rise over September.
The Nissan Sakura EV was Japan’s electric bestseller for a fourth consecutive year in 2025, but it could lose its crown to the Racco, which gives buyers more battery for less money, at least before subsidies. It starts at ¥2.145 million with a 22.4-kWh pack and 130 miles (210 kilometers) of WLTC range, while the Sakura starts at ¥2.449 million with a 20-kWh battery and 112 miles (180 km).
Even the longer-range Racco, with a 35.8-kWh pack capable of 199 miles (320 km), undercuts the entry-level Nissan at ¥2.398 million. The BYD also gets sliding rear doors instead of the Nissan’s conventional ones. What could help the Sakura stay ahead is the larger government subsidy it benefits from, which can make it cheaper to buy despite its higher sticker price.
It’s a tad early to call the Racco a Japanese sensation, but buyers are clearly interested. This newcomer is already selling roughly seven cars for every ten Sakuras in one month, so it definitely deserves attention.

title: Bentley’s First EV Is Already Sold Out, And Production Hasn’t Even Started
content:
Bentley’s First EV Is Already Sold Out, And Production Hasn’t Even Started
Customers of the $220,000+ Bentley Torcal who order now will need to wait until 2028 to get their cars.
- The Bentley Torcal electric crossover is proving to be an initial hit.
- The British automaker’s first EV is already sold out, even though production hasn’t even started yet.
- Based on the same underpinnings as the Porsche Cayenne EV, the Torcal’s starting price in the U.S. is over $200,000.
Bentley’s first electric car, the Torcal SUV, looks like a hit already. Even though production hasn’t started yet, the $220,000+ EV is sold out for 2027, according to Frank-Steffen Wallier, the company’s head honcho, quoted by Automotive News.
The British luxury automaker said that all available production slots for next year have already been allocated and that the company is now taking orders that will be delivered in 2028. Bentley didn’t say how many EVs it will build in 2027, but the initial customer response has made the marque quite happy with the outcome.
“Needless to say, we’re very pleased with the response and position we’re in,” a company spokesperson told Automotive News.
That’s great news for Bentley, which isn’t doing great in terms of sales and profit. From January through September, it sold 5,970 cars globally, 17% fewer compared to the same period last year. Meanwhile, the profit dropped by more than half to $54.1 million through the first nine months of the year.
The Torcal, which is smaller than the Bentayga SUV, is the brand’s cheapest model, though it still costs a pretty penny. The base Torcal starts at $222,495, followed by the more powerful Torcal S at $262,695, and the Torcal First Edition at $300,995. All things considered, Walliser said that the smaller size and relatively lower price compared to the Bentayga have attracted new and younger customers to the brand.
So far, the Torcal S has proved to be the most popular version of the new EV, but when it comes to personalization, the sky’s the limit. “We see cars spec’d north of 300,000 pounds ($397,086),” said Walliser. “Individual content does not stop in case of an electric car. There have been some assumptions, and some people have been critical if people would be ready to do so.”
Based on the same underpinnings as the electric Porsche Cayenne, the Bentley Torcal is powered by a 113-kilowatt-hour battery that can be charged at up to 400 kilowatts. It can go from 10% to 80% in less than 20 minutes, and the estimated EPA range is expected to be over 300 miles.
Built on the Premium Platform Electric (PPE) architecture, it has two electric motors that make 810 horsepower and 881 pound-feet of torque in the standard Torcal and a whopping 876 hp and 996 lb-ft of torque in the Torcal S. When the model debuted in September, Bentley said it was the most powerful and quietest model to come out of the factory in Crewe.
To make the Torcal a reality, Bentley invested $463 million to upgrade its factory in England, plus at least the same amount for supply chain preparations and research and development, Walliser said.
Despite the electric SUV’s initial success, the British automaker is still heavily invested in gas and plug-in hybrid models, and the Bentayga isn’t going anywhere. “We have a very good combination with Torcal and Bentayga,” Walliser said. “The segment definitely has space for two cars.”

title: Mercedes Is Bringing Hands-Free Driving To Certain U.S. Highways In 2027
content:
It's kind of like Super Cruise, only with a Mercedes badge.
Photo by:
Mercedes-Benz
3:33pm ET
Mercedes is bringing a new suite of driver assistance features. The two big new ones are Mercedes' MB.Drive Assist Pro,
an FSD-like system we recently tested
, and Hands-Free Highway Assist.
Silly corporate naming conventions aside, this new system is impressive. MB.Drive Assist Pro is a true point-to-point system, capable of taking you from your starting point to your destination on its own in urban environments as long as you directly supervise it. Mercedes is still calling it an SAE Level 2 system, so you still need to pay attention, keep your hands on the wheel, and take over whenever it needs. But it can do the heavy lifting for you.
On the highway, the Hands-Free Highway Assist can completely take over inputs on approved roads at speeds up to 85 mph. You'll need radar cruise engaged to use it. Once it's on, though, it can change lanes, overtake slower vehicles, handle lane merging, and even take off-ramps for you on its own, assuming the conditions are appropriate. Think of it like
Super Cruise
, just from Mercedes.
Photo by: Mercedes-Benz
"By bringing hands-free highway driving together with point-to-point assistance and expanding these technologies across our portfolio, we’re making them available to more customers across the U.S.," said Jason Hoff, CEO Mercedes-Benz North America. "That’s where sophisticated technology becomes meaningful: when it makes everyday driving more comfortable and convenient.”
China has already had the system, but Mercedes is going to begin bringing it to German and the U.S. The latter of which will actually get a sneak preview of it in December, 2026, but only in California. Select Californian customers will be able to participate in an Early Access Program (EAP), which will let them test out these new features. Only lessees of the
2026/2027 Mercedes CLA
, 2027 GLC Electric SUV2, S-Class Sedan, GLE SUV and Coupe, and GLS will be eligible.
Rollout for the rest of the country will happen in Spring 2027, and it will be available for all Mercedes vehicles with the proper hardware equipped. Even owners of existing vehicles with the necessary hardware will be able to buy the feature and have it digitally installed via an over-the-air update.

title: Tesla Keeps Killing Cars. Now It Wants To Build Cybercabs In Germany
content:
A $3.3 billion factory expansion takes Musk’s autonomy gamble overseas as Tesla trims its conventional lineup.
Photo by:
1:32pm ET
Tesla plans a $3.3 billion German factory expansion to build Cybercabs starting in 2029.
The expansion follows the Model S/X’s retirement, Cybertruck’s planned shutdown, and cuts to cheaper variants.
Tesla is betting more heavily on autonomy while European approvals remain limited to supervised driving.
Tesla’s core
lineup is shrinking
as the company focuses in on robotaxis. Now, Tesla boss Elon Musk wants to take his autonomous vehicle manufacturing ambitions beyond Texas and begin Cybercab production in Germany.
The company plans to invest €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its factory near Berlin, targeting production of up to one million Cybercabs. According to
, Tesla intends to apply for permits before the end of the year, begin construction in the first half of 2027, and start German Cybercab production in 2029.
The news comes as
keeps reducing the number of conventional cars on offer. Over the past year or so, it has retired
entire models
dropped cheaper variants
, and earmarked factory space for robots and robotaxis. Knowing that, the new German Cybercab plan starts to look less like an addition to Tesla’s business and more like a replacement for part of it.
Photo by: Tesla
The most significant departures this year were the Model S and Model X. Tesla ended both model lines and announced it would repurpose its former Fremont factory space
to build Optimus humanoid robots
. Granted, the S and X were aging, low-volume products, but they made Tesla look more like a traditional automaker.
The Cybertruck is next, although its departure has become a moving target. Musk initially announced a mid-2027 shutdown to free Texas factory space for Cybercabs, then
extended production through the end of summer
to fulfill its order backlog. But it’s still scheduled for retirement.
Not even the ubiquitous Model Y has escaped. Tesla
dropped its cheapest all-wheel-drive version
earlier this month, less than a year after introducing it. Buyers who want two motors must now stretch to the Premium AWD or just get the base rear-wheel-drive variant, which remains available.
Stay informed with our newsletter every weekday
Tesla isn’t abandoning human-driven cars altogether.
The redesigned Roadster
revealed last month is now promised for 2028, complete with thruster-assisted theatrics. After years of delays and a complete redesign, it’s still a vehicle Tesla promises to build.
Basically, the new Roadster offers spectacle, but it doesn’t fill the practical gaps left by a luxury sedan, a large SUV, and a pickup. Tesla doesn’t even seem to be interested in filling those gaps.
The Cybercab
faces a different issue. Without manual controls, its usefulness depends on Tesla’s autonomous driving capabilities and permission to deploy them. In the U.S., regulators have already opened an investigation into how the vehicle complies with federal safety requirements. A German production facility doesn’t, by itself, settle where its output can operate.
More Cybercab Stories
Tesla’s struggle to get FSD approved in Europe shows how slow that process can be. Dutch regulators cleared the supervised system in April after more than 18 months of testing, but its rollout has since depended on individual countries granting permission. EU-wide approval remains pending, and
Tesla has renamed it “Tesla Assisted Driving”
and tightened its speed settings to address regulators’ concerns.
All that work is for software that still requires an attentive driver. Getting permission for a Cybercab with no steering wheel or pedals is a separate challenge. And now Tesla wants to build those in Europe…
Still, Tesla’s survival doesn’t only rest on the
Cybercab
are still very popular worldwide, and the Semi could give it a foothold in electric trucking. But shrinking its passenger car lineup while spending billions on robotaxis leaves Tesla with fewer alternatives if Musk’s driverless future takes longer or proves less profitable than he expects.

title: Tesla Model 3 Maintenance Guide: What Needs Servicing And What Doesn't
content:
Tesla Model 3 Maintenance Guide: What Needs Servicing And What Doesn't
EVs need a lot less maintenance than a conventional combustion vehicle. That said, they still need some attention.
Everybody knows that electric cars are pretty easy on the owner’s wallet when it comes to regular maintenance. They may cost more to buy new than a comparable gas car, but as the miles pile on, there’s no need to worry about engine oil changes and emissions checks. Plus, cheap EVs are already here, with more to come in the near future.
While all of this is true, EVs aren’t exactly maintenance-free. There are still some things that need to be done to keep an electric car running like new for many years after it rolled off the assembly line.
There might not be an engine under the hood, and no manual or automatic transmission to worry about, but EVs still have transmissions, believe it or not. They also have brake fluid, brake pads, and coolant. And all of these—plus others—need attention over the course of a car’s life.
WHY ERANGE EV TIRES?
ERANGE EV tires are purpose-built for electric vehicles, combining efficiency, comfort and performance with advanced EcoPoint3 technology.
- Engineered for EVs & Hybrids: Designed to meet the unique demands of electric and hybrid vehicles.
- Extended Range: Low rolling resistance helps maximize driving range.
- Reduced Road Noise: Designed for a quieter, more comfortable drive.
- Optimized Performance: Built to balance efficiency, durability and confident handling.
Tesla Service
For this first installment of our new series on EV maintenance, I’ll focus on the Tesla Model 3, one of the best-selling electric models of all time, and a regular occurrence on roads everywhere in the United States, Europe, and beyond.
I’ll go through what maintenance is required by Tesla to keep the warranty intact, and also discuss items that are not part of the company’s service schedule but might still be worth considering for the long run.
Tesla Model 3 Maintenance: What Tesla Recommends
The following list may seem a little too simple for someone who has switched from a gas or diesel car to an EV, but there’s no shortage of high-mileage electric cars out there, including countless Teslas, that are still going strong with minimal maintenance. Here’s what Tesla recommends owners look out for on the Model 3:
Cabin air filter replacement: every two years
High-Efficiency Particulate (HEPA) filter and carbon filter replacement: every three years, for vehicles that have them from the factory
Brake fluid test: every four years
Similar to a combustion vehicle, the Tesla Model 3 uses brake fluid to push the brake pads onto the rotors. Brake fluid is hygroscopic, meaning it naturally absorbs moisture from the air. If there’s a lot of moisture contamination, hydraulic pressure drops, which leads to a softer brake pedal and longer braking distances. A brake fluid test reveals if it’s still good or if it needs replacing.
Brake cleaning: every year or every 12,500 miles in areas where roads are salted during winter
Even though all modern EVs use their electric motors to slow down, they still rely on mechanical brakes to increase safety, and the Model 3 is no different. To keep things running smoothly, Tesla recommends cleaning and lubricating the brake calipers, especially for cars that live in areas where the roads are salted during the winter.
The thickness of the brake pads also needs to be checked, though there have been plenty of cases out there of Tesla EVs with over 100,000 miles on the clock and the original brake pads still in good condition.
Radiator cleaning: when needed
Yes, the Model 3 doesn’t have a hot engine, but it still needs a radiator to keep the thermal system running cool. Depending on where the car is located, debris can build up over time, reducing the radiator’s efficiency and limiting the car’s performance.
Precision-cleaning the windshield area in front of the camera: when needed
Tesla Model 3 windshield camera precision cleaning
Tesla’s advanced driver assistance systems rely on video cameras to react, but they can’t perform as intended if they’re obstructed. The company says that cleaning the inside of the windshield in the camera area is vital for clear visibility and optimal camera function.
To check if cleaning is required, owners can tap the Maintenance tab in the infotainment system.
Tire rotation: every 6,250 miles or if the difference in tread depth is 2/32 inches or higher
EVs are known for being harder on tires than gas cars because acceleration and brake regeneration will put stress on the rubber. To prolong the life of a tire set, Tesla recommends rotating the tires every 6,250 miles.
This is also when you want to check the tires themselves. Because EVs often wear out tires quicker, it's important to keep an eye on tread depth. When it gets below 4/32nds of an inch, it's time to start looking for new tires. If your tread depth is below 2/32nds, replace them immediately.
Wheel balancing: when needed
If the driver notices vibrations in the steering wheel while driving, the wheels may need balancing. With unbalanced tires, handling, tire life, and steering components are affected.
Wheel alignment: when needed
If the vehicle pulls to one side when the steering wheel is straight, or if there’s uneven wear on the tires, a wheel alignment may be needed. The procedure is also recommended after installing new tires.
All of the vehicle’s maintenance needs can be viewed in the Maintenance Summary on the central touchscreen, which provides a record of when common actions were last performed and recommends when to perform them next.
Tesla says that all of these items need to be performed at an authorized service center. This includes servicing the low-voltage and high-voltage batteries. However, there are some maintenance actions that should be considered by owners who want to treat their EVs as their forever cars.
Tesla Model 3 Maintenance: What Tesla Doesn’t Say
We’ve all heard of “lifetime fluids,” but ask any well-versed mechanic out there, and they’ll say that they don’t exist. Instead, car manufacturers refer to them when it’s their job to maintain the car under warranty. After the warranty expires, the owner is on the hook for all repairs, including those that could have been avoided.
The following recommendations are nowhere to be found in Tesla’s maintenance plan, but some technicians still recommend them. Even though they’re not required actions, Tesla has service procedures for all of them, and its service centers can perform them if the owner asks.
Drive unit fluid change: between 60,000 and 100,000 miles
Tesla used to recommend changing the transmission fluid in its drive units every 100,000 miles, but that went the way of the dodo. Now, the company’s transmissions, which transfer power from the electric motor to the wheels, have built-in filters, but plenty of mechanics out there believe that it’s good practice to renew the fluid every 100,000 miles at the latest.
Coolant check: Every four years
The Model 3 uses coolant to keep the high-voltage battery at an optimal temperature. Just like on a combustion car, the coolant needs to be checked and replaced if it becomes contaminated.
Drive unit, steering, and suspension bushes: inspect and replace as needed
Over time, rubber bushes will lose their elasticity or even crack. If this happens, knocks or rattles will make their presence felt, requiring a visit to a service center. Even though Tesla implemented many manufacturing novelties over time, it still hasn’t figured out how to replace the age-old rubber bushes found in all cars.
Where to service the Tesla Model 3
Under warranty, Tesla's authorized service centers should handle all maintenance items. However, after the warranty expires, many of the maintenance actions found on this list can be easily done at home by the owner. Air filter changes and radiator cleaning are DIY jobs that shouldn't take hours to complete, even for people who haven't done any mechanical work before.
Best of all, though, Tesla has published all of its service manuals online, and anyone can follow the service procedures to do maintenance jobs. What's more, in recent years, plenty of independent EV shops have popped up, and they can usually handle repairs and maintenance at lower costs than Tesla. That said, Tesla's own shops will happily inspect and repair older models, too.
Key takeaway
Keeping an EV on the road should be much cheaper than a gas car, but it still requires some maintenance. Over a five-year period, the main maintenance items should include at least one set of new tires, multiple tire rotations, two brake fluid tests and maybe one flush, two cabin air filter replacements, several brake checks, and at least one set of wiper blades.

title: The Electric Baby Land Rover Defender And Range Rover GT Will Begin Production Next Year
content:
The baby Defender will still be built on the same EV platform as the Range Rover GT.
Photo by:
Automedia
4:34pm ET
JLR's all-electric
baby Defender
is coming soon. According to
Car and Driver
, JLR boss PB Balaji recently said on an earnings call that the smaller, all-electric Defender will go into production at the end next year, alongside the upcoming Range Rover GT. There's no official name for the bite-sized Defender, but Balaji reportedly didn't want to call it the Defender Sport.
While JLR didn't give much info on what the electric baby Defender will be, we do know that it will be built on the same Electrified Modular Architecture (EMA) platform that underpins the
Range Rover GT
. So it makes sense that it'll be built at the same factory. That factory currently builds the existing piston-powered Discovery Sport and the Range Rover Evoque. So JLR is basically just replacing the current combustion cars with their new electric counterparts.
Despite both cars being built in the same factory, Balaji seemed to suggest that only the Defender will go into production in 2027. There's not much word on any technical specs just yet, but EMA supports 800-volt architectures and is capable of housing both pure battery-electric powertrains and hybrids. The baby Defender could very well offer both, but whichever powertrain it has, it'll need to be capable off-road to deliver on its name.
Photo by: Automedia
According to
, Mark Cameron, managing director of Defender and Discovery brands, said "We have got to make sure everything we do as Defender has the DNA of the brand: epic built-to-last, go-anywhere capability."
Pricing, specs, and range are all still under wraps, although it might make sense for either new electric product to have the same 118.5-kWh battery as the current
Range Rover Electric
. With it, the electric Rover is capable of 333 miles of range, and that uses a conventional platform. The battery is also capable of 350 kW DC fast-charging, which would be very competitive in the segment, so it might make sense for JLR to roll with that battery tech. The big Range Rover Electric has a dual-motor powertrain, with 542 horsepower, but that might be a bit much for a baby Defender. Although, there could be a go-fast version with that much power, similar to the current Defender Octa.
Land Rover pushed the current full-size Defender's electric replacement out to sometime in the 2030s, so there shouldn't be any confusion between the full-size and bite-size models. If production begins in late 2027, that means we could see the baby Defender soon.

title: “流星雨之王”狮子座流星雨今晚至明日迎来极大期，专家建议后半夜肉眼观测
content:
IT之家 11 月 17 日消息，据新华社及央视报道，有着“流星雨之王”美誉的狮子座流星雨将于 11 月 18 日凌晨迎来极大期，最佳观测窗口为 18 日凌晨至天亮前。狮子座流星雨以速度快、亮度高为特色，偶尔会出现耀眼的火流星。
狮子座流星雨的母体是坦普尔-塔特尔彗星。星联 CSVA 联合发起人、天文科普专家蒋晨明介绍，坦普尔-塔特尔彗星在绕日运行中，尘埃弥散在整个轨道上。每年 11 月地球穿过这条尘埃轨道，尘埃颗粒闯入大气层形成流星雨，因流星看起来以狮子座为辐射点向外散开而得名。
狮子座流星雨以速度快、亮度高为特色，偶尔出现耀眼的火流星。它不在北半球三大流星雨之列，却因此前几场大爆发而家喻户晓，收获了“流星雨之王”的称号。其爆发具有一定周期性，大约每 33 年有机会迎来大规模爆发。
在非爆发年份，狮子座流星雨流量表现较为平稳，ZHR（IT之家注：天顶每时出现率，指辐射点位于天顶时每小时可见流星数）一般在 10 至 20 之间。蒋晨明表示，今年 ZHR 约为 15，只要耐心守候，仍有机会邂逅转瞬即逝的流星。
狮子座流星雨活跃期为每年 11 月 6 日至 30 日，极大期通常出现在 17 日左右。蒋晨明介绍，辐射点要等到午夜之后才会升到适宜高度，最佳观测时段主要在后半夜，尤其是天亮前。
月光是观测流星雨的主要干扰因素，好在 18 日零点过后，我国多地月亮已经或即将落下，月光影响消失或大幅减弱。
蒋晨明提醒，观测流星雨优先用肉眼观看，尽量远离城市光污染，选择暗夜环境。观测时不必一直盯着狮子座方向，流星可能出现在夜空任意方位。眼下正值初冬时节，天气寒冷，观测时需注意防寒保暖。

title: 哈工大破解热电器件“长寿”难题，将热能转化为电能
content:
感谢IT之家网友
xxy171070
11 月 17 日消息，据新华社 11 月 16 日报道，哈尔滨工业大学材料科学与工程学院隋解和教授、郭逢凯教授团队开发出一种新型超稳定磷化物阻挡层，
有效解决了热电发电器件长期服役过程中的界面稳定性难题
，让生产生活中的热能加速“变废为宝”。
热电发电技术利用温度差就能直接把热能转化为电能，然而如何让热电器件长期稳定工作，一直是困扰业界的难题。
热电器件通常由热电材料与金属电极焊接而成，在长期高温运行中，两侧材料里的元素容易互相“串门”（发生扩散），
导致器件性能大幅下降甚至失效
。这就需要在两者之间加装一层“防火墙”。碲化铋是目前商业化应用最成熟的热电材料，但多年来一直缺乏可靠的阻挡层，制约了温差发电技术的广泛应用。
针对这一难题，哈工大研究团队优选出磷化镍（Ni2P）作为新型阻挡层。测试结果显示，该阻挡层与碲化铋之间的界面不仅接触电阻低、结合强度高，在约 250 摄氏度的高温条件下老化 90 天后仍保持稳定。在同等高温下，
基于该阻挡层制备的器件连续运行 360 小时，输出性能依然稳定
这项成果有望推动碲化铋热电发电器件商业化应用，为推动工业余热回收与节能减排提供新选择。
这一研究成果于 11 月 15 日发表于国际学术期刊《先进材料》。

title: 开发者让一个 ZIP 文件实现三种用途：支持解压、Multiboot 和 BIOS 启动
content:
IT之家 11 月 17 日消息，开发者 David Oberhollenzer（网名 Goliath）制作了一个特殊的 ZIP 文件 boot.zip。
这个文件既能通过常规解压软件正常读取和解压，也能作为操作系统启动镜像，通过传统 BIOS 启动兼容的老式 PC，还支持 GRUB、QEMU 等兼容 Multiboot 规范的引导程序加载。
Goliath 并不是简单地将启动程序放进压缩包，而是通过精心安排 ZIP 文件结构，让同一组字节同时满足压缩文件格式和计算机启动规范的要求。
实现这一效果的关键，是 ZIP 文件格式与 x86 处理器指令之间存在可以利用的字节重合。ZIP 文件通常以 PK 和 03 04 开头，随后是版本号、标志位、压缩方式、修改时间等文件头信息。开发者将第一个文件 ZIPHEAD.COM 设置为不压缩存储，把启动代码直接放在其数据区域中。
在 Multiboot 启动方面，规范要求有效镜像在前 8 KiB 内包含魔数 0x1BADB002，并附带相应标志位和校验值。开发者将这些信息嵌入 ZIPHEAD.COM 的内容中，使其能够被 GRUB、QEMU 等兼容 Multiboot 的加载器识别。
传统 BIOS 启动则需要满足另一项要求：BIOS 读取磁盘的第一个 512 字节扇区，并检查第 510、511 字节是否为 0x55AA。开发者将这一启动标记放在 ZIP 文件对应位置，同时调整文件头中的字段，使其既符合 ZIP 格式，又能被处理器当作 x86 指令执行。
其中，ZIP 文件头中的修改时间字段发挥了关键作用。开发者利用该字段对应的字节编码一条 x86 相对跳转指令，让处理器执行文件开头的内容后，能够跳过 ZIP 文件头，直接进入后续启动代码。版本号和标志位等字段也经过精心设计，以避免执行时产生破坏性操作。
开发者还在自己的博客中解释了后续启动流程：程序首先在 16 位实模式下运行，完成处理器检测、内存探测、磁盘参数读取以及 A20 地址线启用等工作，随后加载压缩包剩余内容，切换至 32 位保护模式，并跳转至 Multiboot 入口。整个启动代码连同相关文件头共计 817 字节。
在实际测试中，David Oberhollenzer 表示，他将 boot.zip 写入软盘后，在 Pentium MMX、i486 DX2 和 Am386DX-40 等老式 PC 上进行了启动测试。
成功启动后，屏幕会显示压缩包内 boot / MESSAGE.TXT 文件中的文字，证明程序不仅能够完成启动，还能读取自身 ZIP 档案中的文件。

title: 我国成功实现 Q/V 频段最高码速率无线通信实验验证：双向 27Gbps 刷新纪录，为 6G 通信与卫星互联网铺路
content:
IT之家 11 月 17 日消息，据新华社今日报道，中国科学院空天信息创新研究院等单位近日在中国遥感卫星地面站丽江站，联合开展面向新一代卫星互联网低轨高通量卫星的高阶体制高码速率双向通信实验，成功实现我国 Q/V 频段最高码速率无线通信实验验证，关键指标达到国内领先、国际先进水平，将为我国 6G 通信与卫星互联网技术发展提供技术支撑。
科研人员介绍，Q/V 频段作为未来 6G 通信使用的重要频段，可用带宽约 10 吉赫兹（GHz），频谱资源丰富，对于实现高速卫星通信具有良好的承载能力。但这一频段的毫米波信号特性特殊，对射频非线性、相位噪声等因素敏感，导致实现高质量、高码速率传输的技术门槛极高。如何提升频段利用效率、提高星地双向传输速率，是当前 Q/V 频段通信领域的重点攻关方向。
据悉，团队攻克了轻量化 Q/V 天线、智能信号补偿、相位噪声补偿等多项关键技术，基于高阶调制解调技术方案建立了 Q/V 频段对应的技术指标体系，搭建了地面实验平台，模拟卫星在轨状态开展实验验证。
实验按照“有线闭环测试 — 远场无线对接 — 全链路综合性能考核”分步实施，依托全套自主研制的天线、功放、信道及基带等设备，在多调制模式、多码速率、不同信噪比条件下完成了传输性能测试。
IT之家从报道获悉，实验在国内首次系统性测试了 64 正交幅度调制（QAM）、128QAM、256QAM 及 512QAM 等多种调制模式对 Q/V 频段双向通信传输速率的提升效果。测试实验结果显示，采用 512QAM 模式时，Q/V 频段单通道最高双向传输速率可达 6.75 吉比特每秒（Gbps），是国内现有同频段单通道传输速率的 2.25 倍。配合双载频和极化复用技术，双向通信速率可达 27Gbps，刷新了国内 Q/V 频段通信速率的最高纪录。
实验成果充分验证了高阶调制解调技术在 Q/V 频段通信的可行性与工程应用价值。后续团队还将继续进行技术指标提升，争取实现双向超 50Gbps 通信传输能力。
