title: Sunkean unveils ETL-certified 2000 VDC TRUNK-T system at RE+ - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The manufacturer’s trunk system and factory-assembled PV wire harnesses are designed to simplify DC cable routing and reduce field wiring, offering configurable power collection options for different module arrangements and utility-scale solar plant layouts.
Sunkean Cable
17 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Utility-scale
For utility-scale PV projects, the DC collection network influences both construction efficiency and long-term connection reliability. Across large arrays, cable routing and repeated wiring operations require careful coordination. SUNKEAN addresses these challenges through two product groups: factory-assembled trunk systems and PV wire harnesses.
At RE+, SUNKEAN officially launched its ETL-certified 2000 VDC TRUNK-T
system, extending its pre-assembled collection portfolio to higher-voltage applications. Designed for large ground-mounted solar plants, the system integrates trunk cables and branch connections into a single assembly that collects DC power from PV strings and delivers it to a disconnect box.
supports customized configurations to accommodate string positions, equipment locations, and project-specific layouts. Its vertical cable exits facilitate branch cable routing, helping installers follow the planned collection layout. Factory pre-assembly reduces the number of individual connection tasks performed on site, helping standardize connection work across the array.
The system’s current collection architecture addresses a separate concern: localized temperature rise. Where several branch currents converge directly at one point on the trunk conductor, this concentration of current can lead to localized heating. TRUNK-T
instead uses a staged approach, combining incoming branch currents before feeding the combined current into the trunk cable. This design is intended to reduce the risk of excessive localized temperature rise.
SUNKEAN also offers copper-to-aluminum and all-aluminum options, giving customers greater flexibility to select conductors in line with the project’s electrical design and material requirements.
Alongside its trunk system, SUNKEAN offers PV wire harnesses with multiple branch configurations, including S-Y, S-X, and S-T designs, to accommodate different module layouts. Factory assembly helps reduce connection errors and maintain consistent installation quality. Matching the harness configuration to the module layout before construction also helps contractors prepare for installation.
For EPC contractors, the combined portfolio helps plan wiring assemblies around the project layout and better manage on-site workloads. For developers, it offers a way to balance construction costs with the need for reliable DC connections throughout the plant’s operating life.
SUNKEAN’s product innovations reflect its commitment to advancing solar connectivity. By addressing both construction needs and connection performance, the company aims to help customers build more reliable PV systems that support stable, long-term operation and greater sustainability.

title: Vietnamese provinces back floating PV projects - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Vietnam’s uptake of floating solar projects continues with three provinces progressing utility-scale projects, including a groundbreaking ceremony for a 35 MW array.
Patrick Jowett
17 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Authorities in three Vietnamese provinces have advanced plans for utility-scale floating solar projects, with installations ranging from 30 MW to over 300 MW.
The province of Gai Lai in southcentral Vietnam is preparing a groundbreaking ceremony for a 35 MW floating solar project this week.
The Bau Can floating solar power plant is expected to span 47 hectares in total, 30 of which will cover the surface on the Bau Can lake.
Local press lists Bau Can Solar Energy joint stock company (JSC) as the investor, with total costs expected to reach VND 613 billion ($23.8 million).
Installation is due for completion in July 2028, with commissioning scheduled for a month later. Once completed, the project is expected to supply nearly 59 GWh
annually over a 50 year operating life.
The province of Lam Dong, southern Vietnam, has backed investment in a planned floating solar array to be installed on the Dak Sin 1 hydroelectric reservoir in Quang Ting commune.
The floating PV project has a planned capacity of 30 MW. It will utilise around 33 hectares of land, 31 of which will be on the water surface.
It will be implemented by VRG Dak Nong JSC, with total investment expected to reach VND 499.5 billion. The project is due to be completed and put into operation by the fourth quarter of 2028.
The province of Dak Lak, just south of Gai Lai province, recently granted a 50-year lease for a large-scale floating solar project to be built on the Srepok 3 hydropower reservoir, located across Ea Nuol and Ea Wer communes.
Developer Srepok 3 Solar Power JSC has been given permission to cover 354 hectares of the reservoir with the solar installation.
A letter confirming the approval states the developer has full exemption from land rental payments for the entire 50 year lease period but says it must complete the relevant legal procedures before using the reservoir’s water surface.
The letter does not state a planned capacity for the floating PV project but details on the provincial government of Dak Lak’s website states a proposed capacity of 304 MW, alongside investment of VND 7.661 trillion. It also gives a target commissioning date by the end of 2027.
Earlier this month, authorities in Dak Lak
approved a 452 MW floating solar project
on the Ea Sup Thuong reservoir. The project is scheduled for completion by the end of 2028 and would rank among the world’s largest inland floating PV installations.
The country’s Ministry of Industry and Trade recently announced
new regional electricity generation price ceilings
for ground-mounted and floating solar projects. Floating solar projects are subject to higher ceilings than ground-mounting projects, ranging from VND 1,340.21 ($0.052)/kWh in the south to VND 1,939.74/kWh in the north.

title: ClearVue secures solar cladding supply deal for Singapore project - pv magazine Global
content:
ClearVue Technologies has received a letter of award (LOA) for a sub-contract worth up to almost AUD 860,000 ($579.261,6) to supply its energy-generating
solar cladding technology
for a Singapore government-owned building in the city-state.
The contract, valued at between AUD 573,000 to AUD 859,800 and awarded through an unidentified Singapore-based façade contractor, covers approximately 4,000 square metres of façade area on the building.
ClearVue said it will manufacture and supply
solar energy-generating laminated glass panels
, finished in grey with matching aluminium edge framing, for the project. The system has been designed to deliver a combined 670 kW of electricity generation capacity, contributing to the building’s overall annual renewable energy target.
The company said it will also manufacture bespoke framing for the project and will utilise its
thermal bridge junction box
technology on a sealed-face façade, the specific application the technology was designed for.
While unable to name the contractor or the specific project due to commercial confidentiality, ClearVue Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Doug Hunt said the contract is “strong commercial validation” of the company’s technology.
“Being selected to supply a government project in Singapore is a significant achievement, not just for this project, but for the business we have spent years building,” he said, adding that the importance goes well beyond the value of this project in revenue.
“We are taking Australian-developed technology into international government infrastructure,” he said. “That is a substantial commercial milestone and strengthens our credibility as we pursue major projects across Asia and around the world.”
The LOA remains subject to project design approvals and final approvals of the manufacturing plan. Final contract value will reflect quantities supplied and delivered.
This latest contract adds to ClearVue’s growing list of projects. It follows a contract to supply its building-integrated PV glazing for a 169 kW project in Cyprus, and a $600,000 subcontract to supply and install its solar products at Canva’s new global headquarters in Sydney.
Earlier this month, ClearVue secured a$500,000 (AUD 742,363) grant from the United States Department of Energy (DOE) to accelerate its push into the American market.
In partnership with North American solar manufacturer Silfab Solar, the company will use the funds to advance its spandrel technology. The grant will support technical development of the technology, performance validation, and evaluation of viable US manufacturing pathways.
ClearVue has also recently established an office and showroom in Hong Kong to support its growth ambitions in the region.

title: Fresnel-based agrivoltaic system redistributes sunlight beneath solar modules to boost crop yields - pv magazine Global
content:
A research team in India has proposed a novel agrivoltaic system that uses linear-diverging Fresnel optics to redistribute transmitted sunlight into shaded regions. Named Even Solar Sharing Agrivoltaics (ESS-AV), it uses diverging Fresnel optics, which are thin, transparent sheets patterned with tiny grooves that spread incoming sunlight outward.
Fresnel optics
use thin, lightweight lenses or sheets with precisely engineered grooves to bend and redirect incoming light. Unlike conventional lenses, they can control how sunlight is concentrated or dispersed while requiring significantly less material.
“The central novelty of our research is demonstrating that how sunlight is distributed beneath photovoltaic modules is as important as how much sunlight crops receive over the course of a day,” said corresponding author Adersh Asok to
pv magazine
. “Our ESS-AV system continuously redistributes sunlight into shaded regions, producing a more homogeneous light environment beneath the photovoltaic array.”
Asok explained that the conventional fixed-tilt agrivoltaic configurations often create alternating regions of intense sunlight and deep shade, which might influence crop growth underneath. “Importantly, we compared ESS-AV with a conventional checkerboard agrivoltaic configuration having identical PV coverage and nominal electrical capacity. This enabled us to isolate the influence of instantaneous light distribution on crop productivity without compromising electricity generation,” he added.
The researchers compared two 1.1 kW rooftop agrivoltaic systems at Thiruvananthapuram, southern India, each with 15 PV modules and 50% PV coverage. One used a conventional checkerboard layout, while the ESS-AV system incorporated Fresnel sheets between modules to redistribute sunlight. The team designed the optics in AutoCAD, simulated them in COMSOL Multiphysics, and fabricated them using a laser machine.
The team grew spearmint hydroponically for 60 days beneath both systems and in an uncovered rooftop control. The team measured crop-level light intensity and uniformity, temperature, and humidity, then assessed plant dimensions, fresh biomass, photosynthetic pigments, water status, membrane damage, and phenolic and flavonoid content. Essential-oil composition was analyzed using gas chromatography mass spectrometry, and treatment differences were evaluated statistically.
“The most striking finding was that our ESS-AV system produced approximately 13% more spearmint fresh biomass than the conventional checkerboard configuration, even though both systems provided comparable daily average photosynthetic light and electricity generation,” Asok said. “In fact, the measured average photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD) was slightly lower under ESS-AV than under the checkerboard system. However, ESS-AV achieved instantaneous light uniformity above 0.922, compared with approximately 0.21 for the conventional configuration.”
The ESS-AV system also achieved a land equivalent ratio (LER) of 1.81 relative to full rooftop PV coverage and 2.04 relative to conventional ground-mounted PV installations, indicating improved combined agricultural and electricity productivity per unit area. “By eliminating separate maintenance gaps between PV rows, our analysis suggests that relative PV installation capacity could potentially increase from approximately 50% to 73% of a conventional ground-mounted PV reference, while preserving the intended optical design,” added the researcher.
“Our long-term objective is to move beyond treating agricultural productivity and solar electricity generation as competing objectives,” Asok concluded. “Instead, we aim to develop agrivoltaic infrastructure in which the optical environment can be engineered to support crop productivity while maintaining commercially relevant electricity generation.”
The research “
Beyond daily average irradiance: Instantaneous homogeneous light distribution unlocks higher productivity in fixed-tilt agrivoltaics
” was presented in
Renewable Energy.
Scientists from India’s
CSIR–National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology
Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR)
have contributed to the research.

title: Havells unveils battery energy storage systems - pv magazine Global
content:
Havells India showcased its battery energy storage systems (BESS) at the REI Expo 2026, highlighting its energy storage solutions as part of its broader renewable energy portfolio, which also includes hybrid inverters, EV chargers, solar inverters and modules.
The company established a dedicated renewables business unit in April to expand its presence across the sector.
“Our primary focus is to address the residential and commercial and industrial (C&I) segments first,” said Reshu Madan, President & SBU Head, Havells. “We also plan to expand into utility-scale and agricultural applications.”
Havells has partnered with Norway-based Pixii to introduce modular battery storage solutions with software-defined controls in India. Its initial portfolio will cover applications from 3 kW to 125 kW, with plans to expand into larger systems. The company also plans to offer integrated solar-plus-storage solutions for residential, commercial and institutional customers.
Modular battery storage portfolio
Havells’ modular battery storage system portfolio will include the PowerShaper family, featuring the PowerShaper XLP with capacities of 112kW/225kW, and the PowerNode family, starting at 125 kW for larger commercial and industrial applications.
“The modular design will allow individual units to be added or replaced while the system is operating, enabling customers to configure storage capacity according to their requirements,” said Aseem Goyal, BU Head – Renewables, Havells India Ltd. “Neither undersizing nor oversizing will be required. That’s where a lot of innovation plays a role,” Goyal added.
The partnership with Pixii is intended to bring the technology to Indian customers at competitive costs while leveraging Havells’ distribution network and installer base. Havells also plans to introduce a new product family, MegaNode, for utility-scale energy storage applications in the future.
The company sees opportunities for off-grid and microgrid storage in remote areas, despite the expansion of grid connectivity.
“Off-grid markets are gradually going away. The Indian government has done a fantastic job in ensuring that electricity reaches every corner of the country,” said Goyal. “However, pockets in states such as Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, along with remote locations, continue to offer opportunities for off-grid and microgrid installations.”
Mining operations are another potential market for battery storage, Goyal added.
Solar manufacturing and localisation
Havells’ solar module portfolio includes monocrystalline PERC bifacial and TOPCon technologies, with TOPCon modules rated up to 620 Wp. The company manufactures some grid-tied inverter models in India, while importing higher-capacity models.
Havells is also a strategic investor in Goldi Solar, which has 16 GW of solar module manufacturing capacity and is expanding into solar cell production.
The partnership combines Goldi Solar’s manufacturing capabilities with Havells’ distribution network and customer reach. “Goldi plays more on the IPP market side, and we play on our strengths on the distribution market side,” said Goyal.
Havells manufactures and markets non-DCR modules under its own brand. The company expects to secure ALMM List-II approval for its DCR modules soon.
The company is also localising its battery storage supply chain, focusing on four key components: power electronics, batteries, software and racking systems. It has already started localising its energy management software and is working on localising the racking system. It plans to begin local battery manufacturing in the near future.
Focus on integrated solutions
Havells aims to strengthen its position in the renewable energy market by moving beyond individual product offerings towards integrated solutions.
“Our aim is to gain the confidence of customers and deliver a better consumer experience. This will not come only from the product; it will come from providing a complete solution,” said Reshu Madan, President & SBU Head at Havells. The company expects to become a significant player in the renewable energy sector over the next three to four years.
Product reliability, warranties and after-sales support are also central to its strategy. Havells offers a 10-year warranty on its inverters, compared to industry offerings that typically range from six to eight years, according to the company. Its battery storage products come with a minimum 10-year warranty, extendable by another five years.

title: A Startup Emerges From Stealth With Highly Personalized AI
content: OpenAI’s ChatGPT remembers details of its users and what they look up, while Anthropic’s Claude Code uses its “auto memory” to take notes on users’ preferences and feedback. A new startup thinks AI models can get even more personalized. First Person Labs , founded seven months ago by two PhD students in the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory , a research institute at the university, is developing tech to make “user models,” the term for more personalized AI models and agents trained on an individual’s data. The startup is coming out of stealth Tuesday and has raised around $10 million in a funding round led by Andreessen Horowitz’s infrastructure team. “Any interface you talk to knows you,” Ken Liu , the company’s co-founder and CEO, said, adding that the company’s tech is “like a biographer—someone that follows you around and sees everything.” To do this, First Person Labs is making an agentic harness, or software infrastructure that wraps around a large language model. The harness—which the company has named Second , like second to one’s own consciousness—takes raw activity from your computer and makes inferences about you based upon it. For example, if your computer logs that you’re often writing at 2 a.m., the model will infer that you’re a night owl. It then constructs a personalized model of what you do and how you think. (Harnesses have also been used by a handful of large tech companies, like Uber , to help them swap between AI models to cut costs .) The company uses a mixture of open-source models like GLM , DeepSeek and Jev as well as some close-source models like Gemini and OpenAI for its harness. It uses this mixture because some inputs don’t require sophisticated models, whereas understanding the intent behind a particular action, like why you worded a delicate email in a particular way, might necessitate some analysis from Anthropic’s high-intelligence model Fable , for instance. Liu said the company plans to generate revenue through subscriptions rather than advertising. The company will be “no ads, forever,” Liu said, because he thinks ads would detract from the personalized feel of the product. Like a personal assistant, people will mostly interact with Second by chatting with it. They can also connect Second directly to other apps, like OpenAI’s Dot , Meta’s Muse and Instinct . Liu thinks First Person Labs’ Second will be able to use the data it collects about you to help these tools arrive at better, more personal results, faster: For example, if your personal assistant knew when school vacation started, it could more seamlessly help you book flights. “Existing personal assistants…can do things, but they don't know you,” he said. “So for user models, it’s almost exclusively focused on the context—understanding you so deeply, and then serving that understanding elsewhere.” First Person Labs lets its individual users control their data, including determining what their Second can and can’t be trained on, and choose which models they’d like their Second to use. That was important to Liu, who researched the intersection of AI and data privacy in his computer science PhD at Stanford, as well as the startup’s investors at Andreessen Horowitz. “As we weave AI into our lives it will come to learn the most sensitive things about us,” Andreessen Horowitz partner Joel de la Garza said. “We invested in First Person Labs because they treat that as an architectural question rather than a policy question, they give control to the user, and we deeply believe that is the right answer.” Here’s what else is going on… People on the Move: Jason Wei Jason Wei , a high-profile AI researcher who worked on OpenAI’s reasoning and deep research models before joining Meta Superintelligence Labs in July 2025, is now joining data curation firm Mercor as its first chief scientist, Wei told The Information exclusively. Wei will be focused on building out an AI research team at the startup. Specifically, he hopes to build more benchmarks that focus on economically valuable tasks in areas like accounting, legal, health and finance, as well as benchmarks for areas in which AI models are rapidly improving and potentially exceeding human capabilities, such as software engineering and the ability for AI to conduct AI research. Wei also said that Mercor wants to conduct research into how to improve model post-training, or the process of tweaking models after they’re already trained. The startup hopes to help business customers cheaply specialize open-source models using their own data for their own specific applications, Wei said. In doing so, Mercor will begin to compete more with other highly-valued AI startups such as Applied Compute in this area, otherwise known as reinforcement-learning-as-a-service. It could also encourage businesses to use more open-source AI rather than closed-source AI from the very frontier labs Mercor serves.— Stephanie Palazzolo Here’s what else is going on… More People on the Move Google DeepMind ’s chief strategy officer Jasjeet Sekhon has left for a role at Anthropic , he said Monday. “I am working to ensure that Claude practices and values epistemic rigor,” he posted on X. An Anthropic spokesperson confirmed the hire. The new committee, chaired by Nvidia director Suzanne Nora Johnson , will retain independent, outside experts to provide legal, national security and trade compliance expertise. The committee will also include two other Nvidia directors, Stephen Neal and John Dabiri . title: AMD and Google Chip Away at Nvidia as Huang Exit Shakes Customers
content: Even before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO last week, AI chips from smaller rivals such as Advanced Micro Devices were starting to win converts. Huang’s departure is likely to reinforce that shift in sentiment. Cirrascale, a 16-year-old cloud provider that operates 25 data centers, started fielding significant interest last year from customers interested in running AI workloads on AMD’s specialized AI chip, according to CEO David Driggers. He said AMD’s chips are particularly suited for running AI models—the process known as inference—which is becoming more popular among businesses. “I’d say the first two years of the company, it was like chewing glass to convince the customer that AMD was a viable option,” said Piotr Tomasik, chief operating officer of Tensorwave, a young cloud provider backed by AMD that runs the company’s chips. Last year, things turned around as outside research showed AMD’s chips being comparable or better than Nvidia on some benchmarks. Google, AMD, Amazon and a host of up-and-coming chip startups have been trying to unseat Nvidia’s dominance in the market for graphics processing units for years. Those efforts are finally starting to bear fruit, in part due to improvements in the rivals’ chips’ performance and their lower cost at a time when Nvidia chips are still expensive and hard to come by. Since late 2025, OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta have said that they would use AMD’s chips to run their AI models (earlier this week, OpenAI said it would use TensorWave’s cloud). Nvidia’s ability to play defense has likely been weakened by last week’s departure of Jensen Huang as CEO, after reports of multiple affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, came to light. The board tapped Nvidia chief financial officer Collette Kress as an interim replacement for Huang. To be sure, Nvidia remains far ahead of AMD and others in terms of its business. Nvidia projected revenue of $108 billion for its fiscal third quarter, which it is reporting Tuesday night, about eight times AMD’s third-quarter revenue reported on Nov. 3. History shows that a successor CEO to a high-profile personality can sometimes outperform the better-known person. Tim Cook, for instance, built Apple into a much bigger company than it had been under Steve Jobs. But Daniel Svonava, CEO at inference provider Superlinked, which specializes in running open-source models, said that in the wake of Kress’s appointment he is less confident that Nvidia will invest enough to make more of its chips available. “CFOs are not known to be very aggressive in the capital deployment, which is what needs to happen to meet the demand to alleviate the compute crunch,” Svonava said. “This latest Nvidia news is the final nail in the coffin for us to switch from experimenting to real deployment.” Cost-Effective Svonava’s company had been testing AMD chips for a few months but began to take them more seriously in recent months, after small open-weight AI models were released from firms like DeepSeek. AMD’s chips are ideal to run such models, he said. AMD chips are much cheaper than Nvidia’s, which makes running some models with AMD chips a higher-margin business for Superlinked. AMD has also managed to improve its RocM software, according to Tomasik, which developers use to program AI models to work on AMD chips. RocM is AMD’s response to Nvidia’s Cuda software, whose popularity with programmers has long been an Nvidia advantage. Before these improvements, TensorWave had dedicated staff to help customers figure out AMD’s software. Tomasik said the amount of time staffers have to spend helping customers crackROCm has dropped 80% to 90% since last year. ROCm’s improvements could give AMD more opportunity to dislodge CUDA. Interest in AMD is helping cloud firms running on AMD chips. TensorWave expects to be generating revenue at an annualized recurring rate of $210 million by the end of 2026, compared to $125 million at the end of 2025. Another AMD-focused cloud provider Sciforium has tripled its customer base since June, when it signed its first commercial contract, and in the past year has grown its capacity five-fold and nearly tripled its team, said CEO Hassan Akbari. The startup, which AMD has invested in, is raising additional funding to add more capacity, Akbari said. Google Google has been spending heavily to expand the market for its TPU AI chips, including by helping finance the building of data centers that will use the chips outside Google Cloud. In July, the company revealed it had agreed to cover as much as $44 billion in data center lease backstops, under which Google would be on the hook if the tenant defaults. Cirrascale recently became one of the first providers of Google’s TPUs outside of Google Cloud. Already, customers have signaled interest in spending hundreds of millions of dollars on computing using Google’s TPU 8 chip, Driggers said. More companies that rely on Nvidia’s chips are starting to use Google’s TPUs. Last month, for instance, The Information reported that Google would sell its TPU chips to OpenAI—the same day Oracle announced it would offer the chips to its own customers. Google has also said it has updated its software to make it easier for customers to run TPUs. The autonomous delivery platform Autolane has primarily used GPUs on Google Cloud but since September, has started moving workflows, like evaluations, to TPUs, Chad Agate, the company’s cofounder and chief technology officer told The Information. The company is now considering heavier, more complex workloads for TPUs, citing a lower cost, Agate said. “We’re looking at moving more workloads, it’s promising,” he said, noting that the company is still heavily reliant on GPUs. “We’re not abandoning ship, we’re looking at which workloads make sense.” TPUs still pale in comparison to Nvidia’s chips. Of the cloud software firm DoiT’s roughly 5,000 customers, only 16 are using TPUs in “real volume,” Vadim Solovey, the CEO of the company said. “These chips are a second supplier, not a replacement.” Nvidia’s Edge Nvidia still has a litany of advantages that rivals must contend with. Because of its large production volumes, Nvidia gets priority for manufacturing capacity during supply crunches from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the dominant manufacturer of AI chips, The Information has previously reported . As a result of that relationship, Nvidia chips remain plentifully available, some customers have found. One startup founder said they were in talks to rent the newest AMD chips at the beginning of this year, but learned they could only get access to the chips by the end of this year at the earliest. Because the startup could get comparable Nvidia chips sooner, it ultimately walked away from using AMD, the founder said. The first time a customer of cloud provider Megaport asked to use AMD chips to run AI workloads was three or four months ago, driven by the difficulty of securing Nvidia chips, said CEO Michael Reid. But the customer would have had to wait six months to get the AMD chips, whereas the lead time for Nvidia chips was 12 to 14 weeks, Reid said, so the customer decided not to use AMD. Nvidia has also built up a robust sales and marketing organization that goes above and beyond traditional vendor relations, an advantage that industry executives say rivals like AMD still cannot match. “Nvidia has been the most proactive vendor I’ve ever worked with in my life,” Reid said. “Nvidia is the only one I’ve ever worked with who will help you with customers, who will help you like they try to connect you with finance people, they try to find you data centers. The rest of them do nothing.” Driggers said that his customers were still increasing their orders of Nvidia chips. Even so, he said, “Nvidia is still dominating, but … they’re losing market percentage.”

title: Microsoft Data Shows Claude Is Stalling Against Copilot in Office
content: Anthropic’s latest push into enterprise apps rattled Microsoft investors last week. Microsoft’s own internal data paints a less threatening picture, at least so far. Usage of Anthropic features that allow people to do work inside Microsoft’s Office apps with Claude , such as sorting email or generating slide decks, has been falling further behind usage of Microsoft’s Copilot in recent months, according to internal Microsoft data described by an employee with knowledge of it. The number of weekly users of those features, known as Claude for Microsoft 365, is less than one-tenth the number of weekly users of the paid version of Copilot, Microsoft’s own AI tools, in Office, which has been growing at a much faster rate, the person said. The idea behind the Anthropic features, which launched in May, was to get existing Microsoft Office customers to use the Claude app as their preferred AI assistant when doing work in Office apps. The slow growth in usage of those features is one reason some Microsoft executives, including Charles Lamanna and Jacob Andreou, who share oversight of Copilot, remain confident they can keep customers from defecting to Anthropic in the long run, the person said. Still, Anthropic gets some benefit from the Copilot usage, as some Copilot features are powered by Anthropic models that Microsoft pays for. The fate of Microsoft’s core apps business was thrust into the spotlight after Anthropic last week launched features that let its customers make spreadsheets, digital whiteboards and dashboards using Claude, without needing Office. Microsoft shares fell as much as 3% that day, as the move revived some of the “SaaSpocalypse” concerns stock investors had earlier in the year about traditional enterprise applications losing their influence with workers. Anthropic, which plans to go public this week, has a smaller enterprise business than Microsoft does, but it’s growing rapidly. Revenue in Microsoft’s 365 Commercial Cloud—which includes Copilot as well as sales of its Office software—rose 17% to $27.7 billion in the September quarter, a slight acceleration from the prior quarter. Anthropic generated $17 billion in revenue in the September quarter, more than twelve times its revenue from a year earlier. Like Microsoft, Anthropic is pushing enterprise customers to pay based on their use of Claude rather than only through subscriptions. Microsoft initially sold Copilot mainly as a $30-per-user monthly subscription. It is now betting on features that bill customers based on how much they use AI, and it recently began offering steeper discounts on the per-seat fee, The Information previously reported. At least two large private equity firms have recently been spending more on usage-based AI tools in Copilot than they previously spent in total on Office 365 subscriptions, the person with knowledge of Microsoft’s plans said. Both firms increasingly use Copilot agents to automate data analysis. The rivalry between Anthropic and Microsoft is more tangled than it looks, and the two companies need each other more than ever. Microsoft plans to invest $1 billion in Anthropic’s initial public offering, and Anthropic has signed up to spend $49 billion renting Nvidia cloud servers from Microsoft’s cloud unit over the next seven years, a critical contract for Microsoft that allows it to lessen its reliance on server rentals to another customer, OpenAI. Microsoft, meanwhile, is on track to pay Anthropic billions of dollars a year to use its AI to power features in Copilot, such as the Copilot Cowork agent that can automate complex tasks like creating financial models in Excel or moving data between different types of documents. Still, Microsoft has recently been working to swap out those Anthropic models in favor of OpenAI models , which are cheaper for it to use thanks to a commercial deal with OpenAI. Product Response Microsoft is preparing its answer to Anthropic’s latest salvos at Ignite, its annual conference for IT professionals and business customers, which begins Tuesday in San Francisco. Its moves target several pressure points: the cost of running AI agents, data-security guarantees, and getting existing Copilot customers to spend more on AI. Microsoft’s Azure cloud unit has developed a new system for hosting AI agents that it believes can drastically cut the computing power they consume and help them finish tasks faster, according to three Microsoft employees with knowledge of the effort. Microsoft plans to debut it at Ignite, they said. The system lets an agent save a snapshot of its work and shut off until it is called on again, then reactivate from that snapshot, one of the people said. That means an idle agent costs customers little to nothing. In doing so, Microsoft will catch up to Google Cloud, which unveiled a similar service, Agent Compute Engine, on Oct. 22. Microsoft hopes the new tools will make running agents on Azure cheaper than on rival cloud providers or from startups offering their own AI agents. Always-On Costs The cost of running always-on AI agents has become a sore spot for companies that offer them. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, for instance, said on the company’s earnings call last month that Meta hasn’t launched its Muse agent globally because of the servers required to run it. The Microsoft agents and their snapshots sit in secure sandboxes within Azure, a feature Microsoft plans to pitch to customers worried about where their data goes when they use AI tools, one of the people said. Microsoft also plans to showcase features that guarantee that the software customers generate with Copilot’s vibe-coding tools will remain in a so-called “sandboxed environment” within Azure, meaning it isn’t connected to the internet and is separate from other customers’ data. As it has done in the past, Microsoft plans to pitch the feature as a contrast to the data-handling policies of Anthropic and OpenAI, another one of the people said. In another prong of its offensive against Anthropic, Microsoft last month made its Office applications accessible directly inside the Copilot app, aiming to keep customers from switching between Microsoft software and competing chatbots like Claude. In sales pitches to customers, Microsoft has also been promoting Copilot as less of a data-governance headache than Claude features that work within Office apps, which require companies to agree to export some data from their Office 365 software to Anthropic’s servers to run, one of the people said. Microsoft also plans a wider launch of vibe-coding tools, previewed in September, that let Copilot customers build custom apps inside Office and share them with co-workers. A customer could, for instance, describe in plain English a widget that pulls contract information from a sales database and alerts salespeople when a contract is about to expire, one of the people said. All of those features bill customers for usage on top of the monthly Copilot fee. Microsoft also plans to unveil tools that help companies monitor how employees use Copilot and what costs they are running up. Convincing existing customers to use more Copilot AI is crucial to Microsoft’s effort to grow its software revenue. The company highlighted that strategy on its earnings call last month. CEO Satya Nadella said the number of customers paying for usage-based features in Copilot rose 75% in the September quarter, and CFO Amy Hood said average revenue per user grew thanks to increased use of the pay-as-you-go AI tools.

title: Nvidia’s Board Should Come Clean on Huang’s Resignation
content: Memo to the board of Nvidia: Folks, you need to explain why you pressured Jensen Huang to resign. Otherwise, a bring-back-Jensen movement will only grow and could theoretically escalate to the point where it threatens your roles on Nvidia’s board. Even President Donald Trump has weighed in, supporting Huang. The board could use Nvidia’s earnings update on Tuesday to provide everyone with some answers. As quixotic as the Jensen loyalists’ effort may seem right now, some of their complaints are on the money. A letter from investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker posted on X on Friday, for instance, made the point that there was “massive uncertainty associated with recent events surrounding” Huang’s departure. The pair were correct to say that a “slow, measured and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia” was in everyone’s best interests. Remember, when Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, it gave zero explanation for why the board had changed its tune from its announcement on Sunday that it had “confidence in Jensen” but would investigate the Chinese spy allegations. Yes, there was the news on Wednesday that he’d had an affair with a subordinate, but that didn’t seem to be enough to prompt the board to short-circuit its previously announced inquiry and push Huang out immediately. Plenty of reports have suggested that Nvidia under Huang at the very least turned a blind eye to smuggling of Nvidia chips into China. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s statements on Sunday that the board needs “to go outside the company” to replace the CEO were based on questions about Nvidia’s awareness of chip smuggling. If that’s what prompted the board’s change of heart, now’s the time to say so. So far, the board doesn’t seem to be paying much attention to the brouhaha. That could be a mistake. Nvidia’s bylaws allow shareholders “owning at least 15% of our shares” to ask for a special meeting of stockholders. Theoretically, then, shareholders could get together to try to overthrow the board. Sure, assembling a group owning 15% to convene a meeting wouldn’t be easy. Jensen Huang owns 3.6%, while other big shareholders are mostly institutional—BlackRock owns 8%, while Vanguard owns 7%, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence. It’s hard to imagine institutional shareholders agitating to overthrow the board, particularly given the circumstances. And the bylaws say shareholders in such a group have to have owned their shares for at least a year—which rules out an activist group buying stock now and then agitating for a meeting. Even if the Huang loyalists succeeded in calling a meeting, there’s no guarantee they could amass the votes to replace the board, which presumably would require at least a majority. Still, even the threat of such a vote would be destabilizing for Nvidia, intensifying the uncertainty surrounding the company. The board might want to think of ways to calm everyone down. Nvidia’s Descent Shares of Nvidia fell another 4% on Monday, a slide likely fueled by multiple news reports that the company’s board wasn’t considering reinstating CEO Jensen Huang despite growing pressure. At Monday’s close of $156.14, the stock has fallen 16% in 10 days and 35% since early October. And yet, it hasn’t been that long since Nvidia shares were last at $156—in fact, it was only 16 months ago, in July of last year. It’s easy to forget, but the stock has rocketed since OpenAI released ChatGPT in late 2022: Nvidia stock was trading around $16-17 back then. Right now Nvidia stock looks cheap relative to smaller rivals like AMD on a multiple of future earnings. But given the uncertainty about what Nvidia’s future revenue will look like—how much it would decline if the Chinese market was properly cut off—the current price makes sense. In Other News • Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust on Monday said it was acquiring a 75% stake in two joint ventures with Amazon Web Services to launch its strategy of buying data centers that have long-term lease contracts with major cloud providers. Blackstone’s data-center focused real estate investment trust is valuing the deal at around $5 billion. • Microsoft this week is planning to debut new features in its Copilot AI software and Azure cloud service aimed at rebuffing competing products from Anthropic and other AI competitors, The Information reported . • California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced a lawsuit on Monday against OpenAI over an attack by a swarm of its agents against the open-source repository platform Hugging Face in July. In the 31-page lawsuit , filed in the Superior Court of the State of California, Bonta asks for an injunction against OpenAI to prevent OpenAI from any practices that constitute unfair competition, as well as civil penalties. • The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security announced a long-awaited rule on Monday that restricts Chinese AI companies from accessing otherwise restricted chips through data centers, primarily in Southeast Asia. Earlier, Shares of Chinese AI firms MiniMax and Z.ai plunged further Monday on fears that the U.S. will tighten Chinese companies’ access to export-controlled chips after the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. • Gates Ventures, the private office of Bill Gates, and West Health, a group of non-profits funded by philanthropists Gary and Mary West, said on Monday that they will offer up to $15 million in philanthropic funding to scientists and researchers trying to develop AI tools to advance research for Alzheimer’s disease. title: OpenAI’s Astra Is a Boon to Robotics, Says Nvidia Robotics Chief Deepu Talla
content: When OpenAI released its Astra model in September, users quickly found that it excelled at tasks that require understanding the physical world. One of those most impressed by its performance was Nvidia’s robotics chief Deepu Talla, who told The Information it is a breakthrough in efforts to create robots that can handle a wide variety of jobs. Astra has made it 100 times faster to create some kinds of data for training robotic AI models and could help automate the process of putting robots to work in factories, Talla said on the latest episode of AI Deep Dive. (The full episode, which was recorded before Jensen Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO, is available here .) “The Astra moment happened, where agents are now truly able to basically use all the physical AI tools that are available—whether it’s for simulation, whether it’s for training,” he said. As a result, the ability to create useful robots is on “completely a different rocket ship than where we were a year ago.” Among Astra’s physical-world feats, it could model mechanical parts using engineering software, and it outperformed some specialized robotics AI models when controlling robot arms. One person even gave an Astra-powered robot a canvas and brushes, and the model painted scenes of the Golden Gate bridge. Roboticists have long relied on computer simulations to train AI models to power robots, but that approach was in part limited by the speed of creating simulated versions of the objects the robot might interact with and the environment it would work in, which could take months. Thanks to Astra’s ability to automate that process, new robotic AI models trained in simulations and released over the next 6-to-12 months will be able to work with much higher accuracy than today’s leading models, Talla predicted. Running those simulations requires AI chips like the ones Nvidia designs, which are also used in training AI models and running them on robots. Talla also discussed the three speeds at which robots have to think, why he expects a ‘ChatGPT moment for robotics’ in the next 1-to-3 years and the role for humanoid robots in manufacturing. The following transcript of the conversation has been lightly edited for clarity. Drew: Welcome back to the Information’s AI Deep Dive. On this show, we get to the bottom of the hardest technical problems in AI. I’m your host, Rocket Drew. My guest today is Deepu Talla. Deepu is Vice President of Robotics and Edge AI at Nvidia. Deepu, welcome on the show. Talla: Rocket, how are you? Drew: I’m doing well. How are you? Talla: Great, thank you. Drew: I’m really excited for this conversation. I think there’s a lot happening in robotics and physical AI is such a hot topic right now. It’s always a pleasure to talk to you about this. So excited to get into it. Talla: Yeah, looking forward to it. Drew: Well, one thing that just happened is Nvidia had its developer conference in Berlin, GTC Berlin. You were there, is that right? Talla: That’s right. Drew: How was Berlin? Talla: I mean, Berlin was amazing. I mean, if you think about some of the toughest problems we have to solve as a human race. We’ve been trying to solve robotics, physical AI, for a long time. As you know, automation has been around for 50 plus years, right? And the technology was not good enough until recently we reached a tipping point. And what was so exciting in Germany? Obviously, a lot of German companies were there, but also a lot of European companies from the region. A lot of the deployments there are tailored towards small and medium manufacturing enterprises. If you think about Europe, Germany, Mittelstand, it’s really small and medium precision, super specialized applications. And robotics, the technology was never really good enough to be deployed in an autonomous manner, and because these are small and medium enterprises, the jobs tend to be extremely high mix. So you can never really program a robot to work in those kind of environments. So you need really autonomous capability, and now the technology is reasonably maturing to address those type of problems. Literally, I mean it felt like all of Europe, everybody working on all the startups, all the researchers, all the developers, large companies, everybody was in Berlin. It was supremely vibrant for me. Drew: You mean to actually do the deployment autonomously, to do the integration work? That that’s something that has to happen autonomously, or to get automation in place. Talla: Yeah. So there’s two parts to it, right? First of all, the intelligence in order to do a task or a set of tasks needs to be good enough. Good enough meaning it needs to be accurate. It needs to be reliable. Do it all the time the same way. And it needs to be safe (and economical and so on). So that general purpose brain that can comprehend the physical world, the environment, we haven’t reached that tipping point yet. Like what happened in November 2022 with ChatGPT for the digital world. So the best in the world from researchers to developers to labs, everybody is trying to work towards that problem of making that physical AI brain accurate enough. That’s the first step. Now, once you are able to create that brain, you still need to deploy that brain into specific robot embodiments into existing workflows, and that’s a fairly complicated endeavor as well because program you can’t program the robot, and they need to work with other robots of different capabilities, they need to work with digital AIs, and of course, they also need to work with humans. So that integration step is not easy because it’s going to be custom on a case by case basis. So that technology was not available either until suddenly, like a month or so ago, the Astra moment happened, where agents are now truly able to basically use all the physical AI tools that are available, whether it’s for simulation, whether it’s for training, whether it’s for runtime deployment, and they’re able to iteratively take good robot brains and see if they can integrate into existing workflows. So progress on both fronts is necessary. Number one, the general purpose brain is accurate, reliable and safe. Number two, you can integrate that into existing workflows. Drew: The importance and the significance of that integration work, I imagine, is something that’s really salient for people in these traditional manufacturing centers in Europe. On the West Coast, here in California, there’s a kind of AI arrogance, sometimes that AI is everything. That’s the only important part of the problem. I mean, is there something that roboticists here in California stand to learn from traditional manufacturers in Europe? Talla: Yeah, I don’t know if it’s we are being in the Silicon Valley we are being, how would I say, too brave or too proud—I don’t think it’s that. What really it is is again, there’s two parts to the puzzle, right? Since we haven’t really solved the general purpose accuracy in the first place, we really never had to go and solve the integration problem at scale. So the integration problem is really scaling out the intelligence. But luckily, the whole agentic AI revolution—Gee, what was it? Just happened in February of this year in the digital world. And that advance is going incredibly fast now. And just when Astra was released, we were pleasantly surprised. I for sure was because what we were doing, in order to train the robot brain, for example, you have this lot of data collection that’s required. As you know, in the physical world, the accuracy requirement is much higher than the digital world. And what was happening was we had to basically collect lots of real world data, and that’s kind of happening. But that was not going to be sufficient. So synthetic data generation was an obvious concept, but the problem with synthetic data generation was that you needed artists or needed CAD models to create accurate 3D representations of all the different objects and the spaces. And as much as AI has progressed, still creating those environments and those assets was extremely time-consuming to the point of several months. If you wanted to create a digital twin of an environment, it would take several months, including using generative AI to do that. Now, suddenly, what happened with this agentic AI, like Astra, for example, was trained on the physical world. It has a good idea of the physics of the world, it has a good idea of the space and time relationship, what you call spatial-temporal relationship. So, because of that, it is able to basically study the properties of the objects. It’s going to go on the internet and probably pull out a CAD that may be available from it, or from a picture or a video, which need not be a full, accurate 3D scan per se, but just by taking some pictures and video, it’s able to construct those environments. Which essentially means what used to take months in generating synthetic assets and environments suddenly got 100X boost and speed up. Which means now suddenly we can use that capability, agentic AI capability, to create good data to train our models better, faster, to converge faster, to increase the intelligence. So that’s the number one observation. And then number two, equally important, if you had a reasonably good enough brain that you can deploy for whatever application, that integration work—typically, imagine you have to put it in a factory. The factory, there’s machines. Some of them are controlled by PLCs that might be 20–30 year old. Most likely it is, and they have some bespoke, programming language to control that. And sometimes you have to connect that to a ERP system. If you’re talking about the supply chain. It might have to be connected to a building management system, so on so forth, right? So who’s writing all that glue code? It’s actually pretty boring to write the glue code. There’s not that many people actually who know that, and the manuals are all out there somewhere. But if you throw agents at them, and the agents are actually able to study all those manuals and understand all the glue code and write it, that’s another 100X lift, I think. So because while you’re trying to create intelligence, the pre-work has gotten 100X better. The post-work, which is basically the deployment, has gotten 100X better. Now suddenly, the pace at which we can create useful physical AI intelligence is, I think, we are on a completely a different rocket ship than where we were a year ago. Drew: Yeah, I think both of those are really great examples of ways that LLMs are removing bottlenecks to deployment, and in kind of unintuitive ways. Like I don’t know if people would have appreciated how useful it is to be able to develop these sim-ready assets using a model like OpenAI’s Astra. Why do you think Astra got so good at that capability? Why now is it all of a sudden really good at CAD and Blender and this physical understanding? Talla: I think the first modality that was being solved in the last three to five years was all about language, and then when language got added, and a couple of years ago video got added and other sensors got added. But however, I think this is just the next evolution, right? Physical AI quite simply is the largest opportunity. As language has gotten good, as video’s gotten good, now it’s about combining all of those to solve spatiotemporal problems. And I think I actually believe that they actually did a good job of training the model to actually do this very type of tasks that we really need to be solved. Drew: I see. It was a deliberate decision. OpenAI decided the time is right to target these physical capabilities, and so maybe they went out and bought a lot of reinforcement learning environments to train those CAD capabilities. But they targeted this capability. Talla: Yeah, I didn’t ask them explicitly, but my guess is it didn’t happen accidentally, but it was really interesting to solve this sort of a problem. Drew: Yeah, that would be my guess too. So my question—I think both of these are real accelerants: using LLMs to create these simulation assets, using LLMs to write that kind of glue code to enable faster deployment. The question that comes to mind for me, though, is is that really the hardest part of the problem? Even if we were able to use LLMs to automate that and make that as fast as possible, aren’t there other bottlenecks or other frictions that are going to still get in the way? For example, dealing with the IT guy at the factory, getting the IT person to agree to put the robots on the Wi-Fi. That’s a very human problem that LLMs, I don’t know if they’re going to solve that. Talla: Yeah, you’re right. The thing to remember is, we have several orders of magnitude improvement needed before you go and deploy these things at scale. For example, what’s a good accuracy in the digital world, if your model is 90, 95% accurate, that’s a pretty good accuracy because in most cases in the digital world, especially if it relates to consumer type of applications, it’s more of a hint and there’s a human in the loop to close the last 5 or 10%. In the physical world, it’s not about 90, 95; it’s 99-point how many nines of accuracy do you need after that? Because in almost all cases, there’s no human in the loop. So, if you think from that perspective, in where we are today and where we need to go, 100X improvement is very good. But let’s say you’re at 99, it basically means that you went from 99 to 99.99. That’s impressive. But you need to get to 99 point maybe six nines or eight nines. So we need lot of these step function exponentials that are happening. So I think what happened right now with respect to LLMs agents solving the asset creation and also the post is a step in the right direction, necessary but not sufficient. To your point, right? So, at the end of the day, there will be some element of human that’s going to do the judgment of what is the right thing and what’s not the right thing. But hopefully, a lot of these, especially in the manufacturing, logistics, these kind of settings, there’s definitely rules because those rules are coming from first principles. They’re coming from safety. They’re coming from efficiency. They’re coming from, combination of all of these different things— Drew: and bureaucracy, I’ll say it. Talla: There’s obviously, there’s different—bureaucracy is one way to look at it. The other one would be there’s probably a good reason for that rule because there’s a benefit in some other scenario that’s the reason there’s probably that rule. And all of these are reasonably well codified actually as it turns out, which means they’re all documented well, which means LLMs can actually read through all of those and follow those instructions and create this intelligence create the software essentially that is actually going to strictly follow those rules, and then there’s always going to should be a human in the loop to make sure that all of these are exactly being done in the way they’re intended to. Drew: I take your point that first things first, we have to get to reliability before we can deal with these hard problems of deploying at scale. Still, I feel like if you have an LLM that can process all of these, all of this documentation, that’s still not the same as convincing the company that they’ll get good ROI if they get your robots. Making the factory manager happy with having the robots in the factory. Making the person who has to interact with the robots day to day on the line feel like they actually want the robots to be there. Those seem like really hard problems. I wonder how fast you could see deployment getting, say, five years from now for a factory. How quickly will they be able to go from no robots to automating a big process? Talla: Yeah. So if you step back for a second, right? In fact, the best place to build and test these systems actually is not in the real world first, right? Because it’s going to be slow. It is potentially dangerous, and it’s also expensive. Because if you have a wrong game plan and you don’t want to find out that you did all of the work and wrong, so the robot— Drew: The robot breaks or something gets damaged. Talla: Absolutely. So the answer is you want to do this in simulation, right? Now we talked about simulation, and the idea of simulation is not new. For example, the best example I use is because we’re Nvidia, we build a lot of silicon chips. In the chip industry, we’ve been using simulation emulation for well over 30 years. Until we 100% are confident of the simulation and emulation, we never send it out the design to tape out at say TSMC or whichever fab you’re using, and then somehow when it comes out, almost always it works, right? So the same idea should apply to physical AI and robotics problems, and we’ve been working on this for 15 years inside Nvidia and working with partners, worldwide. And luckily even simulation because of all the AI capability, the tools, which is basically what we build, the tools and acceleration libraries, whether it’s Isaac Lab for policy evaluation, reinforcement learning, or Isaac Sim for basically doing all the virtual environments to work together. Because of AI technology, this simulation technology has reasonably matured. Where now we can literally do this data generate data in emulation, generate it synthetically, or bring real world sensors in software in the loop or hardware in the loop, and we can basically test all of these whether it’s an individual brain on a robot or test fleets of robots interactions with digital AI. You can do the orders of magnitude, maybe 1000, if not a million times more in simulation first, which is also faster, safer, and cheaper. We do all of this. So, to your question of how do you know it’s going to work in the factory? Is it going to be scaling out or not? You want to do all of this in simulation as much as possible. And the good news also is these agents are actually using all these simulators as tools. In fact, one of the coolest thing that Jensen showed last week at GTC Berlin, the keynote, incredibly cute. The Micro Ducks. I don’t know if you caught a lot of people saw those, Micro Ducks. Essentially the AI model was running on a PC and it was communicating on RTX part PC and was communicating with the Micro Ducks. It was so cute and so cool, right? Drew: They are so cute. I like to say that they’re superhuman at one capability and it’s being cute. Talla: Yeah, being cute and yeah, and then semi following instructions like a kid would, right, or a dog puppy would. But my biggest takeaway from all of that was like, you know how long it took for us to create that whole demonstration? I think it was less than a week, from idea to deployment. And if we did this, if we tried to do this six months ago, there’s no way we would have done it that fast. The reason it happened so quickly was this Astra type of capability. Essentially, basically, you are able to say, “Build me a environment for these robots to operate in.” So it’s essentially created a digital twin. And then you said, “Put all these different objects in the digital twin.” So in the case of a factory, you can say, “Here’s my factory size. Here’s pictures and images of the factory.” And by the way, if you have CAD, you can give it, but you just gave pictures and video, it can kind of identify what it’s looking at. Is it looking at a machine? Is it looking at table? It’s looking at a desk. Because it has spatiotemporal capability, it can kind of exactly know what’s the size—Just like you and I, if you saw an object, you can kind of tell approximately how big this, how long this mic is. What’s the volume approximately, what’s the strength would be approximately the same thing. So it could create all those environments, and then it could basically create synthetic data. It would basically train the model. That’s basically calling another agent to go and train the model. And then for testing the model, how do you know that these ducks are going to operate properly with their mechatronics? That mechatronics was fed into Isaac Lab, and then it basically ran all the policy evaluation in Isaac Lab and Isaac Sim, all using agents. Agents did that just iterative loop, and then finally when it came to a reasonable good answer, you deploy that brain. In this case, it was a PC because the duck didn’t have a big enough chip in there. So this is exactly illustrated… So my takeaway from that demo was, of course, the ducks were cool. But if you’re a warehouse operator, if you’re a factory operator, you’re trying to make your factory more automated. Make it more autonomous. How do you do it? Before it would take a long time to even generate the assets, but now with this capability, literally you’re up and running within a week. And then, these agents are super good at using the best tools that are already available.
