Molten Industries Commissions World’s First Plant to Produce Battery-Grade Graphite – and hydrogen – from Natural Gas
Building a domestic supply of critical materials, Molten’s Oakland demonstration plant is now operational, producing battery-grade graphite and clean hydrogen in an end-to-end, commercial-scale, modular process
OAKLAND, Calif.–(
BUSINESS WIRE
)–Molten Industries, an industrial manufacturing startup scaling a breakthrough technology to produce critical minerals and chemicals, today announced the commissioning and start of operations at its demonstration plant in Oakland, California. This milestone marks the world’s first plant to produce battery-grade graphite from natural gas, creating a new domestic source for a critical battery material and demonstrating Molten’s methane pyrolysis technology end-to-end at commercial scale.
Molten’s technology converts natural gas into two valuable products — battery-grade graphite and hydrogen — by splitting methane into its elemental components, carbon and hydrogen, without oxygen, combustion or CO₂. Compared with conventional synthetic graphite, Molten’s process uses 4× cheaper feedstock and 3× less electricity, needs no graphitization furnace, and produces zero process emissions. The process also produces clean hydrogen as a by-product, an ingredient used in global production of ammonia fertilizer, refined petroleum products, methanol, semiconductors, and steel.
Graphite is the primary material that holds charge in a lithium-ion battery, making it essential to electric vehicles, data centers, grid storage, robotics, drones, and other battery applications. Graphite is also used in nuclear reactors, semiconductor processing, jet engines, gas turbines, steelmaking, and thermal energy storage. While domestic sources of graphite for steelmaking and nuclear exist, the United States remains entirely dependent on foreign sources for battery-grade graphite, and
of global battery graphite processing is controlled by China.
Molten’s process demonstration unlocks a 100%-U.S.-made pathway for this critical material based on a widely available domestic resource, natural gas. The company’s Oakland plant has a capacity of 300 metric tons of graphite anode production per year, with reported natural gas-to-graphite yields above 95%, using a single full-scale modular reactor that serves as the building block for future plants.
Kevin Bush,
CEO and co-founder of Molten Industries, said:
Splitting natural gas into carbon and hydrogen was first patented in 1889, but nobody could figure out how to create high-quality graphite,
“We’ve created an entirely new technology to become the first to produce battery-grade graphite and hydrogen from natural gas. The Oakland plant proves that we can make these products from an abundant domestic resource in a single modular reactor — a critical step toward scaling the technology.”
Caleb Boyd,
CTO and co-founder of Molten Industries, said:
Going end to end from pipeline natural gas to battery material in a single facility at scale is modern alchemy,
“We’ve gone from a concept in the lab to an operating plant that is producing graphite and hydrogen every day and serves as the building block for larger production facilities.”

ProLogium and TDAC Announce Prospective Investments of $85 Million
Non-binding term sheets signed for approximately $85 million of investment
Existing and strategic investors investing at the business combination to participate at $10.00 per share.
Proceeds expected to support the build-out of ProLogium’s Dunkirk, France gigafactory driving it to the first 4 GW of capacity, further expansion of revenue opportunities in new markets, and other general corporate purposes.
TAIPEI, Taiwan and NEW YORK, Nov. 18, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — ProLogium Holding Inc. (“ProLogium” or the “Company”), a global leader in next-generation lithium ceramic battery technology, and Translational Development Acquisition Corp. (“TDAC”) (Nasdaq: TDAC), a special purpose acquisition company, today announced the signing of non-binding term sheets with a number of existing and strategic investors for proposed investments totaling approximately $85 million.
Under these term sheets, several existing investors in ProLogium and other strategic investors have indicated an intention to invest in connection with ProLogium’s previously announced proposed business combination with TDAC (the “Transaction). Each PIPE investment is expected to be made in common shares at $10.00 per share concurrently with the closing of the Transaction. One term sheet with a strategic partner contemplates follow-on investments after the closing of the Transaction, on terms to be agreed as part of a broader partnership plan. The proposed investments remain subject to the negotiation and execution of definitive transaction documents. ProLogium expects to use the proceeds for the build-out of its gigafactory in Dunkirk, France including unlocking further reimbursements from the $1.5bn French Government subsidy, accelerating expansion into new business applications for revenue expansion in new markets such as drones, and other general corporate purposes. The Transaction is expected to close in December 2026, subject to approval by TDAC’s shareholders and other customary closing conditions.
Vincent Yang,
Founder and Chief Executive Officer of ProLogium, said:

”The additional capital would help us advance construction of our Dunkirk gigafactory in France and support our continued expansion into automotive, unmanned systems, AI data centers and other application markets, serving customers in Europe and globally,”
Michael B. Hoffman,

content:
Recycling – Charging towards the battery electric future
The Battery Innovation Programme has awarded £28.6m to 27 projects to strengthen the UK battery sector and boost national capability.
Delivered by Innovate UK on behalf of the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, the competition is designed to support UK businesses and researchers to develop new battery technologies.
The competition focused on sourcing and processing battery materials, recycling valuable materials, strengthening UK manufacturing and reducing reliance on overseas supply chains.
Recycling batteries
Lithium Battery Recyclers Ltd has been awarded more than £1.2 million to lead project Reclaim, to develop a new UK process for recycling end-of-life electric vehicle batteries.
The process, developed by the University of Leicester, uses a tiny quantity of vegetable oil in water to separate valuable battery materials, including graphite, without acid leaching or hazardous chemicals.
The project will scale up the technology at a pilot facility in Widnes, Cheshire, and test the recovered materials for reuse in new batteries.
It aims to reduce the energy needed for recycling and keep valuable battery materials in the UK to support domestic manufacturing.
Reducing waste
Hyperbat, now part of Unipart Manufacturing Group, has received more than £2.4 million to lead a project.
This aims to reduce the number of electric vehicles written off because their batteries are damaged or no longer working as expected.
At present, it can be difficult to assess whether these batteries are safe to repair or reuse.
This can lead to unnecessary vehicle write-offs, higher insurance costs and valuable materials being lost.
The project will develop a clear process for checking each battery and deciding whether it can be repaired, reused , given a second life for energy storage or safely recycled.
The work could keep batteries in use for longer, reduce waste and create skilled jobs in the UK.
Feasibility studies
The competition has also awarded just over £6.2 million to 15 shorter feasibility studies exploring new ideas across the battery supply chain.
Running for between six and 12 months, these projects will test whether early-stage technologies could improve how batteries are made, used, reused and recycled.
This will help the most promising ideas move towards further development and commercial use.
SuperDielectrics Group and Sytronix have been awarded almost £500,000 to test a new type of battery that could help data centres manage the rapid changes in electricity demand.
The water-based battery is designed to store and release power quickly, helping data centres run more AI servers without placing additional strain on local electricity networks.
The project will build on an existing battery pack and test how it responds to the changing power needs of AI systems.
If successful, the technology could help data centres make better use of their existing grid connections and expand without requiring immediate upgrades to local power supplies.
It could also provide a safer alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries and reduce reliance on imported battery materials.
Investment in skills
The Battery Innovation Programme has also awarded £3.6 million to three regional skills initiatives.
These will accelerate the development of the UK’s battery manufacturing workforce and strengthen national capability across the battery value chain.
The investment will support the delivery of industry-focused nationally accredited training programmes across England.
These will equip learners with the skills needed to secure careers in one of the UK’s fastest-growing advanced manufacturing sectors, and help businesses access talent to meet increasing demand.
University Centre Somerset will deliver Level 2 and 3 battery manufacturing training for the South West battery cluster.
University College Birmingham, and Newcastle University with New College Durham in the North East, will expand their training to Levels 4 and 5.
Dr Valentina Gentili,
Director of the Battery Innovation Programme, said:
As global demand for batteries continues to grow, it is increasingly important that the UK focuses on the areas where it can deliver the greatest impact and strategic value.
The projects supported through this competition demonstrate the breadth of innovation taking place across the UK battery sector.
Minister for
Reindustrialisation Blair McDougall,
This funding will give Britain’s battery manufacturing industry the support they need to power the industries of the future and keep our country at the cutting edge of innovation.
Through our Modern Industrial Strategy we’re doubling down on Britain’s high-growth sectors like advanced manufacturing, and I want to congratulate all the winners on their success and their role in reinforcing Britain’s leadership in this fast-growing industry.

Partnership expands access to U.S.-manufactured lithium-ion cells, flexible stocking and scheduled releases for aerospace, defense and other demanding applications
TAMPA, Fla., Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Sensible Micro Corporation today announced an authorized distribution partnership with American Lithium Energy (ALE), expanding customer access to U.S.-manufactured cylindrical and pouch lithium-ion cells and coordinated supply planning services.
Through Sensible Micro, customers can evaluate ALE cell options, coordinate technical discussions and sourcing documentation, and develop stocking and delivery plans aligned with production needs. Supporting Domestic Battery Sourcing
As aerospace and defense programs assess changing battery sourcing requirements, the partnership offers an additional path to evaluate domestically manufactured cells.
Section 842 of the FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act
addresses certain defense procurements involving advanced batteries and foreign entities of concern. Customers should assess applicability and compliance for their specific programs and products.
U.S. Battery Technology and Manufacturing
Founded in 2006, ALE designs and manufactures advanced lithium-ion cells and custom battery solutions for aerospace, defense, medical, mobility and energy storage applications. Its portfolio includes cylindrical and pouch cell designs, SafeCore™ safety technology and ZeroVolt™ technology, which supports repeated discharge to zero volts in applicable designs. Availability and performance depend on the selected product and application.
Flexible Distribution and Supply Planning
Sensible Micro can structure custom stocking programs and scheduled releases around agreed forecasts, order commitments and delivery requirements. These services can help customers plan availability, manage working capital and align inventory with production schedules.
Executive Perspectives

Chief Executive Officer & Co-Founder, Sensible Micro Corporation, said:
Defense and aerospace customers are increasingly focused on battery sourcing, supply continuity and long-term availability.
”By pairing ALE’s U.S.-manufactured cell technologies with Sensible Micro’s stocking and distribution capabilities, we can help customers evaluate options and plan for ongoing production.”

, Founder & President, American Lithium Energy, said:
Our partnership with Sensible Micro expands access to ALE’s U.S.-manufactured lithium-ion technologies.

title: AI Workloads Hit by Power-Quality Issues at Data Centers
content:
Electrical problems are constraining AI deployments at US data centers, with nearly a third of respondents to a Fluke survey saying power-quality issues have reduced their ability to deploy or operate high-density AI and GPU workloads.
The survey, which polled 500 data center operators and professionals across the United States, suggests facilities are facing internal infrastructure constraints alongside the broader
struggle to secure electricity
“The biggest risk is whether a data center’s internal infrastructure can reliably distribute and support that power at scale,” Michael Stuart, senior manager and technical fellow at Fluke, told
Data Center Knowledge.
Power, Cooling, and Cabling Failures Create Risks
About three-quarters of respondents (76%) reported experiencing electrical or power-system issues. Separately, 79% said power-quality problems had contributed over the past year to delays, service disruptions, unplanned downtime, or serious near-misses.
Related:
Rethinking High-Voltage Commissioning for AI Data Centers
The figure groups operational failures together with incidents that did not result in an outage. It does not mean nearly four in five respondents experienced downtime.
Stuart said weaknesses often emerge where power, cooling, and cabling systems intersect. Problems can include harmonics, voltage sags and swells, thermal hotspots, deteriorating cooling systems, and infrastructure connections that have not been adequately documented or verified.
“Since each data center is so complex and diverse, determining weaknesses within facilities should be done on a case-by-case basis,” he said.
Those conditions can limit the computing capacity a facility can support even after an operator has secured sufficient electricity.
“If electrical, mechanical, and network systems aren’t performing to specification, operators may be unable to fully utilize the capacity they’ve already secured from the grid,” he added.
Testing and Monitoring Before GPU Rollouts
For operators preparing to
install high-density GPU racks
, Stuart recommends measuring power quality as close as possible to the GPU loads along the electrical distribution chain.
The appropriate measurement points will vary by facility and may change during commissioning as actual load conditions become clearer. Electrical distribution and cooling also need to be evaluated together to establish whether they can sustain the intended workloads.
Related:
New Approaches to Data Center Power Procurement
“If measurements reveal that either system cannot reliably support the intended GPU workloads, operators should address those issues before proceeding with deployment,” Stuart said.
The survey also identified gaps in operators’ ability to detect developing problems. Some 78% of respondents said they lacked comprehensive, continuous, real-time visibility across critical electrical systems. Another 15% said electrical problems were identified only after performance degradation, equipment failure, or downtime had already occurred.
Stuart said operators should assess existing monitoring coverage to identify where additional visibility would most improve reliability. Potential areas include power distribution, backup power, batteries, and switchgear, although priorities will depend on each facility’s infrastructure and current monitoring capabilities.
Labor Shortages Add Pressure to Maintenance
Recruiting qualified electrical technicians
has become harder for 57% of respondents, adding pressure to the teams responsible for installing, testing, and maintaining infrastructure.
That hiring difficulty has not uniformly translated into slower expansion. Some 65% of respondents said skills shortages had not delayed infrastructure upgrades or new capacity.
Related:
AI’s Expansion Hits the Limits of Local Power
Still, Stuart said workforce constraints can contribute to localized delays, inconsistent installation practices, and additional work to correct problems or verify quality.
“Not every problem is visible during an initial inspection; some only surface once electrical systems are operational,” he said.
Stuart said qualified electricians should perform and validate the work, supported by testing and diagnostic tools to identify faults that may emerge after installation and help ensure long-term reliability.

title: Nvidia AI Surge Comes with $118 Billion in Guarantees
content:
Nvidia reported $107.6 billion in data center revenue Tuesday, up 110% from a year earlier, and disclosed up to $118 billion in financial guarantees tied to AI infrastructure projects. The guarantees put Nvidia on the hook for financing arrangements designed to help customers secure the land, power, and facilities needed to deploy its systems.
The impressive quarter comes on the heels of a startling scandal that led to CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and
dominated headlines
around the world. Huang
resigned
Nov. 12 after reports of multiple affairs, including one with a woman suspected by US intelligence officials of having ties to Chinese intelligence. CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while the board seeks a permanent successor.
The campaign to bring Huang back attracted prominent supporters, including Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and President Donald Trump. A public petition drew more than 180,000 signatures, including thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees. Huang said Tuesday he would be honored to return if the board decided it was in the company’s best interests.
Related:
Huang Resigns: Nvidia's AI Infrastructure Roadmap in Question
The board rejected that possibility during Tuesday’s earnings call. Chairman Harvey Jones said directors unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and did not intend to reinstate him. The board will consider internal and external candidates for a permanent CEO.
The leadership upheaval comes as Nvidia takes on a larger role in financing and securing the infrastructure needed to sustain its AI growth.
For data center operators, Nvidia’s guarantees address a constraint that comes before server deployment:
financing and building facilities
with enough power to support large AI workloads. Nvidia is helping customers bridge that gap while securing the components needed to manufacture its next generations of systems.
The largest guarantee supports SB Energy’s PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio. Nvidia is providing credit support for approximately 4.25 GW across nine buildings. The campus will host Nvidia infrastructure under 20-year leases to OpenAI, subject to limited exceptions.
As buildings come online, Nvidia’s guarantee exposure will build. Each guarantee takes effect only after its associated building is completed and ready for service. The first is expected in fiscal 2029. Exposure will reach a maximum of $105 billion and then decline over the lease terms as OpenAI makes payments. Nvidia said it had made no guarantee payments as of Oct. 25.
The $118 billion maximum gross exposure also includes $9.5 billion in power and systems credit support guarantees and $3.5 billion in land, power, and shell guarantees for neocloud providers.
Related:
AMD Launches Epyc SP7, Helion as AI Rack Demand Rises
Nvidia separately reported $32 billion in future commitments under neocloud agreements. Those commitments depend on providers securing financing, purchasing Nvidia infrastructure, and deploying and operating the computing capacity.
Stephen Sopko, practice lead for semiconductor and deep tech at HyperFrame Research, cautioned against treating the full guarantee figure as exposure to neocloud financing problems.
“Of $118 billion in guarantees, $105 billion backs land, power, and shell for one campus, PORTS-Pike, which is leased to OpenAI for 20 years. The neocloud commitments are $32 billion and only apply once the operator secures its own financing and the capacity is accepted,” he said.
Nvidia Locks in Supply Years Ahead
Nvidia’s supply commitments climbed to $390 billion at the end of the third quarter, up from $279 billion three months earlier. The company attributed most of the $111 billion increase to multiyear memory procurement.
The rest of the increase reflects deals across the manufacturing supply chain, including
new substrate agreements
with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics and packaging expansions at Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and Amkor Technology. Kinsus plans to increase advanced ABF substrate capacity dedicated to Nvidia by more than 3.5 times, with the additional capacity targeted for the third quarter of 2028. SPIL’s expansion runs through mid-2029.
Related:
Google Adds TPU 8tx, 8i Max for Enterprise AI
Nvidia is securing components years before deployment, putting pressure on manufacturing capacity used by competing AI chip programs. The agreements cover memory, substrates, and advanced packaging – components that require substantial capacity and long lead times.
“It’s no longer just leading-edge wafers. It’s memory, substrates, and packaging, and that capacity takes years to build,” Sopko said.
Nvidia also has manufacturing relationships with suppliers including IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics, and Unimicron Technology. The company’s Vera Rubin platform will draw on the same TSMC 3-nanometer, 5-nanometer, and CoWoS manufacturing base that the broader semiconductor industry depends on, Sopko said.
“Nvidia is locking in supply two to three generations ahead, which squeezes everyone else, including custom ASIC programs, for that same capacity,” he said.
Nvidia also reported $102 billion in combined cloud service agreements and data center lease commitments, up from $74 billion in the previous quarter. Those arrangements provide infrastructure for research and development, including chip engineering, product testing, and AI model development.
Vera Rubin Ramps as Power Limits Persist
Nvidia began volume shipments of Vera Rubin NVL72 systems during the quarter, calling it the fastest product ramp in company history. Racks are running at CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and Nebius, with systems expected soon at SpaceXSI.
Oracle Cloud Infrastructure announced general availability of Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs. Google Cloud also announced general availability of its Vera Rubin-powered A5X instances. Nvidia expanded its collaboration with Meta, which plans to deploy Vera Rubin systems, Vera CPUs, Spectrum-X networking, and BlueField-4 data processing units.
Nvidia reported that Vera Rubin delivered 10 times more tokens per watt than GB300 on the MLPerf Endpoints benchmark. The result measures performance under a specific test, not expected electricity savings across data center fleets.
“In power-capped sites, yes. Watts are the scarce input, so more tokens from the same grid allocation is real revenue capacity. But that 10x is an MLPerf result versus GB300, not a fleet average,” Sopko said.
He expects operators to use efficiency gains to run more workloads rather than reduce electricity consumption.
“They won’t bank the savings. They’ll spend them on bigger models and longer-running agents. Cost per token falls; total power demand doesn’t,” he said.
Nvidia Forecasts $130B in Fourth-Quarter Revenue
Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in total third-quarter revenue, up 103% year over year and 20% sequentially. Data center revenue reached $107.6 billion, up 110% year over year and 21% sequentially. Net income was $65.3 billion, compared with $31.9 billion a year earlier. GAAP diluted earnings per share were $2.70, up from $1.30.
Nvidia expects fourth-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%. The forecast assumes no data center compute revenue from China. The company expects fourth-quarter GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins between 71% and 72%, reflecting the initial Vera Rubin ramp.
Sopko said the guarantees reflect a constraint beyond the availability of chips: getting powered facilities financed and built.
“The bigger shift is that powered shells are now the bottleneck, and Nvidia is acting as a credit enhancer to get them built,” he said. “It has also said it will be selective as other capital sources mature.”

title: Rethinking High-Voltage Commissioning for AI Data Centers
content:
rapid global buildout
of digital infrastructure to support the artificial intelligence boom is reshaping the design, construction, and commissioning requirements of data center projects. As computing capacity grows and rack densities rise to unprecedented levels, facilities are increasingly demanding power supplies measured in the tens and hundreds of megawatts. For many developments, securing that capacity means moving beyond conventional distribution networks and, where possible, connecting directly to high-voltage (HV) transmission infrastructure.
Those connections can provide the capacity needed to support the next generation of AI facilities. They also significantly increase the complexity of the electrical environment. That raises both the difficulty and the risk for commissioning teams. Yet not every project fully acknowledges that the demands of HV data center commissioning extend well beyond conventional low-voltage (LV) certification and verification.
Related:
Speed Is the New Capacity: Why AI Infrastructure Needs a New Power Strategy
HV infrastructure must be treated as a specialist engineering discipline, with its own competencies, testing methodologies, safety procedures, and assurance requirements. Incorporating it into an existing data center commissioning scope without appropriate specialist oversight risks leaving critical elements of the project insufficiently verified.
The Changing Electrical Landscape
Traditionally, data centers have relied on utility supplies delivered through distribution networks, with transformers stepping voltage down before electricity reaches the facility’s LV infrastructure. From there,
uninterruptible power supplies
, switchgear, and distribution systems provide the conditioned power required by critical IT loads.
Now, the scale and nature of the AI boom are changing that equation.
As AI data center development trends toward gigawatt-scale demand, local distribution networks in some markets cannot support new projects without major upgrades. That has contributed to extended approval processes and multiyear delays for some projects. Direct connections to higher-voltage networks, including 66kV, 110kV, and 150kV systems, are becoming an increasingly compelling alternative.
However, connecting a data center directly to transmission infrastructure introduces additional complexity and cost. Substations,
power transformers
, HV cables, switchgear, protection systems, and utility interfaces all become integral parts of the critical power architecture. In many cases, some or all of those elements would have sat well outside the project boundary only a few years ago.
Related:
Powering Behind-The-Meter Power: Where LNG and Process Safety Meet Digital Resilience
HV Commissioning Requires Specialist Expertise
HV commissioning differs fundamentally from conventional LV commissioning in both its technical requirements and its safety implications.
At higher voltage levels, electrical hazards include arc flash, flashover, and fatal electric shock, even when personnel are exposed without direct contact with live conductors. The consequences of incorrect installation, protection settings, or switching procedures can be severe. Equipment failure during energization can damage expensive infrastructure, disrupt the wider electrical network, and cause significant project delays, in addition to the personal risk to teams working on the system.
HV commissioning is its own discipline, with its own standards, testing methodologies, and safety protocols. It is not simply an extension of LV commissioning. The stakes are higher, and developers need to assess a project’s HV commissioning requirements during project planning rather than treating them as an extension of the broader electrical commissioning program.
Related:
HV Commissioning from Installation to Verified Performance
A structured HV commissioning program should define the inspection, testing, and acceptance requirements for every major component, supported by detailed inspection and test plans.
The process begins with a comprehensive review of design documentation, equipment specifications, installation records, and manufacturer requirements. Site inspections then verify that equipment has been installed correctly, that connections and terminations are satisfactory, and that the installation reflects design intent.
Individual equipment testing forms a substantial part of the program:
Power transformers
require electrical testing to confirm insulation integrity, winding condition, and the correct operation of associated monitoring and protection devices.
HV cables and terminations
must be tested to verify insulation performance and installation integrity.
Switchgear and circuit breakers
need both mechanical and electrical verification, including checks of operating mechanisms, interlocks, contact resistance, and switching functionality. Any deficiencies identified during testing must be resolved and documented before the equipment progresses toward energization.
Protection-system verification
means relays must be checked against approved protection studies and settings schedules, with secondary injection testing used to verify relay operation.
Grid-interface testing
is particularly important because data center supply performance often depends on interactions among multiple systems delivered by different contractors and organizations.
Power-quality assessment
forms part of this broader assurance process as well. Voltage stability, harmonics, reactive power performance, and other relevant electrical characteristics must be evaluated against connection requirements and applicable standards.
All these testing and certification activities require early engagement and collaboration among developers, utilities, electrical designers, equipment manufacturers, and the specialist commissioning teams conducting the tests. When that coordination is lacking, it creates serious program risks.
It is also important to recognize that completing individual equipment tests does not automatically prove that the entire HV installation is ready for activation. Before energization, the commissioning team must confirm that all required inspections, tests, defect resolutions, and safety checks have been completed and appropriately authorized. That includes confirming protection settings, verifying switching schedules, checking grounding arrangements, and ensuring that the required permits, procedures, and personnel authorizations are in place.
Commissioning assurance should not end at the day-one handover. It needs to continue beyond energization. Performance monitoring, periodic inspection, protection-system verification, and planned maintenance all help preserve the integrity of the installation throughout its service life. That is especially important given the demands placed on HV systems and the consequences if something goes wrong.
Bringing HV Commissioning into the Project from Day One
One of the greatest risks in large-scale data center development is treating HV commissioning as a late-stage activity, introduced only when the substation and associated infrastructure are nearing completion.
For developers delivering increasingly power-intensive AI facilities, HV is both a solution and a new source of project risk. Bringing the right expertise into the project at the earliest possible stage is essential. The electrical infrastructure supplying the critical IT environment deserves the same level of scrutiny as the systems within the data hall itself.
As data center power requirements continue to grow, HV connections are likely to become an increasingly common feature of the digital infrastructure landscape. Successfully managing that shift will require a new layer of rigorous, specialist commissioning expertise that verifies every element of the power chain, from the transmission interface to the facility’s electrical distribution, before and after energization.
Recognizing HV commissioning as a dedicated discipline, rather than an extension of conventional LV assurance, is an important step toward meeting the demands of the AI boom safely, reliably, and on schedule.

title: Green Flexibility starts construction of 480 MWh battery portfolio in Germany - Energy Storage
content: Green Flexibility has launched construction of a large-scale battery storage project in Geestland/Bad Bederkesa, Germany. It said the facility, its first large-scale battery project in the German state of Lower Saxony, will have a power output of 10 MW and storage capacity of 25 MWh. Commercial operations are scheduled to begin in the second quarter of 2027. Green Flexibility plans to build six large-scale battery storage facilities in Lower Saxony, with a combined power output of 120 MW and storage capacity of 480 MWh. The company puts the total investment required at around €150 million. Lower Saxony’s Green Party energy minister, Christian Meyer, also attended the symbolic construction launch. As with its other projects in the state, Green Flexibility will use its self-developed REGIOlink concept, which it describes as a grid-neutral operating approach. Under the model, the battery responds not only to electricity market price signals but also adjusts its operation to meet the requirements of the regional grid. Green Flexibility said it had implemented a flexible connection agreement (FCA) with grid operator EWE Netz for all six projects in Lower Saxony. The company said the agreement would allow the batteries to operate economically while meeting regional grid requirements. Green Flexibility is also developing battery storage projects elsewhere in Germany. Its facility in Obergünzburg, in the Ostallgäu district of Bavaria, is largely complete. The system has a power output of 40 MW and storage capacity of 90 MWh. Shortly before its official commissioning, the company opened the facility to the public. Green Flexibility has invested around €35 million in the Obergünzburg project. It also built its own substation to connect the battery to the high-voltage grid operated by LEW Verteilnetz. The facility will also operate under the REGIOlink concept. title: Italy authorizes five standalone battery projects totaling 598 MW - Energy Storage
content: Italy’s Ministry of Environment and Energy Security (MASE) has issued five single authorizations for standalone BESS developed by Zhero Group, Opdenergy, Neoen, Reden and Chiari Srl, with a combined power output of 598.3 MW. The largest project is Atena Storage, for which Milan-based Atena Storage Srl, a subsidiary of Dutch group Zhero Group, secured authorization under Decree 341/2026. The 200 MW facility will be built in Selargius, in the province of Cagliari, Sardinia. Construction is scheduled to take 12 months. In Lombardy, Milan-based Chiari Srl received authorization under Decree 339/2026 to build a 151.2 MW BESS in the municipality of Chiari, in the province of Brescia. The project comprises 200 battery containers, each with 3.44 MWh of capacity, for a total of approximately 688 MWh. This equates to slightly more than four and a half hours of storage. Construction is expected to take 10 months. In Brindisi, Spanish developer Opdenergy, controlled by investment fund Antin Infrastructure Partners, secured authorization through its subsidiary Opdenergy Italia 2 Srl for the 99.165 MW Greentuke BESS. Decree 340/2026 covers the project, which will be divided into northern and southern sections. Construction is scheduled to take around 600 days. In Campania, French developer Neoen, controlled by Brookfield, obtained authorization through its subsidiary Neoen Renewables Italia Srl for a 97.92 MW BESS in Benevento. Decree 342/2026 sets out the approval. Construction is expected to take around nine months, the shortest schedule among the five projects. Finally, Electricity Time Shifting 3 Srl, a subsidiary of Reden, received authorization under Decree 338/2026 for a 50 MW BESS in San Severo, in the province of Foggia. Construction is expected to take around 24 months. The project appears to be a twin of the 50 MW facility authorized on Oct. 30 for Electricity Time Shifting 4 Srl in the same municipality. On Nov. 2, the ministry had authorized Miura Storage’s 280 MW project in Tuscania, in the province of Viterbo, and the 200 MW Bess Castegnero project developed by BESS Pieve Srl in the municipality of Castegnero Nanto, in the province of Vicenza. title: Japanese trial taps home EV charging for demand-response flexibility - Energy Storage
content: Panasonic Electric Works and electricity retailer TG Octopus Energy said a three-month trial in Tokyo showed that home EV charging can be shifted automatically in line with electricity market prices with few user overrides. The trial ran from March to May 2026 at 30 detached homes with battery-electric or plug-in hybrid vehicles. It linked TG Octopus Energy’s EV Octopus tariff with Panasonic Electric Works’ home EV charging app and an internet-connected 200 V charging outlet, which uses a control module made by Nature Inc. Charging was controlled remotely in 30-minute blocks, under schedules based on market prices and other factors. Participants accepted 98.7% of the 30-minute control instructions, the companies said. Measured by actual charging volume, 83.6% of the electricity charged was delivered within the assigned schedule. EV charging accounted for about 30% of the households’ total electricity use. Without remote control, charging tended to cluster at particular times of day. With it, charging moved to periods when market prices were relatively low. Some users overrode the system manually or changed their schedules, which the companies said had a limited effect. The amount of load available to shift varied because vehicles were sometimes away from home or already fully charged. The companies did not disclose any cost savings, volumes shifted or reductions in peak demand, although lowering electricity costs and shifting peaks were stated aims when the trial was announced in November 2025. That announcement targeted 100 households. The results cover 30, and the companies did not explain the difference. In a post-trial survey, 70% of the 30 respondents said they would keep using the service if it were formally launched. The partners said they will consider a phased commercial rollout based on the trial data and user feedback, without giving a timeline. Japanese utilities and retailers have been testing other household devices as grid resources. Tohoku Electric Power has used Sharp’s PV-linked home batteries for grid balancing , and Kyushu Electric Power launched a residential battery demand response pilot with Sharp in March. Osaka Gas began selling Kyocera home batteries that it plans to pool for Japan’s balancing and capacity markets in July. Panasonic has separately been testing an energy management system that combines solar, heat pumps and batteries . title: UK battery developer begins building 125 MWh system in Germany - Energy Storage
content: Battery storage developer Voltwise has started construction of a 56 MW/125 MWh battery in Leopoldshöhe, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. The system will use Fluence’s modular, AC-based Smartstack battery platform and can discharge at full power for slightly more than two hours. It will connect to Bielefelder Netz’s Bechterdissen substation at 110 kV. The site covers about 4,000 square meters and includes a fire-water tank and a 4-meter noise barrier. Vattenfall, which contracted Fluence last month to supply a 1 GWh battery in Germany , is a project partner, though Voltwise did not specify its role. Santander CIB acted as arranger, lender and hedging counterparty for the financing, the terms of which were not disclosed. Thorsten Klöpper, managing director for Germany at Voltwise, said the project marks a decisive step in building the company’s German business and that it plans to develop and build more storage sites in the country. Voltwise, founded in 2023 and owned by Sandbrook Capital, is developing further projects in the United Kingdom and Germany. The company has called for a reliable long-term framework to support the economics and bankability of market-driven storage, having urged Germany last year to extend the grid fee exemption for large batteries to 2034 . Germany’s Federal Network Agency (Bundesnetzagentur) said in May that batteries commissioned before Aug. 4, 2029, will keep their grid fee exemption . The Leopoldshöhe system would fall within that window if commissioned as planned in the second half of 2027. title: e-Storage to supply battery energy storage system for X-Elio projects totaling 1.43 GWh - Energy Storage
content: Brookfield Renewable-owned Spanish clean energy developer X-Elio has selected Ontario-based Canadian Solar subsidiary e-Storage to supply five projects with its battery energy storage systems (BESS) for projects across the US and Australia. Across a total supply agreement of 590 MW / 1.43 GWh (DC) , the split will be across four in Texas, US, and one is in New South Wales, Australia. Backed by a 22-year long-term service agreement (LTSA), all five projects will use e-Storage’s SolBank 3.0 battery system, power conversion systems (PCS) and plant controls manufactured at Canadian Solar facilities. One specific project, a 200 MW / 482 MWh site in Texas, will run on EQ-S, e-Storage’s own energy management system developed in North America. The SolBank 3.0 has a nominal capacity of 5 MWh, and supports 2-hour and 4-hour configurations with a rated power output of between 1.2 MW and 2.35 MW. All five projects are expected to reach commercial operation in the next two years. Other X-Elio projects are active in Australia, and include the 300 MW / 1,200 MWh solar-plus-storage project near Goulburn, located approximatley 200 kilometres southeast of Sydney, and two in the Central West Orana Renewable Energy Zone ( CWO REZ ) that includes the under-construction Forest Glen Hybrid 90 MW solar, 90 MW / 180 MWh BESS project 16 kilometres west of Dubbo , and the Puggoon 264 MW solar farm and 110 MW / 440 MWh BESS near Mudgee. Signed at RE+ 2026 in the US, the agreements follow a 6 October 2026 announcement by e-Storage, which had entered an agreement to supply and commission a 100 MW / 200 MWh BESS for OX2’s Muswellbrook Solar Farm and Battery, also in NSW. title: Aptera (SEV) completes its first customer solar EV — for its top crowdfunder
content:
Aptera (SEV) has finished building its first solar electric vehicle for a paying customer. It’s going to Martin Hartono, the startup’s No. 1 “Accelerator” investor, and it’s being exported out of the US.
It’s a real milestone for a company that has pushed back its delivery dates since 2022. And it comes a week after Aptera reported $9.2 million in cash against the roughly $25 million it says it needs to start series production.
A matte black Aptera for Accelerator #1
Aptera announced today from its Carlsbad, California headquarters that it completed what it calls its first production solar electric vehicle. The car is finished in “Noir,” a matte black exterior, and was built for Accelerator #1.
Accelerators are investors from Aptera’s community funding program, where delivery priority goes to whoever invests the most. So the first customer car went to the biggest check.
Hartono is the CEO of GDP Venture, the Jakarta-based venture arm of Indonesia’s Djarum Group. Aptera didn’t say which country the car is going to, what he paid for it, or when it will actually be handed over.
In the release, Hartono said Aptera is a fit for people who want to “minimize their energy consumption without compromising the ability to travel long distances.” Co-CEO Chris Anthony called it “the moment our team has worked toward for years” and said the company is working to finish more vehicles for early customers as soon as possible.
No number was given for how many more.
Where Aptera actually stands
The timing is interesting. Just seven weeks ago, Aptera cut its estimated cost to start production to about $25 million, down from $40 to $45 million, and said the first 40 production vehicles would start building by the end of 2026, with customer deliveries in early 2027 “subject to financing.”
Its Q3 report last week didn’t change that picture much. Aptera ended September with $9.2 million in cash, and $4.1 million of that is refundable reservation fees. It lost $14 million in the quarter, and its own filing says substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern “has not been alleviated.”
On November 10, it priced a $6 million registered direct offering at $1.75 per share. SEV closed at $1.67 on Tuesday, with a 52-week high of $7.
The solar side of the pitch holds up better. In August, TÜV Rheinland measured 4.23 to 4.75 kWh per day going into the battery from the car’s integrated panels in Carlsbad, which works out to roughly 40 miles of daily driving. But that conversion relies on Aptera’s 100 Wh/mile efficiency target, and today’s release itself notes that figure isn’t yet confirmed for production vehicles.
The release’s risk factors are also worth reading. They list export, import, certification and registration requirements, state dealer licensing, single-source suppliers, and whether reservations will convert into binding orders. Shipping car No. 1 to an investor overseas sidesteps most of those for now.
Electrek’s Take
Credit where it’s due. Aptera has a finished car built to a customer’s spec, which is more than Lightyear or Sono Motors ever got to before they ran out of money. We’ve followed this company since it came back in 2019, and plenty of people (us included, at times) didn’t think we’d see this day.
Top comment by GreenBoomerang
A positive achievement, but the question remains: Is this essentially a hand-built prototype and a token delivery to one very rich customer, or is it the first of many more vehicles that will roll off an assembly line for regular people over the next couple months?
But I have to be honest, this looks more symbolic than like the start of a production ramp. This is a single vehicle, built before Aptera has raised the money it says it needs for series production, and it went to the person who put the most money into the company. That’s a thank-you and a good press release ahead of what will likely be another raise. It doesn’t tell us much about Aptera’s ability to build cars at a cost that works.
The real test is still the first 40 cars, and whether they reach regular reservation holders in the US. Aptera says it needs about $25 million to get there. It has $9.2 million, $4.1 million of which customers can ask back for, and it’s raising money at under $2 a share, which means a lot of dilution for every dollar.
We want this to work. Ultra-efficient cars are the only way vehicle-integrated solar makes sense, and Aptera is the last serious attempt standing. So can it fund those 40 cars before the cash runs out?
If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, even if your car doesn’t have panels built into the body like the Aptera. title: Elon Musk announces another Tesla vehicle no one asked for
content:
Elon Musk says Tesla plans to build a version of the Model Y with no steering wheel and no pedals, a driverless people-mover he describes as “good for transporting groups of 6 or 7 people.”
It’s yet another vehicle nobody asked for, from a company that ended Model S and Model X production this year and is about to end the Cybertruck. And the data says very few car buyers want a car they can’t drive.
What Musk said
Musk made the comments on stage at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday.
He pitched it as the answer to the Cybercab only carrying two people. “We still need autonomous vehicles if you’ve got 4 or 6, or a whole family,” Musk said, before adding that Tesla plans “an autonomous version of the Model Y that won’t have steering wheels or pedals.”
There was no timeline, no price and no word on where it would be built.
Six or seven seats points straight at the Model Y L, the stretched three-row Model Y that Tesla launched in the US in July for $61,990, or the regular Model Y with the $2,500 seven-seat option Tesla brought back in January.
The Model Y L wasn’t supposed to need to exist
Here’s the funny part. When Tesla launched the Model Y L in China in August 2025, Musk said it might never come to the US, “given the advent of self-driving in America.”
The idea was that autonomy would make a bigger family car pointless. Less than a year later, Tesla was building the Model Y L at Giga Texas and selling it at the top of the Model Y lineup.
Now Musk wants a driverless version of that same car. So families still need a big vehicle, self-driving or not. That’s what we said in 2025.
Tesla’s Model Y robotaxis already have a steering wheel
The robotaxi argument doesn’t hold up either. Tesla’s Robotaxi fleet is mostly Model Ys, and those cars have a steering wheel and pedals.
The wheel isn’t what’s stopping them from driving themselves. Removing it mostly makes the car useless outside Tesla’s geofences.
We’ve already seen what that looks like. Tesla opened personal Cybercab orders last week at $29,990, but the car only works inside Robotaxi service areas and requires a $299 per month subscription to operate at all.
There’s also the regulatory mess. Tesla self-certified the Cybercab as compliant with federal safety standards even though FMVSS 135 calls for a foot-operated service brake, and NHTSA responded with a Special Order in September. Zoox took the slower route and got a Part 555 exemption, which caps it at 2,500 vehicles a year. A second vehicle with no controls means a second round of that fight.
Buyers don’t want cars without controls
Cox Automotive’s 2026 Autonomous Vehicle Study asked US consumers which level of autonomy they’d find most appealing in a vehicle they own. Only 10% picked fully driverless Level 5, down from 17% when Cox first asked in 2016.
The most popular choice was Level 4 at 28%: full autonomy, but with the option for a human to drive. And only 38% said they’d feel safe in a Level 5 vehicle, compared to 87% for a modern car with basic driver aids.
So after a decade of exposure to self-driving tech, interest in a car with no controls went down, not up.
Electrek’s Take
Tesla already makes the Model Y. It already makes a six-seat Model Y. Just make the Model Y.
In 2016, Musk’s Master Plan Part Deux promised to “expand the electric vehicle product line to address all major segments.” Ten years later, once the Cybertruck ends next summer, Tesla’s consumer lineup is the Model 3 and Model Y. That’s it. No affordable car (Musk called a non-robotaxi $25,000 Tesla “pointless” in 2024), no compact crossover, no minivan, no midsize pickup.
Top comment by Doug T
Teslafsdtracker is the only real source of Tesla ADS/ADAS capability.
It shows a safety critical intervention is needed every 2000 miles. That is less than 1% of whats needed to remove a human from the real time loop. Hence Tesla's hiding of intervention data and operational parameters, and the control centers where humans watch real time video feeds and initiate interventions when needed.
Tesla L4 is all smoke and mirrors. All they have is a L2 system driving in geo restricted zones with driver oversight shifted from the front seat to a control center
Every time there’s a gap in Tesla’s lineup, Musk gives the same answer: autonomy will fill it. The Model Y L was going to be unnecessary. The cheap car was pointless. The Model S and X made way for Optimus, and the Cybertruck for the Cybercab.
But Tesla’s own robotaxi fleet proves you don’t need to remove the steering wheel to run a robotaxi. Keeping it costs Tesla almost nothing and keeps the car useful for the roughly 90% of buyers who still want the option to drive. Taking it out only adds a federal compliance fight and shrinks the market to people who live inside a geofence.
If Tesla wants to sell more cars, it should build cars people are asking for. Who exactly is asking for this one?

title: Porsche’s newest electric car is a tiny 50 mph replica of a legendary racer
content:
Micah Toll
| Nov 19 2026 - 3:36 am PT
Porsche’s latest electric vehicle isn’t a new Taycan or Macan EV. In fact, it’s not even a full-sized car. Instead, the German automaker has teamed up with British luxury miniature car builder Hedley Studios to create an 80%-scale electric replica of one of Porsche’s most iconic racing cars, the legendary 550 Spyder.
Known as the Porsche 550 J, the pint-sized electric sports car will make its public debut at the Icons of Porsche festival in Dubai on November 21-22, celebrating 75 years of Porsche motorsport.
Hedley Studios
sounds familiar, that’s because we’ve covered the company before, back when it was known as The Little Car Company. Among its more entertaining projects was
a life-sized recreation of the famous Japanese Tamiya Wild One RC dune buggy
, turning a childhood remote-controlled favorite into an actual drivable electric vehicle. We’ve also covered the company’s ultra-luxurious miniature electric cars, including its
stunning Bentley Blower recreation
Now the company has turned its attention to Porsche, and the result is perhaps its most impressive miniature EV yet.
There’s something I love about miniature electric cars, combining the fun of four-wheels with the right-sized (or pint-sized) magic of mini-mobility.
The Porsche 550 J is based on the original 550 Spyder, Porsche’s first purpose-built racing sports car, which debuted in 1953 and went on to become a motorsport legend.
Despite being scaled down to 80% of the original’s dimensions, the new electric version still seats two adults. It weighs just 350 kg (772 lb), thanks partly to its lightweight tubular steel spaceframe and hand-formed carbon fiber bodywork.
The standard version features an 8 kW (11 hp) electric motor operating on a 48V system, providing a top speed of 40 mph (65 km/h) and a range of up to 30 miles (50 km).
For those who want a bit more performance from their miniature Porsche, an optional RS Pack doubles the power to 16 kW (21 hp), increases the top speed to 50 mph (80 km/h), and extends the range to 50 miles (80 km) thanks to additional batteries. The upgrade also includes drilled disc brakes and adjustable suspension.
The attention to detail goes well beyond the exterior. The car features Brembo brakes, Bilstein suspension, Continental tires, and even a wood-rimmed Nardi steering wheel, just like the original. The classic dashboard retains its three-dial layout, though the fuel gauge has been replaced with a battery meter and the original choke lever now serves as a drive mode selector.
Even the charging port is cleverly hidden beneath the chrome fuel filler cap.
The project was developed in close collaboration with Porsche over six years, with Hedley Studios gaining access to original engineering drawings, archival materials, and historic vehicles in Porsche’s museum.
Only 250 examples will be produced, with buyers able to choose historic racing liveries or custom paint finishes, including colors matching their full-sized Porsches.
Of course, this level of craftsmanship doesn’t come cheap.
Prices start at £69,500
(approximately US $91,000), before taxes and options. Orders are already open through Porsche dealers and Hedley Studios, with deliveries expected to begin in spring 2027.
That’s a lot of money for a car that’s only 80% there, but then again, this isn’t really meant to be practical transportation. It’s a collector’s piece that just happens to be electric, drivable, and capable of hitting 50 mph. When there are only 250 of these being built, the £70k price is really just the entry ticket to a special, ultra-luxury club of electric mini-Porsches.
And if you ask me, that sounds like a pretty fun combination. I don’t think I’ll ever be in the market for one of these personally, but I’d sure love to be friends with someone who is!

title: The Volkswagen ID. Buzz Beach is an electric van built for camping, but it's not cheap
content:
Volkswagen
ID. Buzz
Peter Johnson
| Nov 19 2026 - 7:51 am PT
Volkswagen introduced the
ID. Buzz Beach,
a fun spin on its electric van that’s built for camping and overnight stays. However, it won’t be cheap, starting at over $70,000.
Meet the Volkswagen ID. Buzz Beach
Volkswagen’s original microbus became a cultural icon thanks to its open, customizable interior, making it perfect for large families, road trips, camping, and, of course, music festivals.
The ID. Buzz brings the classic Type 2 microbus into the electric era with a retro-new style, modern tech, and a flexible, spacious cabin.
Building on its reputation as a symbol of freedom and adventure, Volkswagen is adding a new member to the electric people mover lineup.
The new ID. Buzz Beach “brings adventure into the electric age,” Volkswagen said after introducing the new variant on Thursday. Designed for camping, longer road trips, and overnight stays, the electric van will be available in 5-, 6-, and 7-seat configurations.
Volkswagen said it sleeps two comfortably with a removable bed frame and a custom-fitting folding mattress.
Volkswagen ID. Buzz Beach fold-out mattress (Source: VW UK)
The mattress is a decent size at about 6.5 feet long by 4 feet wide (2.0m x 1.2m), roughly the size of an average small double bed.
In the 5-seat configuration, the bed frame tucks away in the trunk, while in the 6- and 7-seat layouts, it’s stored vertically behind the third row of seats.
For camping and other longer stays, Volkswagen added a new Overnight mode that uses the vehicle’s battery to provide up to 48 hours of continuous, off-grid climate control. The new mode can be accessed on the center touchscreen.
It also includes blackout curtains throughout the cabin and ventilation grilles on the front side windows.
The ID. Buzz Beach offers vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities. A 230V power socket adaptor comes standard, letting you power an e-bike, charge a smartphone, run camping equipment, or power other external electronic devices. A camping connector is available as an added option.
To top it off, Volkswagen added a hidden foldable table and chairs set that can be tucked away without taking up internal space.
Volkswagen will open orders for the new ID. Buzz Beach in the UK later this month, starting at £53,955 (excluding VAT), or about $71,000. Including VAT and OTR costs, it will start at £65,837, or roughly $86,500.
What about those in the US? VW introduced the 2027 ID. Buzz with
a new Tourer model
that was essentially the same as the Beach variant in the UK, with a fold-out mattress, Overnight mode, blackout curtains, and a table and chairs set.
However, VW told its US dealers in September that it would be
delaying the ID. Buzz’s return
until the 2028 model year.
The 2025 Volkswagen ID. Buzz started at about $60,000 in the US, which is one of the biggest reasons it failed to catch on with buyers. The original VW microbus was an affordable people mover.
A custom camper variant would likely cost more than $70,000. Would you pay $70,000 or more for Volkswagen’s electric camper van?

content:

11月17日，亿纬锂能在北美RE+2026展会上发布AIDC全场景储能解决方案，产品涉及储能、调频及备用电源等环节。
此次发布的产品包括20尺5MWh 1P高功率储能系统、调频专用电芯、Mr.Giant 3.0储能系统、超高倍率BBU+CBU、磐盾6C/10C备电柜以及混合超级电容器，共六款产品，分别应用于源网侧、配电侧和机架侧。

title: 光储一体不是简单拼装，晶澳为何强调“同源”？
content:
光储一体是行业公认的方向，但从概念到落地，始终少有一份让人满意的答卷。
行业擅长把单品做到极致，却不擅长让它们作为系统彼此成就。客户需要的从来不是一件高效率组件加一台大容量储能的简单叠加，
而是一套更确定、更省心的能源系统
真正的挑战发生在设备之间：时序错配、出力波动，以及多供应商、异构协议带来的策略割裂、联调低效与责任难辨。当负荷、光照、电价不断变化，谁来动态决定充放电的时机？出了问题，又该找谁？
面对这些追问，11月16日的JA光储同源生态发布会上，晶澳给出的答案，落在了
答案写在研发基因里
在晶澳，一直流传着
“量产一代、储备一代、研发一代”
——这是光储同源的基因来源。三个“一代”如同彼此咬合的齿轮，各自承担不同的协同任务：
聚焦当下产品的成熟与兑现，让稳定交付中的每一次优化，都转化为光储协同价值；
着眼下一轮升级，通过性能、工艺与可靠性验证，提前考察光储之间的适配与能量流转；
面向未来，围绕新原理、新材料、新结构、新工艺探索，用真实场景积累的经验寻找更具协同性的技术方向。
三个层次彼此衔接，让光伏与储能从设计之初就为同一个系统结果负责，也为完整的产品矩阵和长期客户价值打下基础。系统如何高效运行、绿色价值如何衡量、长期服务由谁负责——这三个问题的答案，都藏在这套基因里。
让光储协同走进多元场景
研发协同的优势，最终要由产品承接、在场景中兑现。晶澳整合光伏、储能与智慧能源，构建面向多元应用场景的光储产品矩阵，并以此为基础
推出八大光储融合系统解决方案，覆盖AIDC、集中式、工商业、农业/农场、光储充一体化、并/离网微电网、矿山及户用。
八大方案并非统一配置的简单复制，而是依据不同场景的负荷特征、供电要求与资源条件，匹配相应的产品组合与控制策略。
以并/离网微电网为例，偏远地区、海岛等场景常面临电网薄弱甚至无电可用的问题，传统方案依赖柴油发电，燃料成本高，供电保障也面临挑战。对此，晶澳采用光储柴一体化方案：光伏作为成本最低的能量主力，尽可能压低昂贵的柴油用量；电压与频率的稳定性，交由柴发与构网储能支撑。落到产品上，以5MWh微网集装箱储能系统为核心，搭配晶澳DeepBlue系列组件；PCS支持多机并联最大3MW及PQ/VF等多种控制模式，可在20毫秒内与柴发联动切换，并具备黑启动能力，实现自主复电与系统能量重建。多能互补之下，供电更稳定、柴油依赖更低、运维更高效，这正是客户价值的直接兑现。
其他场景则围绕高可靠供电、绿电消纳、用能优化和灵活配置等不同需求，形成各有侧重的产品组合与运行策略，让光储系统真正适配不同客户的实际用能场景。
从系统协同到价值兑现
场景适配解决了系统如何部署，长期价值的兑现，还需要贯穿项目全周期的协同保障。为此，晶澳进一步构建调控同源、绿电同源、服务同源三大能力：
调控同源，让光与储协同运行。
通过光伏、储能与EMS的深度适配和统一调度，让发电、储能与负荷协同运行，提升系统运行效率。
绿电同源，让绿色价值可量化
。统筹光储运行数据与减排测算，让绿电利用效果和绿色价值有据可循、可追溯。
服务同源，让项目全周期有人承接。
贯通前期方案配置、项目交付与投运服务，减少客户多方对接，让项目全周期获得持续支持。
从场景配置到系统运行，再到绿色价值管理与长期服务，三个同源共同保障光储方案发挥综合价值。
落到收益上，数据同样直观：
一个典型1MW工商业项目，配储后综合IRR由7.15%提升至9.76%，回收期由11.13年缩短至7.98年（具体随项目条件而定）。从西西里岛渔场100%就地消纳，到西北算力中心柔性适配，从非洲地区矿山削减柴油依赖，再到内蒙古光伏治沙把受限电量转化为收益，光储同源正从理念走向不同地区的真实场景。
让同源价值经得起验证
真实场景之外，价值还需要一套可测量、可验证的体系来支撑。TÜV莱茵将与晶澳联合制定白皮书，围绕光储系统协同、全生命周期可靠性及资产价值等维度展开研究；同时，共同推动电站综合评价标准，以六维26项、四维分级让不同电站横向可比。从组件、储能系统到整座电站，第三方验证将把“光储同源”从理念变成一套可测量、可追溯的价值体系。
三代研发机制夯实技术协同基础，完整产品矩阵支撑多元配置，八大场景方案回应差异化需求，三个同源构筑价值护航，再到第三方验证与真实项目实践——晶澳构建的，是一条从技术研发到价值兑现的完整路径。
光储一体的标准答案，不是光伏与储能的简单相加，而是让每一个环节从源头开始协同。这份答卷，经得起验证，也经得起时间。以同源之力，促光储共生。晶澳将持续推动光储融合走向更深层次，让每一度绿电在需要的时候发挥更大价值。

title: 宁德时代、欣旺达、阿特斯等5企储能业务再传新动态
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，近日，储能产业接连落地多项订单与合作。海外市场方面，阿特斯储能获美澳1.43GWh储能订单，欣旺达签署5GWh储能合作备忘录，昱能科技签约斯里兰卡10MWh工商储项目；国内方面，卫蓝新能源与煜邦电力围绕固态电池储能达成合作，宁德时代则与斯莱克敲定电池壳体“厂边厂”供应协议。
欣旺达与Acelerex签署5GWh储能合作协议
当地时间11月17日，在美国拉斯维加斯举行的RE+2026展会上，欣旺达与能源自动化及控制技术企业Acelerex正式签署合作备忘录。根据协议，双方计划在未来五年内，围绕大型电力储能、工商业储能及微电网等应用场景，累计推进5GWh储能项目部署。同期，双方还签署了首个合作项目合同。
根据合作规划，双方将整合欣旺达在储能电池、电池管理系统（BMS）及系统集成领域的技术积累，以及Acelerex REX™平台在能源管理、电站控制、数据采集与监控（SCADA）及微电网控制方面的能力，推动储能硬件与智能控制系统融合。
在微电网应用方面，双方将重点关注印度、非洲、南美洲及加勒比地区市场，探索模块化微电网解决方案。其中，联合方案将采用欣旺达261kWh液冷一体式储能系统，结合Acelerex智能控制平台，实现储能设备与光伏、风电等分布式电源的协同运行，以满足不同规模微电网项目的建设与运营需求。
阿特斯储能获1.43GWh储能订单
近日，阿特斯储能（e-STORAGE）与全球可再生能源开发商X-ELIO签署合作协议，将为其位于美国得克萨斯州和澳大利亚新南威尔士州的五个储能项目提供总规模达590MW/1.43GWh的电池储能系统（BESS），并提供为期22年的长期服务协议（LTSA）支持。上述项目预计于2027年至2028年陆续投入商业运营。
根据协议，五个项目均将采用阿特斯储能SolBank 3.0储能系统，该方案集成由阿特斯自主生产制造的储能电芯、储能变流器（PCS）及电站控制系统。项目投运后，将通过储能系统的削峰填谷和电力调节能力，将日间富余的太阳能电力转移至晚间用电高峰时段，为当地电网提供电力支撑。
卫蓝新能源与煜邦电力签署储能战略合作协议
11月17日，卫蓝新能源与煜邦电力在北京签署战略合作协议，双方将围绕新型储能技术研发、电芯应用、生产集成及国内外市场拓展等领域开展合作。
根据协议，双方将结合各自在混合固液电池、全固态电池研发制造、储能系统集成及构网型控制等方面的技术积累，推进储能电芯、储能变流器（PCS）、能量管理系统（EMS）及协调控制设备等技术与产品应用。
在产业协同方面，双方拟推动卫蓝新能源储能电芯在煜邦电力储能系统集成中的应用，面向电网、矿业及海外市场探索合作，并依托煜邦电力的储能电池PACK生产线及系统集成能力推进生产合作。同时，双方还将结合各自渠道和业务优势，开展重点区域储能项目开发、系统集成及新产品应用等合作。
昱能科技签约斯里兰卡10MWh工商储项目
近日，昱能科技与斯里兰卡上市集团E.B.Creasy&Co.PLC正式签署战略合作协议，双方将围绕工商业储能系统、光储融合等领域开展合作，共同拓展斯里兰卡及南亚储能市场。
根据合作安排，昱能科技近期将向当地交付10MWh储能电站系统，涉及组串式液冷储能系统APstorage 261L等核心设备。
未来，E.B.Creasy将作为昱能科技在斯里兰卡的工商业储能领域战略合作伙伴，面向斯里兰卡及南亚市场持续提供本地化渠道分销、项目拓展等配套服务。
宁德时代与斯莱克签署电池壳配套供应协议
11月17日，苏州斯莱克精密设备股份有限公司公告称，其控股子公司分宜和骏新能源科技有限公司近日与宁德时代签署《厂边厂配套供应协议》，将在江苏苏州、福建泉州两地建设生产基地，为宁德时代提供电池壳体等配套产品。
根据协议，苏州、泉州生产基地的产能将优先供应宁德时代。若宁德时代相关基地订单不足，还将分别向分宜和骏下达溧阳工厂、厦门工厂的订单，以提高其产能利用率。协议有效期至2028年12月31日，具体供应价格及合作内容以双方后续签订的订单或采购合同为准。

title: 航天机电：拟转让土耳其光伏15%股权项目
content:
11月18日，航天机电发布公告称，公司下属卢森堡控股公司拟转让其持有的航天光伏(土耳其)股份有限公司15%股权。转让完成后，公司不再持有土耳其光伏股权。本次交易尚处于前期启动阶段，交易对方尚不明确，是否构成关联交易无法确定。
对于出售原因，公司表示，航天光伏（土耳其）经营承压，2025年营收较前年大幅下滑85%，致亏损8500万元。截至2026年9月30日，土耳其光伏资产总额为3.35亿元，负债为4.14亿元，净资产为-7,891 万元，资产负债率为124%。为进一步降低境外经营风险，卢森堡控股拟转让其持有的土耳其光伏15%股权。
