title: Can AI Really Engineer Its Way to Superintelligence?
content:
Yet trying for it may still be disastrous
12 min read
McKibillo
Many people were caught
off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon
announced
his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science,
, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently
told CNN
, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”
These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as
recursive self-improvement
(RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than
artificial general intelligence
(AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.
These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.
Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.
I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an
annotated bibliography
of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.
Objection #1: Recursive Self-Improvement Is Speculative
RSI is an old concept. In
a 1965 paper
, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the
Extropians
, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as
Eliezer Yudkowsky
(who later founded the rationalism movement) and
Nick Bostrom
(who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).
Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled
“When AI Builds Itself,”
Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of
developing an automated researcher
But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for
, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After
, however, continued scaling began
yielding diminishing returns
. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from
reinforcement learning
are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.
Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and
mathematics
, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher
François Chollet
recently
hypothesized
, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.
Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of
backpropagation
, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The
influential 1986 paper
on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.
An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent
research
led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.
Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or
data centers
that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.
Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.
Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be Computable
There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.
We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.
But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937
, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.
We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.
A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge
pointed out
, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.
At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.
Objection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)
Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The
was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.
To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the
system card
for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”
Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to
hack into
Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a
cybersecurity
evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion
The Hill
articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”
These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.
Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.
In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.
I believe that pursuing RSI
is an act of
negligence
The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.
Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.
The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.
The Dangers of Chasing Superintelligence
Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after
multiple warnings
that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.
This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have
described
RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from
futurism
and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.
What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”

title: Human Posts Beat AI Slop
content:
This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!In one year, the number of developers working for themselves has more than doubled. Stack Overflow’s annual survey of more than 30,000 developers showed that freelancers and sole proprietors went from about four percent of respondents to ten percent.
You can read this as a polite way of saying, “I got laid off and I’m figuring it out.” But I don’t think the number can be ignored.
Whatever the case, it leads to the question I keep hearing from engineers right now: What can I do to stay employable? One tried and true answer is to build a personal brand.
But what does that actually mean?
Over the last six years, I grew my LinkedIn audience to 40,000 followers and YouTube channel to 10,000. I don’t think you should aim to be famous (unless you’re into that sort of thing) but I do think it’s worth exploring how to be discoverable online in 2027 if you want an advantage in the open market.
A personal brand is a discovery mechanism
Strip away the follower counts and the AI-generated thought leadership, and a personal brand comes down to a simple question: Does the internet know who you are? When a hiring manager goes looking for someone who has your skills, do you show up?
You can think of this as search engine optimization for your employability. Recruiters have mostly consolidated around a single platform to find people: LinkedIn.
Those 40,000 followers and millions of impressions came with barely a viral post to my name. Nobody is begging me to do sponsorships. But I rarely have trouble finding work, and far more opportunities come to me than I go looking for. That has much less to do with fame than with being easy to find.
You don’t need 10,000 followers. You need a trail of breadcrumbs.
Don’t write AI slop
LinkedIn is notorious for being overrun with AI-generated posts. It’s become a running joke. That’s good news for you, because the bar to stand out is “sound like a human being.”
Write about what you actually achieved: a hairy bug you squashed, how your team handles deployments, why you picked some obscure library, the migration that went sideways at 2 a.m. Specifics are hard to fake and easy to trust. (But be careful not to post sensitive information.)
And post a picture of yourself once in a while. People connect with faces a lot faster than with walls of text.
Hot takes, with caution
Posts with an opinion tend to outperform tutorials, but you don’t have to dunk on anyone to have one. For instance, if you work on a tech stack people love to mock (VB, .NET, some ancient Java monolith held together with prayer), try something like “What people get wrong about .NET.”
You’ll attract a few trolls in the comments—free engagement, honestly—plus people who want an actual conversation. These comments can turn into actual connections and even… friends.
A routine you can follow
Posting twice a week is not a big ask. Pick a simple, repeatable format so you’re never staring at an empty text box: what you worked on, what broke, and what you learned. Even a post that gets 10 views leaves one more breadcrumb about who you are and what you know.
Over time, the people who comment become your network. And because so few engineers post about their work on LinkedIn, you can become a big fish in a small pond surprisingly fast.
Write for the people a few steps behind you
The best audience is engineers one or two steps behind where you are now. Answer the questions you had a year ago. It helps them, it sharpens your own thinking, and every so often it turns into mentorship in both directions.
It also tells a future employer more about how you think than any résumé bullet ever could.
The engineers who grab the most opportunities are the ones employers can find. You don’t need to become an influencer to be one of them. You just need to leave enough breadcrumbs that the right person can follow them back to you.

title: A Tesla Model Y Without A Steering Wheel Is Coming: Musk
content:
The Cybercab is Musk's solution for most rides. But he thinks a six- or seven-seat autonomous Model Y is important, too.
Photo by:
9:08pm ET
Tesla is working on a version of the Model Y without a steering wheel or pedals.
The proposed vehicle is meant to operate fully autonomously, like the steering-wheel-free Cybercab.
CEO Elon Musk says that it's meant to service the 10% of rider miles that require more than two seats.
Tesla has already built one model without a steering wheel or pedals. But one was not enough, and CEO Elon Musk is eyeing another model for an autonomous upgrade.
Musk said Wednesday that Tesla will build a steering-wheel-free, fully autonomous version of the Model Y.
Musk revealed the plan at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, noting that Tesla wants to take the basic premise of what it can offer with the
Cybercab
—a fully autonomous vehicle that can operate as a managed fleet car—to a platform that can seat more than just two people.
"It's going to make sense for us to make cars that can seat different amounts of people,” said Musk. “We still need autonomous vehicles if you've got four or six, or a whole family. What we plan to do is have an autonomous version of the Model Y that won't have steering wheels or pedals and would be good for transporting groups of six or seven people."
Now, before getting too far—yes, you’re still going to be able to order a regular-size Model Y with a steering wheel for the foreseeable future. But Tesla wants a robotaxi that can accommodate an actual family.
Tesla already uses the Model Y in its autonomous fleet. However, those cars retain the basic driving controls that Tesla now wants to eliminate in its fully autonomous variant. Musk’s proposed version would seemingly delete them from the factory and create a larger autonomous car that passengers could ride in, but not drive—similar to the Cybercab.
To Musk’s point,
Cybercab is intentionally tiny
. Its two-seat configuration “covers 90% of all passenger miles,” according to Musk. That means that Tesla can cut down on production costs by reducing the interior complexity in order to make the Cybercab cost under $30,000.
Stay informed with our newsletter every weekday
Musk didn’t say when (or if) this variant would be offered to the public to purchase. The Cybercab only
recently became available for hand-picked private buyers to purchase
, and even then, there are a number of asterisks involved (like where the car can operate, and the mandatory $300 per month autonomy subscription required for the car to move).
Nevertheless, if Tesla is going to build driverless cars, an autonomous Model Y makes sense if Tesla can keep costs down and safely deploy it in enough usable areas. But with a $300 per month cost on top of the vehicle, would Tesla’s ideal audience be fleet operators or private buyers?

title: Americans Bought More Used EVs In October. Fewer Of Them Were Teslas
content:
Tesla still led the U.S. used EV market, but the Chevy Equinox EV, Kia EV6 and Nissan Leaf all gained ground from September.
Photo by:
Mack Hogan/InsideEVs
7:56am ET
U.S. used EV sales hit 48,678 in October, up 73% year over year.
Tesla still led despite a 5.4% monthly sales drop. The Equinox EV, EV6 and Leaf gained.
Used EV asking prices averaged $36,582 last month.
September was a good month to be selling a used Tesla Model Y. Sales jumped nearly 14% from August, and the Ford Mustang Mach-E did even better. The Chevrolet Equinox EV beat both, though, with a nearly 42% increase. A month later, only one of those three electric crossovers was still gaining buyers: the Chevy.
Americans bought an estimated 48,678 used EVs in October, according to the latest EV Market Monitor from
Cox Automotive
. That’s up 4.7% from September and 73.2% year over year. Used Tesla sales, meanwhile, fell 5.4% from September, with the Model 3, Model Y, and Model X losing ground.
Cox says used EV sales rose 4.7% from September to October. However, its September report put sales at 47,862 vehicles. October’s total of 48,678 is 816 higher, which is a 1.7% gain; Cox doesn’t explain the discrepancy.
Photo by: Patrick George
Tesla still dominated the used EV scene, though. The change was one spot down, with Chevrolet moving ahead of Ford into second place. Hyundai and BMW rounded out the top five. The Equinox EV and Blazer EV added to their September gains, while the Kia EV6, Nissan Leaf and Volkswagen ID.4 also found more buyers than in the previous month.
Cox says this is because a growing supply of cars coming off lease is giving shoppers more choices across brands and price points.
That 73% jump over last year deserves a little context. October 2025 was the first full month after the federal EV tax credit ended and Americans bought about 30,000 used EVs. In March,
sales hit a record of nearly 43,000
. EVs made up 3.3% of U.S. used car sales in October, matching
September’s record
and up from 2% a year earlier.
Stay informed with our newsletter every weekday
For used EV shoppers, the more useful number might be $36,582. That was the average asking price for a used EV in October, down from $36,767 in September and 1.9% below a year earlier. The Equinox EV, ID.4, Mach-E and Nissan Ariya all got cheaper.
Used Teslas didn’t for a second consecutive month, rising 1.8% to an average of $34,109. Even after that increase, the average used Tesla was listed for about $2,500 less than the average used EV.
Used EVs still carried a $2,236 premium over gas cars and hybrids, up slightly from $2,137 in September. Dealers had 38 days’ worth of used EVs on hand at October’s sales pace, versus 47 days for gas cars and hybrids.
More On This
At October’s sales pace, traditional dealers had enough used Teslas to last 32 days, the shortest supply of any major brand Cox tracked. Cox’s count leaves out Tesla’s own stores. Another study looked at
how long each used EV spent on dealer lots
in September. The Audi Q4 E-Tron Sportback sold the fastest, and no Tesla made the top ten.
Over on the new-car side, Americans bought 83,262 EVs in October, down 3.9% from September but up 3% from a year earlier, marking the first year-over-year gain of 2026. EVs’ share of new sales slipped from 6.5% in September to 6.2% last month. The average buyer paid $56,221 for a new EV, even with incentives averaging $6,375 per vehicle. Dealers had 85 days’ supply of new EVs, more than double their used inventory.
October wasn’t all bad for Tesla. While sales of second-hand Model Ys fell, Americans bought 36,366 brand-new examples, up 9.4% from September. It accounted for nearly 44% of all new EVs sold in the country.

title: Ford Just Started Fathom LFP Battery Production In Michigan. It's A Big Deal
content:
Ford Just Started Fathom LFP Battery Production In Michigan. It's A Big Deal
Ford’s BlueOval Battery Park Michigan is now shipping production-grade batteries for testing in Fathom prototypes.
Ford just reached a critical milestone in the development of its Fathom electric truck. The company has started manufacturing low-cost lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) battery packs at its $3 billion BlueOval Battery Park Michigan, located a couple hours west of Detroit, in Marshall, MI. These are production-grade LFP batteries which will first be used in Fathom prototypes before full-scale manufacturing begins next year.
One can’t overstate how important the Marshall plant is for Ford. It’s the first plant in the U.S. to manufacture LFP batteries for mainstream consumer vehicle use domestically. LG Energy Solution also produces LFP batteries in the U.S.—supplying to GM and Tesla—but they’re dedicated to stationary energy storage systems. Ford’s 2 million-square-foot facility is dedicated to automotive LFP batteries.
Gallery: Ford BlueOval Battery Park Michigan
It has an annual production capacity of 20 gigawatt-hours and can manufacture 50 battery packs every hour. It’s a vertically integrated plant, where materials like raw lithium and iron-phosphate powder go in one end, and fully assembled, ready-to-install battery packs come out the other. All anode and cathode production, as well as major production processes in between, happen inside the plant.
Alan Clarke, the vice president of advanced development projects at Ford, said the company is moving fast to bring the Fathom to the market. In a relatively short time period, he claimed, Ford had developed the all-new Universal EV Platform that will underpin its future EVs, an all-new production system at the Louisville Assembly Plant, and domestic LFP battery production.
“Not having a team that existed to have a battery factory, a unicasting factory, an entirely new most automated vehicle production facility that Ford's ever produced in less than five years would be I think faster than China speed,” Clarke said during a media roundtable at the BlueOval Battery Park Michigan on Tuesday.
Clarke previously worked at Tesla for 12 years, helping create the Model S, followed by development work for the Model X, Model Y, Model 3, and Cybertruck.
BlueOval Battery Park Michigan drone photo
I toured Ford’s LFP plant this week, and I think it’s one of the most advanced, highly-automated battery facilities in the U.S. Michigan, America’s automotive manufacturing hub for a century, certainly hasn’t seen anything like it in its history.
Part of the reason why the facility is so cutting-edge comes from Ford’s LFP licensing deal with China’s CATL, the world’s largest and the most advanced battery maker. The U.S. has been lagging behind China and Europe in the battery technology race. Ford is now bringing that technical know-how back to the U.S. even if that means licensing technology from CATL.
More importantly, Ford officials said the new plant is fully compliant with the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) rules. Raw materials used to make batteries here do not come from what the U.S. government designates as Foreign Entities of Concern (FEOC). Even though the technology is from CATL, the critical materials aren’t sourced from U.S. FEOCs such as China, Russia and North Korea. (China controls the vast majority of the global critical materials supply chain.)
Final inspection of the Ford Fathom's LFP prismatic cells.
The plant is fully owned and operated by Ford, but CATL engineers helped the company set up thousands of incredibly complex production tools. They’re also helping train workers to operate high-tech equipment and install tight quality control systems to help Ford deliver the affordable EV that it has long promised. The prismatic LFP cell itself is unique to Ford and not something that exists in CATL’s global portfolio.
Meng Wang, the director and chief engineer of battery cell industrialization at Ford summed up the CATL partnership well. “To shorten our time to market, we decided to learn from the best,” Wang said. “Throughout the process, CATL passed on critical knowledge to Ford, including the equipment functions, manufacturing process, and also quality controls.”
Preorders for the Ford Fathom will begin early 2027 and production and deliveries are expected to begin by the end of next year.

title: Kia Made Its First EV 40 Years Ago. It Shows How Far Electric Cars Have Come
content:
Kia Made Its First EV 40 Years Ago. It Shows How Far Electric Cars Have Come
The Kia Besta EV was made for the 1986 Asian Games. Decades later, the brand is back to making EV vans alongside its other models.
- Kia made its first EV ever 40 years ago by converting the diesel-powered Besta van to electric.
- The Besta EV was made for the 1986 Asian Games, as a way to keep time for marathon runners without exhaust fumes bothering the competitors.
- The Besta EV had an estimated 35 kWh battery.
Kia has cemented itself as one of the world’s premier electric vehicle manufacturers. And it's spent longer experimenting with EVs than you probably think. This week, Kia marked 40 years since its first EV hit the road. It shows just how far the automaker—and the EV industry—has come.
Kia’s first EV launched in 1986 and was very important for several reasons. It was based on a van called the Besta. This was Kia’s first van developed in-house, replacing the Mazda-based Bongo van that it was making before.
Ahead of the 1986 Asian Games, Kia decided to develop a marathon broadcast vehicle that could keep pace with runners and house timekeeping and camera equipment—all while not disturbing runners with exhaust fumes. So the automaker ripped out the Besta's 2.0-liter diesel engine and replaced it with an electric motor and 35 kilowatt-hours worth of lead-acid batteries.
The range wasn’t great, but it was enough to cover the whole 26.2-mile marathon on one charge. Hyundai says it had around 75 miles of range and a top speed of 56 mph. It made another appearance at the 1998 Seoul Olympics.
Most importantly, Kia says the Besta EV was South Korea’s first-ever EV. The brand would go on to continue developing EV prototypes like the 1991 Sonata EV and 1992 Excel. In 1993, the Pride EV hatchback became Korea’s first EV certified for commercial sale, although it didn't get a full production run. This car, which you may have known in gas form as the Ford Festiva, had an (estimated) 17.4 kWh battery and solar panels that Kia said were good for almost ten miles of additional range.
The Kia Ray was the brand's first production electric vehicle, launching in 2011 with 86 miles of range.
Eventually, Kia made its first true production model, the Ray EV, in 2011. It had a 16.4 kWh battery pack and 86 miles of range. Three years later in 2014, the Soul EV came to market, bringing a Kia EV to the U.S. for the first time. And things really took off from there.
There’s only a four-year gap between the 93-mile Soul EV and the 238-mile Niro EV. In a relatively short amount of time, Kia’s EVs went from being useful as a second car to having enough range to be a sole vehicle. Today the company has a deep and competitive line of EV models, including the EV2, EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6 and EV9—although we are missing some of those options in the U.S.
And forty years after the Besta, Kia is back to making electric vans. The PV5 went on sale last year, offering several battery options and a range of up to 258 miles WLTP. Sales are off to a promising start; Kia says it sold some 57,000 of them in the van's first 14 months on the market.

title: Nearly 1 In 5 Tesla Model Ys Failed Their First German Inspection
content:
Inspectors found major defects on 18.5% of Model Ys, while the Mazda MX-30 EV fared far better.
Photo by:
6:03am ET
The Model Y ranked last among 109 models. At its first inspection, 18.5% had major defects, nearly triple the 6.4% average for cars of its age.
Inspectors flagged worn suspension joints on Model Ys 24 times as often as on comparable cars.
The Mazda MX-30 ranked third overall with a 3% failure rate, though it averaged less than half the Model Y’s mileage.
Ask a used
buyer what they’d like checked first, and I’m pretty sure the battery would come up pretty quickly. After reading what German inspectors found underneath some surprisingly young Model Ys, I’d want to know how the suspension was holding up, too.
Germany’s
analyzed 9.7 million mandatory roadworthiness inspections carried out between July 2025 and June 2026. The most revealing comparison was among cars coming in for their first check, at around three years old. EVs won three of the six vehicle classes, but they also occupied the bottom three spots in the overall ranking.
finished last out of 109 models for the second year running. Inspectors found major defects on 18.5% of the Model Ys they checked, up from 17.3% a year earlier and nearly triple the 6.4% average for cars that age. No model in that age group recorded a worse result since the 2015 report. Meanwhile, just 3% of
Mazda MX-30
EVs failed, good enough for third overall behind the
CX-60 and
Mercedes-Benz
Photo by: Andrei Nedelea
For the Model Y, inspectors flagged worn suspension joints 24 times as often as they did on comparable cars. They also found defective brake discs on 3.4% of Model Ys, against a 1% average for the age group. Front lighting drew more complaints than usual, too.
Tesla Model Ys covered more miles than average, though. By the time they showed up for inspection, the Model Ys had traveled an average of 36,000 miles (58,000 kilometers). The average car in the group had driven 29,200 miles (47,000 km), and the average MX-30 had covered only 16,200 miles (26,000 km). Those Teslas had driven more than twice as far as the Mazdas in roughly the same amount of time.
is the first car from a Chinese automaker to appear in the report, and it finished second from the bottom, with a 16% failure rate despite averaging only 23,000 miles (37,000 km). Inspectors flagged brake discs on 10.3% of MG4s, about ten times the average. Suspension defects were also unusually common. Just ahead of the MG was Tesla’s Model 3, with a 12.5% failure rate at an average of 34,200 miles (55,000 km).
Stay informed with our newsletter every weekday
The Model Y’s poor performance in Germany runs counter to its reputation for reliability. American buyers may remember that
Consumer Reports ranked the Model Y as its most reliable new EV
, though that’s based on owners reporting the problems they’d encountered.
Technical inspections, on the other hand, may find play in a suspension joint that the driver hasn’t noticed. There’s also a difference between buying new and buying used, even in Consumer Reports’ own data. Tesla finished last as a brand in its separate survey of five- to ten-year-old cars, which is perhaps more telling.
The German results apply to the Model Y that preceded the Juniper refresh. When
I drove the updated Model Y
, the softer suspension and new frequency-selective dampers made it noticeably more comfortable. Whether this softer suspension setup holds up better is something we’ll learn as those cars cover more miles.

title: Rivian’s Also Spinoff Pauses Deliveries Of Its $3,500 E-Bike After Months Of Delays
content:
Shipments of the futuristic e-bike are paused until Also finds a fix for problematic charging behavior.
Photo by:
Tim Levin/InsideEVs
3:20am ET
Rivian spinoff Also has paused shipments of its futuristic TM-B e-bike.
The startup sent an email to reservation holders, saying it has identified a few software-based issues.
Also originally planned to deliver the first e-bikes this spring, but shipments began just a few weeks ago.
, the electric mobility startup spun off from
, is facing another logistics headache. After delaying deliveries of its futuristic TM-B e-bike, the startup has paused shipments entirely to address some software problems that may lead to problematic charging behavior and phantom battery drain.
email sent to reservation holders
, the company apologized for the delay, saying it has identified a few software-based issues that are impacting some bikes, and that it wants to address the issues before resuming shipments, as first reported by
The Verge
. A firmware update is in the works, and Also estimates that deliveries will resume in approximately two weeks, with another update scheduled for November 24.
This is the latest setback for the mobility spinoff that made headlines last year with its software-heavy bicycles and four-wheeled quads. The TM-B e-bike was originally scheduled to be shipped in the spring of this year, but customers started receiving their orders months later, leading to a barrage of negative comments on the Also subreddit. This prompted Saul Leiken, the startup’s product manager, to post a 661-word apology letter, in which he attributed the setbacks to strict quality standards and “significant supply chain challenges.”
An Also e-bike customer who received his e-bike posted a YouTube video showing how the TM-B behaves when the state of charge gets low, and how the battery drains while the bike is not in use.
Aaron Draczyski
said he charged his bike in the garage up to 70%, but the state of charge went down to 30% in 24 hours without any usage. What’s more, when the battery level became critically low, the bike refused to charge, throwing an error message that claimed the battery was not installed, even though it hadn’t been removed.
The Also TM-B is unlike most e-bikes out there. Designed from the ground up as a futuristic mobility vehicle, its pedals are not physically connected to the rear wheels. Instead, the rider spins a generator, which provides power to the battery and the electric motor that turns the rear wheel via a rubber belt.
The battery can be recharged via a USB-C port, there’s a round touchscreen to control all of the bike’s features, and the rider can also use a smartphone app to keep tabs on the bike remotely.
The base Also TM-B starts at $3,500, but the Launch Edition models, which have yet to be shipped, cost $4,500. Earlier this year, when the startup announced the first delays, it threw in one of its Alpha Wave helmets and a $250 credit to spend on accessories.

title: The BMW i3 Has The Nurburgring Skills To Match Its Impressive Range
content:
The BMW i3 Has The Nurburgring Skills To Match Its Impressive Range
And this is just the standard i3. Can you imagine what the electric M3 will be like?
Who needs the electric M3 when the regular BMW i3 can already dominate at the track? In this new video from Misha Charoudin, the BMW i3 50 takes to the Nurburgring and not only makes it around the Green Hell without issue, it actually beats up on other performance cars.
The BMW i3 50 xDrive is currently the only variant on sale, and while it isn't a full-blown M car, it has the specs to rival most of the real ones. Its dual motors combine for 463 horsepower and 476 lb-ft of torque, making it more powerful than most M3s throughout history. Those motors get fed electrons by a 109 kWh battery, which is far bigger than most electric sedans of its size. Such a big battery might seem like overkill in an i3, especially since its heft might not seem useful on track. However, that massive pack actually helped it at the 'Ring.
When Charoudin started the lap, he had 79% state-of-charge (SoC). When he finished the 12-mile lap as hard as he could, he had 65%. A 14% drop after pushing the i3 hard on the most difficult track in the world is pretty dang good. Even more impressive is that, after three more laps with someone else at the helm, it still had 20% battery. Depending on where that i3 calls home, it could have been driven back after four flat-out laps. That's pretty remarkable, especially considering this is just the normal i3.
What's most impressive, though, is how the i3 50 handled the Nurburgring itself. On a normal day, the 'Ring is clogged up by countless sports cars, and even boring rental cars, so unless you're properly quick, you can get caught behind a train of cars. But not the i3. It carved through the traffic with ease, overtook even some serious performance machines, and looked like the fastest car on the track at times.
During the lap, you can see its sharp turn in, explosive power, and strong braking, both regenerative and friction. What's more, it did all of that on eco-friendly EV tires in the cold. So imagine what one could do on a set of stickier summer tires in good temps. The battery didn't even overheat, with the temp gauge saying "OK" until the very last minute. It did eventually say the battery temps got high, but the lap was basically done by that point.
This is the same BMW i3 50 that gets 468 miles of EPA-rated range and drove from Norway to Spain while only charging for a total of two hours and 46 minutes. If it can smoke performance cars at the Nurburgring, can you imagine what the M3 will be like?

title: The EV Charging Company That’s Quietly Conquering America Is Building A New U.S. Factory
content:
The EV Charging Company That’s Quietly Conquering America Is Building A New U.S. Factory
Alpitronic’s EV fast chargers are popping up everywhere in the U.S. A new factory in South Carolina will boost production.
- Italian EV charging equipment company Alpitronic is building a new factory in the U.S.
- The new $33.94 million plant in Fort Mill, South Carolina, will assemble 400- and 1,000-kilowatt DC fast chargers.
- Alpitronic’s stalls are a common occurrence in Europe, and several companies in the U.S. are using them, too, including Electrify America, Ionna, and Walmart.
Alpitronic, the company that makes the DC fast chargers used by Ionna, Walmart, Mercedes-Benz, BP Pulse, and others, is building a new factory in the United States that will boost output of its 400- and 1,000-kilowatt stalls.
The manufacturer’s new 173,315-square-foot facility, located in Fort Mill, South Carolina, will create 70 new jobs and will also act as a testing lab, repair center, logistics hub, and warehouse.
Alpitronic, which has its North American headquarters in Charlotte, North Carolina, and its global headquarters in Bolzano, Italy, said it will invest $33.94 million in the new facility, with $200,000 coming from York County’s Coordinating Council for Economic Development in the form of a Set-Aside grant to assist with the costs of building improvements.
“North America is central to our next phase of growth, and investing in our manufacturing capabilities is key to supporting that expansion,” said Patrik Herrnegger, Alpitronic Americas CEO. “Our Fort Mill facility will put U.S. production under our direct control, bringing us closer to our customers and enabling us to serve them more efficiently. We thank South Carolina and York County for their partnership as we prepare to begin production in early 2027.”
Back in 2024, the company worked with a third-party production partner to open its first local manufacturing facility in Wisconsin. Now, manufacturing has moved in-house, with Alpitronic wholly owning the production operation.
The new South Carolina plant will assemble HYC400 and HYC1000 stalls, Alpitronic said. The HYC400 all-in-one dispensers can deliver up to 400 kW of power to a single connected electric vehicle without needing a separate power cabinet, and are the current charger of choice for Ionna and Walmart.
The higher-powered HYC1000 system is composed of a 1,000-kW power cabinet and up to four stalls that can deliver up to 600 kW to a single EV. Each stall can have two ports, and the system can dynamically allocate power to each vehicle to make the best use of the available power.
What makes the company's dispensers different from most competitors is the use of silicon carbide components, which lower energy losses and, subsequently, the amount of money EV drivers have to pay for a top-up. According to Alpitronic, SiC modules enable 97.5% efficiency and allow for smaller, quieter, and cooler stalls.
Alpitronic’s new factory in Fort Mill, South Carolina, is scheduled to go online in February 2027.

title: This Hedley Studios Porsche 550 J Is A Shrunken Electric Replica Track Toy
content:
This Hedley Studios Porsche 550 J Is A Shrunken Electric Replica Track Toy
At only 80% scale, the 550 J isn't road legal but it sure looks fun.
This is adorable and I want one. Hedley Studios in the UK just came out with a replica Porsche 550 Spyder, which itself isn't a unique idea. There have been Volkswagen-powered 550 Spyder replicas for decades. What sets this one apart are two things: one is that it's only 80% scale, so it's a little fella, and the other is that it's electric. It's called the Porsche 550 J (for Junior) it looks like a blast.
I can't tell if the 550 J is a track toy or just a toy, but either way it looks like fun. At 80% scale, it looks positively bite-sized next to the real one, which was already one of the smallest production road cars you'll ever see. So it's tiny. So much so, in fact, that I struggle to see how two adults can actually fit in its two seats side-by-side. And, as you'd imagine with such a tiny footprint, the 550 J isn't road legal and is only meant for private roads and race track.
Like a real 550 Spyder, all of the 550 J's weight is behind the driver. Two 1.8 kWh battery packs provide the juice at 48 volts, while a single 11 horsepower electric motor drives the rear wheels. It only weighs 728 pounds, so that power should be enough to have some fun with. Add two passengers, though, and its weight can pretty easily pass the half-ton mark. At that point, 11 horses isn't much. However, there is an optional RS pack that bumps it to 21 horsepower. Top speed also jumps from 40 mph to 50 mph.
The RS Pack also adds two more of those 1.8 kWh battery packs, though, which adds another 44 pounds. That weight penalty might be worth it for the range, though. The standard 550 J only has 30 miles of range, while the RS has 50. That isn't a lot but it's enough for a track day. Plus, with such small batteries, the 550 J will charge up quickly. Lap the track a bunch of times, plug it in and have some lunch, and get back to it.
Track days should be fun, too. Bilstein dampers with Eibach springs handle suspension duty, while Brembo brakes do the stopping. The RS model gets Bilstein adjustable coilovers and drilled brake rotors, too. So despite having Power Wheels-levels of horsepower, it has genuine track car handling bits.
Hedley has done an admirable job of making the 550 J look like a real 550 Spyder that was hit with a shrink ray. It's smaller, sure, but you wouldn't know it from photos. Everything about it looks spot on, from every exterior detail of its carbon fiber body, to the interior switchgear, and even the fuel filler cap. It's a very impressive recreation and one that will look fantastic in owners' garages. Hedley claims it worked closely with the Porsche Museum to get all the details right and it shows.
Only 250 of these will be made, and they'll cost £69,500 ($91,406) each. So it isn't cheap, especially for something that isn't road legal. However, for folks who can afford to spend that kind of cash on a track day toy, this seems like a really fun way to do it.

title: NASA 旅行者 1 号抵达距地球 1 光日位置，深空探测任务前路几何
content:
IT之家 11 月 19 日消息，近日美国国家航空航天局（NASA）的旅行者 1 号探测器（Voyager 1）在太空中达成一项历史性里程碑：它与地球之间的距离已经达到一个光日。这意味着，地球向探测器发送一条指令，光速信号也需要整整 24 小时才能抵达。
自 1977 年旅行者 1 号及其姊妹探测器旅行者 2 号（Voyager 2）发射升空，开启太阳系外侧行星探测之旅以来，两项任务已经取得了大量科学成果。
据IT之家了解，旅行者 1 号曾近距离探测木星和土星，随后改变飞行轨道，飞掠土星最大的卫星土卫六（Titan）及土星环。这条飞行路线使其在 20 世纪 80 年代初飞到了太阳系行星轨道平面之外。
由于旅行者 1 号离开太阳系的速度更快，它已于 11 月 18 日达到距离地球一个光日的位置。相比之下，旅行者 2 号为了依次探测木星、土星、天王星和海王星，选择了稍慢的飞行路线，预计要到 2035 年才能达到同样的距离。
随着两艘探测器不断深入星际空间，接下来它们还将开展哪些探测工作？
继续探索遥远的星际空间
所谓星际空间，是指太阳持续释放的太阳风粒子在日球层顶（Heliopause）之外逐渐让位于星际空间物理环境的区域。
两艘旅行者探测器在这一领域都取得了宝贵成果。旅行者 1 号于 2012 年 8 月进入星际空间，此后一直持续收集数据；旅行者 2 号则于 2018 年 11 月进入星际空间。
NASA 喷气推进实验室（JPL）旅行者号任务项目经理苏珊 · 多德（Suzanne Dodd）向 Space.com 表示，目前的科学研究仍在持续测量磁场强度与方向、等离子体密度以及高能粒子等数据。重要的是，科学家需要了解随着探测器远离太阳，这些现象会发生怎样的变化。
JPL 项目科学家琳达 · 斯皮尔克（Linda Spilker）补充称，探测器还将继续研究周围的等离子体和磁场，并重点关注冲击波、压力前沿等可能由太阳活动引发的现象。
斯皮尔克表示：“旅行者号未来一项重要的科学任务，是观测太阳对星际空间的影响究竟能够延伸多远，一直到旅行者 1 号所在的位置。太阳的影响在哪里结束，真正原始的星际空间又从哪里开始？也许旅行者号能够运行足够长的时间，为我们解答这个问题。”
研究团队还希望继续观测探测器周围磁场方向的变化，了解磁场从受太阳影响的区域过渡到星际空间后会发生怎样的改变。
斯皮尔克指出，这一发现并不在旅行者号最初发射时科学家的预期之内，因此研究团队希望进一步了解其中的奥秘。当然，前提是探测器能够继续正常运行。
电力管理成为最大挑战
目前，两艘旅行者探测器每年都会损失约 4 瓦的电力。1977 年发射时，它们的初始供电功率为 470 瓦。随着核动力电源持续衰减，任务团队不得不在探测器即将迎来运行 50 周年之际，越来越谨慎地分配有限电力。
为了延长任务寿命，部分科学仪器已经被关闭。今年早些时候，两艘探测器还按照计划执行了一项名为“大爆炸”（Big Bang）的电力重新分配操作，尽可能在不牺牲科学研究能力的前提下节省电力。
对于后续安排，多德表示，团队预计在两艘探测器分别迎来发射 50 周年之前，不需要对运行方案作出重大调整。旅行者 2 号于 1977 年 8 月 20 日发射，比旅行者 1 号早了几周，后者于同年 9 月 5 日升空。
JPL 一名代表补充称，“大爆炸”操作预计能够让剩余科学仪器继续工作到这一时间节点。不过，团队还必须兼顾探测器的热状态。
这名代表表示，目前的电力余量已经“非常有限”，尤其是探测器所处的星际空间环境十分寒冷。
此外，还有一些无法提前预测的突发情况。例如，上个月旅行者 1 号曾突然停止响应地球发出的指令，通信中断约 48 小时。所幸，探测器随后很快恢复了正常通信。
JPL 代表表示：“任务的核心目标是科学研究，因此团队关注的不只是与旅行者号保持通信，还包括尽可能延长科学仪器的工作时间。探测器距离地球越远，就越能帮助我们了解日球层顶之外的星际空间如何变化。”
旅行者 1 号背后的几代航天工程师
如今，旅行者 1 号任务团队已经汇集了多代工程师，每个人都承担着不同但不可或缺的工作。
据 JPL 任务经理卡里姆 · 巴达鲁丁（Kareem Badaruddin）介绍，即使是团队中资历最浅的成员 —— 恩尚 · 卡扎里安（Nshan Kazaryan）和巴瓦娜 · 古普塔（Bhavana Gupta），也已经开始承担重要职责，为未来接手更多工作积累经验。
巴达鲁丁在邮件中表示：“他们已经一次又一次地证明了自己对团队的价值。”
卡扎里安负责与深空网络（DSN）协调探测器的跟踪时间安排。深空网络由三组天线组成，分布在不同地区，负责跟踪和通信深空探测任务，确保地面团队能够持续掌握旅行者号的运行情况。
古普塔则负责整理探测器指令与控制系统的相关资料，收集重要技术细节，以便在出现问题时，团队能够根据这些资料制定详细的处理指令。
巴达鲁丁还特别提到了团队中资历最深的成员之一杰克 · 利平科特（Jack Lippincott）。他在深空网络运行机制和数据解读方面积累了丰富经验，为任务提供了关键支持。
谈到位于澳大利亚戈尔德斯通的深空网络天线站时，巴达鲁丁表示，当地过去几周天气状况十分恶劣，利平科特帮助团队了解如何处理由此引发的特殊问题。
目前，科学家还无法确定旅行者号究竟还能在太空中运行多久，但任务团队表示，将尽可能坚持到最后。
多德表示：“旅行者 1 号能够达到一个光日的距离，背后凝聚了数十年来卓越的工程技术。我们希望，在任务结束之前，它还能走得更远。”
巴达鲁丁则表示：“一个光日之所以如此特殊，是因为人类此前从未在如此遥远的距离上与一艘航天器保持联系，而且未来可能也不会再有这样的机会。”

title: 科学家首次直接观测到“恒星吞噬伴星”事件，整个过程持续约 7 年
content:
IT之家 11 月 19 日消息，天文学家借助 NASA 詹姆斯 · 韦布空间望远镜，首次获得恒星吞噬伴星并最终可能合并为一颗恒星的直接观测证据。
研究人员通过追踪仙女座星系外围一组双星系统的变化，重建了两颗恒星从相互绕行、发生吞噬到剧烈爆发的过程，相关研究于当地时间 11 月 18 日发表在《自然》上。
这组双星系统被研究人员亲切地称为“Bao”，正式编号为 AT 2025abao，分别称为“大宝”（Big Bao）和“小宝”（Little Bao）。
根据 NASA 发布的研究介绍，其中较大的恒星质量约为太阳的 7 倍，半径约为太阳的 350 倍，亮度约为太阳的 1.8 万倍；较小的伴星质量约为太阳的 0.7 倍，体积和亮度均小于太阳。
研究人员认为，小宝在进入大宝外围气体包层后，受到气体阻力影响，轨道逐渐收缩，并在约 7 年内不断向大宝核心靠近，最终撞入其核心。
这一过程属于天文学中的“共同包层演化”（Common Envelope Evolution）。在双星系统中，当一颗恒星膨胀到足以包裹伴星时，伴星会在共同包层内受到气体阻力，逐渐损失轨道能量并向主星核心螺旋式下沉。此前，天文学家主要通过理论模型和事后观测推测这一过程，此次研究则获得了较为完整的直接观测证据。
据《自然》论文，大宝在 2018 年左右开始逐渐变亮，研究人员于 2023 年 2 月通过 NASA 已退役的 NEOWISE 红外空间望远镜数据注意到这一异常现象。2024 年 9 月，WINTER 望远镜的观测进一步发现，这颗恒星不仅亮度增加，还开始向周围释放尘埃。
2025 年 10 月 17 日，兹威基瞬态设施（ZTF）探测到该系统发生剧烈爆发。研究人员发现，恒星亮度在短时间内迅速上升，并在不到一周内达到峰值。NASA 的韦布空间望远镜随后于 2025 年 12 月 24 日对其进行观测，距离爆发峰值仅过去 47 天。
研究人员利用韦布望远镜的中红外观测数据，结合其他地面及空间望远镜此前积累的紫外、可见光和近红外数据，重建了双星系统合并前后的演化过程。
研究估算，此次爆发将相当于太阳质量 0.1 至 0.2 倍的物质抛射到周围空间。研究人员认为，小宝最终被拖入大宝核心，两颗恒星由此合并。不过，合并后形成的 Bao 目前具体处于何种状态，仍需要未来进一步观测才能确定。
研究团队认为，NASA 即将开展大规模巡天观测的南希 · 格雷斯 · 罗曼空间望远镜，有望帮助天文学家发现更多类似事件，为研究双星系统演化提供新的观测样本。

title: 腾讯：更多企业转向国产芯片，将助推国内供应链建设提速
content:
11 月 19 日消息，腾讯昨日发布第三季度财报。财报显示，其第三季度实现营收 2073.36 亿元，同比增长 8%；毛利 1159.11 亿元，同比增长 7%；归母净利润为 636.12 亿元，同比增长 0.8%。
据《科创板日报》报道，对于持续增加的 AI 投入，腾讯管理层在业绩会上表示，公司当前资本开支主要用于 AI 基础设施建设。这类投入并非一次性消耗，建成后的基础设施可以持续用于模型训练和 Token 生成。随着 2026 年、2027 年建设的基础设施在后续年份发挥作用，
预计到 2028 年相关投入带来的经营压力有望逐步缓解
管理层同时提到，AI 基础设施的投入成本未来有望出现积极变化。其认为，目前设备采购价格相对较高，预计到 2028 年，同类设备采购价格将明显下降；此外，更重要的是模型训练和推理的计算效率持续提升，在相同基础设施条件下，
未来有望完成更多训练任务、处理更多 Token
算力供给仍是当前 AI 业务面临的现实约束。谈及最新收紧限制的影响，腾讯高管表示，短期内实际可用算力减少，无论租赁还是自建算力都受到影响，模型训练也将承压。腾讯目前混元 Hy4 采用的精度训练效率较高，但下一代模型的推出可能需要更长时间。

Was passiert eigentlich hinter den Mauern von Schloss Birlinghoven? Rund 100 Vertreterinnen und Vertreter Sankt Augustiner Unternehmen und Institutionen nutzten das 18. Unternehmerfrühstück, um genau das herauszufinden. Gastgeber war dieses Mal das Fraunhofer-Institut für Angewandte Informationstechnik FIT, das spannende Einblicke in seine Forschungsarbeit und die Anwendung neuer Technologien ermöglichte.
Organisiert wird die Veranstaltungsreihe von der Interessengemeinschaft Wirtschaftsförderung Sankt Augustin, zu der die VR-Bank Bonn Rhein-Sieg eG, die Kreissparkasse Köln und die Wirtschaftsförderungsgesellschaft Sankt Augustin mbH (WFG) gehören. Das Format schafft regelmäßig Gelegenheiten für den persönlichen Austausch und neue Kontakte innerhalb der lokalen Wirtschaft.
Nach der Begrüßung durch Oliver Kindermann, stellvertretender Firmenkundendirektor Rhein-Sieg der Kreissparkasse Köln, stellte Prof. Wolfgang Prinz, stellvertretender Institutsleiter des Fraunhofer FIT, das Institut vor. Ein Schwerpunkt lag auf den Einsatzmöglichkeiten Künstlicher Intelligenz in Unternehmen. Das Fraunhofer FIT entwickelt digitale Lösungen mit dem Menschen im Mittelpunkt. Dabei untersucht das Institut, wie neue Technologien, z. B. Künstliche Intelligenz, Blockchain oder Virtual Reality, sinnvoll eingesetzt werden können. Besonders spannend für die Unternehmen: Gemeinsam mit Wirtschaft und Verwaltung werden Ideen bewertet, Technologien erprobt und Lösungen für die Praxis entwickelt. Ziel ist es, Prozesse zu verbessern und neue Möglichkeiten für Produkte, Dienstleistungen und Geschäftsmodelle zu erschließen. »Die entscheidende Frage ist nicht, was KI heute schon alles kann, sondern wie Unternehmen daraus einen konkreten Nutzen ziehen können. Genau hier verstehen wir uns am Fraunhofer FIT als Brückenbauer zwischen Forschung und Anwendung«, so Prof. Wolfgang Prinz.
Unter anderem mit dem Fraunhofer FIT auf dem Campus Birlinghoven verfügt Sankt Augustin über renommierte Forschungskompetenz direkt vor Ort. Bürgermeister Dr. Max Leitterstorf unterstrich die Bedeutung dieses besonderen Profils: »Sankt Augustin ist ein starker Wirtschafts- und Wissenschaftsstandort. Das enge Zusammenspiel unserer Unternehmen, Forschungseinrichtungen und der Hochschule Bonn-Rhein-Sieg schafft herausragende Voraussetzungen für Innovation, Wissenstransfer und Fachkräftesicherung. Diese Stärken wollen wir nutzen und Sankt Augustin als attraktiven Standort weiter ausbauen.«
Nach dem offiziellen Programm stand der persönliche Austausch im Mittelpunkt. An verschiedenen Stationen präsentierte das Fraunhofer FIT zudem ausgewählte Entwicklungen und Anwendungen aus seiner Forschungsarbeit. Der persönliche Austausch ist ein wichtiger Baustein der Wirtschaftsförderung: »Ein starker Wirtschaftsstandort lebt vom persönlichen Kontakt und vom Austausch untereinander. Mit dem Unternehmerfrühstück möchten wir genau diese Begegnungen ermöglichen und die Vernetzung unserer Unternehmen fördern«, so Benedikt Bungarten, Geschäftsführer der WFG.
Das nächste Sankt Augustiner Unternehmerfrühstück findet am 3. März 2027 bei der BWLC GmbH Steuerberater Rechtsanwälte statt.

title: AirDrop und Quick Share: CISPA-Forscher findet sechs bislang unbekannte Schwachstellen

AirDrop und Quick Share: CISPA-Forscher findet sechs bislang unbekannte Schwachstellen
Hinweis zur Verwendung von Bildmaterial: Die Verwendung des Bildmaterials zur Pressemitteilung ist bei Nennung der Quelle vergütungsfrei gestattet. Das Bildmaterial darf nur in Zusammenhang mit dem Inhalt dieser Pressemitteilung verwendet werden. Falls Sie das Bild in höherer Auflösung benötigen oder Rückfragen zur Weiterverwendung haben, wenden Sie sich bitte direkt an die Pressestelle, die es veröffentlicht hat.
Visualisierung zum Paper „Protocol Prying: Systematic Vulnerability Research in the Apple AirDrop and Android Quick Share Proximity Transfer Protocols”
| Copyright:
Download
Dateitransfers zwischen Geräten in unmittelbarer Nähe – etwa mit Apples AirDrop oder Googles und Samsungs Quick Share – gehören längst zum Alltag. Doch wie sicher sind diese direkten Verbindungen? Und welche Informationen können Geräte bereits austauschen, bevor Nutzende eine Übertragung bestätigen? Arash Ale Ebrahim hat erstmals systematisch untersucht, wie sicher die Kommunikationsabläufe hinter AirDrop und Quick Share auf verschiedenen Plattformen sind und sechs bislang unbekannte Schwachstellen identifiziert. Die Ergebnisse hat er in seinem Paper „Protocol Prying: Systematic Vulnerability Research in the Apple AirDrop and Android Quick Share Proximity Transfer Protocols” publiziert.
Arash Ale Ebrahim untersucht Software und Protokolle, die vergleichsweise wenig Aufmerksamkeit erhalten, weil sie auf den ersten Blick nicht besonders wichtig erscheinen. So kam er auch auf AirDrop und Quick Share: „Besonders motivierend war für mich, dass diese Dienste sogenannte Zero-Click-Angriffsflächen bieten“, erzählt er. „Das bedeutet in diesem Zusammenhang, dass ein Angreifer aus der Funknähe mit dem Gerät interagieren und bestimmte Protokollfunktionen ansprechen kann, ohne dass die betroffene Person zuvor eine Datei annimmt oder eine Aktion ausführt.“ Ziel seiner Forschung ist es, solche bislang unbekannten Angriffswege aufzudecken. „Seit einigen Jahren gibt es immer wieder Angriffe, bei denen Einzelpersonen gezielt ins Visier genommen werden, etwa Journalist:innen oder Oppositionelle“, so Ale Ebrahim weiter. „Vor diesem Hintergrund wollte ich diese Angriffsflächen untersuchen, Schwachstellen finden und dadurch zu ihrer Behebung beitragen.“
Reverse Engineering und eigener Fuzzer
Um die Sicherheitsmechanismen von AirDrop und Quick Share systematisch zu untersuchen, rekonstruierte Ale Ebrahim zunächst die zugrunde liegenden Protokollabläufe, indem er deren technische Funktionsweise analysierte. Eine besondere Herausforderung stellte dabei Apples proprietäres Funkprotokoll AWDL dar, dessen Funktionsweise die Forschenden zunächst ebenfalls nachvollziehen mussten. „Danach schrieb ich ein einfaches Skript, das ein gültiges Paket an die AirDrop- beziehungsweise Quick-Share-Komponente senden konnte. Als das erfolgreich funktionierte, wandelte ich dieses Skript in einen Fuzzer um“, erklärt der Forscher. So entstand „AIRFUZZ“, ein speziell auf die komplexe, mehrschichtige Protokollstruktur zugeschnittenes Werkzeug zum automatisierten Aufspüren von Softwareschwachstellen. Damit konnte Ale Ebrahim systematisch unterschiedliche Eingaben testen und schließlich mehrere Schwachstellen identifizieren.
Die Ergebnisse: Schwachstellen bei AirDrop und Quick Share
Mithilfe von AIRFUZZ fand Ale Ebrahim Schwachstellen sowohl bei Quick Share als auch bei AirDrop. „Bei AirDrop handelt es sich überwiegend um Denial-of-Service-Schwachstellen“, erklärt der Forscher. „Mit diesen Schwachstellen lässt sich das Zielgerät – beziehungsweise lassen sich bestimmte Funktionen – außer Betrieb setzen.“ Konkret fand er bei AirDrop einen Stack Overflow, eine Null-Pointer-Dereferenzierung und einen fatalen Assert. Einfach ausgedrückt können diese Fehler dazu führen, dass die betroffene Software abstürzt. Dadurch können bestimmte Gerätefunktionen vorübergehend nicht mehr verfügbar sein. Diese Schwachstellen traten unter bestimmten Vorbedingungen des AirDrop-Protokolls auf.
Bei Quick Share waren die Ergebnisse weitreichender. „Zwei Schwachstellen betrafen die Absicherung der Kommunikation, eine weitere betraf die Windows-Version der Software“, so Ale Ebrahim weiter. „Dort entdeckten wir eine Use-after-free-Sicherheitslücke, die die Ausführung von Code aus der Ferne ermöglichte.“ Eine Use-after-free-Sicherheitslücke entsteht, wenn ein Programm auf einen Speicherbereich zugreift, der bereits freigegeben wurde. Je nach den Umständen und der Möglichkeit, die dadurch entstehende Speicherbeschädigung zu kontrollieren, kann eine solche Sicherheitslücke zu einem Absturz oder in manchen Fällen zur Ausführung von Schadcode aus der Ferne führen. Das bedeutet, dass Angreifer solche Schwachstellen ausnutzen können, um eigenen Code auf dem betroffenen Gerät auszuführen. Ale Ebrahim meldete alle gefundenen Schwachstellen verantwortungsvoll an die jeweiligen Anbieter. Nach seinen Angaben sind sie mittlerweile behoben.
Ausblick
Für Ale Ebrahim ist eine wichtige Erkenntnis aus seiner Forschung, dass die Sicherheitsrisiken solcher Dienste offenbar lange unterschätzt wurden. „Möglicherweise lag das daran, dass sich die beiden Kommunikationspartner in räumlicher Nähe befinden müssen“, erzählt er. „Unsere Forschung zeigt jedoch, dass sich auch über solche Dienste komplexe und hochentwickelte Angriffe durchführen lassen. Viele Menschen sind sich der möglichen Auswirkungen nicht bewusst, wenn ihre Geräte über solche Protokolle und Dienste erreichbar sind.“ Ale Ebrahim empfiehlt Nutzenden deshalb, die Einstellungen regelmäßig zu überprüfen und diese Funktionen zu deaktivieren, wenn sie nicht benötigt werden.
Ale Ebrahim, der als wissenschaftlicher Mitarbeiter in der Forschungsgruppe von CISPA-Faculty Nils Ole Tippenhauer arbeitet, ist auch nach der Veröffentlichung des Papers weiter am Thema Zero-Click-Angriffsflächen interessiert. „In unserer Gruppe untersuchen wir AirDrop und ähnliche Dienste weiterhin auf solche Schwachstellen“, erzählt er. „Der Schwerpunkt liegt derzeit vor allem auf Bild- und Nachrichtenparsern von Apple. Auch dabei handelt es sich um Zero-Click-Angriffsflächen. Deshalb müssen wir weiterforschen, um möglicherweise noch schwerwiegendere Schwachstellen zu finden.“ Das ist für den Forscher inzwischen leichter, weil er bereits eine gute Infrastruktur aufgebaut und einen passenden Fuzzer entwickelt hat. „Dadurch können wir tiefer in die Systeme eindringen und weitere interessante Schwachstellen untersuchen,“ so Ale Ebrahim abschließend.

Studierende aus sieben Hochschulen und ein Azubi-Team lösten beim dritten Hackathon hack4GDI_DE an der Hochschule Mainz fünf Challenges mit öffentlichen Geodaten.
Eine Augmented-Reality-App für die Bahnreise, die komfortable Planung von Radtouren, ein Bewertungssystem für Entsiegelungsflächen und eine Onlineanwendung für die Suche nach der zuständigen Behörde: Beim dritten hack4GDI_DE an der Hochschule Mainz entwickelten rund 70 Studierende am 13. und 14. November praxisnahe Lösungen auf Basis öffentlicher Geodaten. Die Teilnehmenden kamen von sieben Hochschulen, dazu trat ein Team von Auszubildenden im Bereich Geomatik an. Veranstalter waren die Koordinierungsstelle GDI-DE und die Hochschule Mainz.
Den ersten Platz sicherte sich das „Team Oldenburg“ mit seiner Bahnorama-Lösung für die Challenge „Zugbegleiter“. Die Augmented-Reality-Webapp macht aus einer passiven Bahnreise eine aktive Sightseeing-Tour mit dem eigenen Smartphone. Platz 2 ging an das Team „Pedal to the Metal“. Deren Lösung in der Challenge „Fahrradtourismus“ ermöglicht die komfortable Planung von Radreisen, inklusive Informationen zu Übernachtungsmöglichkeiten sowie zu geographischen und touristischen Routendetails. Beide Teams waren aus Oldenburg angereist.
Aufgrund der hohen Qualität der Beiträge vergab die Jury den dritten Platz gleich zweimal. Das Mainzer Team „Die 05er Entsiegler – Weck, Worscht & WMS“ zeigte in der Challenge „Flächenentsiegelung“ eine GIS-basierte Lösung, mit der sich Flächen mit Entsiegelungspotenzial in der Stadt Mainz anhand eines Bewertungssystems identifizieren lassen. Das Team „LeBeZi“ – ein gemischtes Team aus Tübinger, Augsburger und Mainzer Studierenden – kombinierte in der Challenge „Zuständigkeitsfinder“ amtliche Informationen aus unterschiedlichen Quellen und Formaten, damit Nutzende die zuständige Behörde für ihr Anliegen finden können.
Vertreten waren Studierende der Hochschulen Bochum, Mainz und Oldenburg sowie der Universitäten Tübingen, Augsburg, Freiburg und Heidelberg. Auch das Azubi-Team der Berufsschule Cuno II Hagen stellte sich erfolgreich den Aufgaben.
Eröffnet wurde der Hackathon von Kanzler Jens Egler, der die Teams von Seiten der Hochschule Mainz herzlich willkommen hieß und den Stellenwert der Veranstaltung für die Studierenden unterstrich. Dr. Jörg Kurpjuhn, Abteilungsleiter im Ministerium für Wirtschaft, Tourismus, Energie und Klima Rheinland-Pfalz (MWTEK), begrüßte die Teilnehmenden im Namen des Ministeriums und der GDI-DE. Er gehörte der Jury an, die die Preisträger kürte. Neben dem MWTEK unterstützte auch die Hochschule Bochum die Veranstaltung. Daten und hilfreiche Tools steuerten das Bundesamt für Kartographie und Geodäsie (BKG), das Bundesministerium für Digitales und Staatsmodernisierung (BMDS), die DB MindBox sowie das Start-Up Tobey GIS Consulting bei.
Die Studierenden zeigten sich begeistert darüber, mit tagesaktuellen Themen und berufsbezogenen Challenges arbeiten zu können. Besonders überzeugte sie die Möglichkeit, anwendungsnahe Use Cases zu entwickeln, die beispielsweise Behörden dabei unterstützen, präventiv tätig zu werden. Auch Organisation und Ablauf der Veranstaltung kamen sehr gut an.
Die hohe Qualität der Lösungsansätze für die bearbeiteten Challenges begeisterte die Jury — und machte ihr die Auswahl der ausgezeichneten Projekte der Studierenden-Teams nicht leicht. „Ich war im Vorfeld des Hackathons sehr gespannt, wie die zum Teil ja noch sehr jungen Teams mit den herausfordernden Challenges umgehen würden. Umso mehr freue ich mich, nun so funktionelle und kreative Lösungen zu sehen.“ stellte dann auch Dr. Jörg Kurpjuhn begeistert fest.
"Es freut uns sehr, dass wir den Hackathon bereits zum dritten Mal an der Hochschule Mainz ausrichten konnten und unsere Einladung auf große Resonanz gestoßen ist“, erklärte Prof. Dr. Markus Schaffert, Professor an der Hochschule Mainz und ebenfalls Jury-Mitglied. "Die studentischen Teams haben sich in kurzer Zeit in komplexe Fragestellungen eingearbeitet, eigenständige Lösungsansätze entwickelt und diese technisch überzeugend umgesetzt“.
Nun geht es für das Team der Koordinierungsstelle GDI-DE darum, die siegreichen Entwürfe so aufzubereiten, dass sie Interessierten in Kürze auf der Webseite präsentiert werden können. So soll die Möglichkeit geschaffen werden, die Nachnutzung und den tatsächlichen Einsatz der Lösungen zu unterstützen.

Staus auf den Zufahrtsstraßen und volle Parkplätze: Die Anreise zu den Salzburger Christkindlmärkten kann in der Adventzeit zur Geduldsprobe werden. Die von Salzburg Research entwickelte Mobilitätsinformation “switsch – Einfach besser ankommen” bietet nun eine Entscheidungshilfe. Die neue Weihnachtsversion gibt einen aktuellen Überblick über Fahrzeiten auf den Zufahrtsrouten, Abfahrtszeiten von öffentlichen Verkehrsmitteln und Auslastungen von Parkplätzen bzw. Park&Ride-Angeboten. Das kostenlose Online-Angebot steht während der gesamten Adventzeit zur Verfügung.
Wer in der Adventzeit den Salzburger Christkindlmarkt in der Altstadt oder den Adventzauber in Hellbrunn besuchen möchte, steht oft vor der Frage: Mit dem Auto direkt ans Ziel fahren oder besser auf öffentliche Verkehrsmittel umsteigen? Gerade an den stark besuchten Adventwochenenden kann die Fahrt in die Stadt oder nach Hellbrunn durch Staus und die Suche nach einem freien Parkplatz viel Zeit kosten.
Salzburg Research hat deshalb die bestehende Mobilitätsinformation “switsch – Einfach besser ankommen” um eine Weihnachtsversion erweitert. Die Website zeigt für die Anreise von den Autobahnabfahrten Salzburg Nord, Salzburg Mitte, Salzburg West und Salzburg Süd kommend zu den Christkindlmärkten in der Altstadt sowie in Hellbrunn aktuelle Verkehrsinformationen, die Umstiegspunkte in den öffentlichen Verkehr sowie aktuelle Auslastungsdaten der Parkplätze.
Auto, Öffis oder Park+Ride: Was ist gerade die bessere Wahl?
switsch stellt Anreiseoptionen gegenüber: Aktuellen Fahrzeiten mit dem eigenen PKW inklusive der Auslastung von Parkplätzen, Abfahrten von öffentlichen Verkehrsmitteln sowie kombinierte Wege mit Auto und Öffis.
Besonders interessant ist dabei das Park+Ride-Angebot: Wer dort das Auto abstellt, kann mit öffentlichen Verkehrsmitteln weiter in Richtung Stadtzentrum fahren und sich so den dichten innerstädtischen Verkehr und die Parkplatzsuche ersparen. Damit können Besucherinnen und Besucher bereits vor der Anreise abschätzen, ob ein Umstieg sinnvoll ist und wo noch Parkmöglichkeiten verfügbar sind.
Das kostenlose Angebot ist online abrufbar und steht während der gesamten Adventzeit zur Verfügung.
Forschung macht Mobilitätsalternativen sichtbar
Die Weihnachtsversion basiert auf dem Verkehrsinformationsangebot “switsch – Einfach besser ankommen”, das Salzburg Research im Rahmen des Forschungsprojekts MUST entwickelt hat. Die ursprüngliche Anwendung wurde im Frühjahr 2026 vorgestellt und bietet Echtzeitinformationen für sechs wichtige Pendelkorridore in die Stadt Salzburg.
Ziel ist es, verschiedene Verkehrsmittel und ihre aktuellen Reisezeiten vergleichbar zu machen. Statt Verkehrsinformationen aus unterschiedlichen Quellen zusammensuchen zu müssen, erhalten Nutzende eine übersichtliche Entscheidungsgrundlage.
Die Weihnachtsversion überträgt diesen Ansatz auf die Anreise zu den Christkindlmärkten in der Stadt Salzburg. Gerade bei Veranstaltungen mit hohem Verkehrsaufkommen können aktuelle Informationen dazu beitragen, Alternativen zur Anreise mit dem eigenen Pkw aufzuzeigen und bestehende Park+Ride-Angebote besser zu nutzen.

MUST („MUltimodale VerkehrsSTeuerung durch Kombination innovativer Informationskanäle“) untersucht, wie intelligente Verkehrsinformationen eine effizientere Nutzung der Verkehrsinfrastruktur und nachhaltigere Mobilitätsentscheidungen unterstützen können. Das Projekt wird von der Österreichischen Forschungsförderungsgesellschaft (FFG) im Programm „Mobilitätssystem, Städte & Digitalisierung“ gefördert.

Das Fraunhofer-Institut für Photonische Mikrosysteme IPMS und PVA TePla bündeln ihre Expertise und gründen das »Center of Excellence for Advanced Metrology« (CEAM) mit Sitz am Fraunhofer IPMS in Dresden. Ziel der strategischen Partnerschaft ist es, modernste Messtechnik von PVA TePla für Industrie und Forschung verfügbar zu machen und optische Messverfahren für die Halbleiter- und Werkstoffanalyse gemeinsam weiterzuentwickeln.
• Plattform für industrienahe Spitzenforschung mit optischen Messtechnologien für die Halbleiter- und Materialcharakterisierung
• Messsysteme von PVA TePla im 300-mm-Forschungsreinraum des Fraunhofer IPMS: ausgestattet wie die Reinräume großer Halbleiterfabriken
• Halbleiterhersteller und Zulieferer können Messverfahren mit eigenen Wafern unter fabnahen Bedingungen erproben
Herzstück des CEAM ist der 300-mm-Forschungsreinraum des Fraunhofer IPMS im Dresdner Norden, der identisch zu den Reinräumen großer Halbleiterfabriken ausgestattet ist. Wafer können daher zwischen den Fertigungsreinräumen der Industrie und des CEAM ausgetauscht und unter realitätsnahen Bedingungen analysiert werden. Unternehmen erhalten so die Möglichkeit, Messverfahren mit eigenen Wafern an den verfügbaren Systemen zu erproben und für ihre Prozesse zu bewerten – ohne die Systeme vorab in der eigenen Fertigung installieren zu müssen.
Hochspezialisierte Messsysteme von PVA TePla bilden das technische Rückgrat des CEAM und unterstützen kritische Schritte der Halbleiterproduktion und Qualitätssicherung. Das Hyperspektral-System VEreveal fusion ist bereits zur präzisen Materialcharakterisierung in Betrieb, demnächst soll LuXpector THEA hinzukommen, das Ellipsometrie und Reflektometrie zur zerstörungsfreien Analyse dünner Schichten kombiniert. Perspektivisch soll das CEAM um weitere Systeme aus dem Portfolio von PVA TePla erweitert werden: Neben einem System zur Messung von Stress im Wafer (SIRD) ist als Ergänzung zum optischen Schwerpunkt auch ein System für akustische Mikroskopie vorgesehen.
»Unser Ziel ist es, neue Standards in der zerstörungsfreien Materialanalyse zu setzen«, sagt Martin Landgraf, Projektleiter am Fraunhofer IPMS. »Im Mittelpunkt steht der industrielle Nutzen: Hochpräzise Materialanalysen sollen dazu beitragen, Fertigungsprozesse in der Halbleiterindustrie effizienter zu gestalten.«
»Mit dem CEAM bringen wir unsere Messtechnik in ein Umfeld, das einer modernen Halbleiterfabrik entspricht«, sagt Dr. Philipp Wollmann, Geschäftsführer von PVA Vision. »Mitten in Europas wichtigstem Mikroelektronik-Cluster können Kunden unsere Systeme dort mit ihren eigenen Wafern und unter realen Fertigungsbedingungen testen. Das kann Evaluierungs- und Qualifizierungsprozesse deutlich verkürzen. Gleichzeitig profitieren wir vom direkten Feedback der Expertinnen und Experten vom Fraunhofer IPMS, das unmittelbar in die Weiterentwicklung unserer Produkte einfließt.«
Fraunhofer IPMS und PVA TePla stärken durch das CEAM die Position Dresdens als Knotenpunkt für Halbleitertechnologien in Europa. Die Partnerschaft verbindet industrienahe Spitzenforschung mit angewandter Messtechnik und setzt damit einen wichtigen Impuls für »Silicon Saxony«. Weitere Multiplikatoreffekte werden sich aus der Integration des CEAM in die europäische APECS Pilotlinie ergeben (APECS - Advanced Packaging and Heterogeneous Integration for Electronic Components and Systems), die im Rahmen des EU Chips Act modernste Produktionstechnologien für neue Halbleiterprodukte verfügbar macht.
Über das Fraunhofer IPMS
Das Fraunhofer IPMS ist ein international führender Forschungs- und Entwicklungsdienstleister für elektronische und photonische Mikrosysteme. Unsere Technologien finden Anwendungen in Industrie, Mobilität sowie Biotechnologie und Medizintechnik. Zugleich adressieren wir zentrale Zukunftsfelder wie Quantentechnologien und neuromorphes Computing. Mit unserer Forschung im Bereich grüner Mikroelektronik leisten wir Beiträge zu einer ressourcenschonenden und nachhaltigen Welt. Mit dem Center Nanoelectronic Technologies (CNT) bietet das Fraunhofer IPMS angewandte Forschung auf 300-mm-Wafern für Mikrochip-Produzenten, Zulieferer, Gerätehersteller und F&E-Partner.
Über PVA TePla
PVA TePla ist ein führendes Spitzentechnologie-Unternehmen für Material- und Messtechnik. Der 1991 gegründete Systemanbieter entwickelt und produziert maßgeschneiderte Lösungen für hochpräzise Materialherstellung, -veredelung und -bearbeitung (Material Solutions) sowie Anlagen zur Inspektion von Material und Bauteilen durch akustische, optische und nass-chemische Verfahren (Metrology).
