title: Brazil, Colombia and Chile lead Latin America’s agrivoltaics market with 60 projects across the region - pv magazine Global
content:
German consultancy AgRadiance has launched the AgRadiance Atlas, an open-access interactive platform mapping agrivoltaic projects worldwide and providing information on regulations, support policies and court rulings.
The atlas currently lists 2,697 projects across 109 countries, compared with just 37 projects identified worldwide in 2018. It provides geographical data for each project and allows users to explore regulatory conditions in different countries and regions.
Each project is linked to its original publicly available source. The database also includes 151 projects classified as postponed or canceled.
The atlas contains 523 regulations, policies and court rulings related to agrivoltaics. Users can select a country or region to view identified projects, applicable regulations and a summary of local market conditions.
Projects can be filtered by development status, agricultural activity – including fruit and berry cultivation, viticulture, horticulture, biodiversity conservation and beekeeping – generation capacity and dates associated with different development stages. Records date back to 2009, allowing users to track project development over time.
Agrivoltaics in Latin America
In Latin America, the atlas identifies 60 agrivoltaic projects across 11 countries. Of these, 36 are operational, 20 are planned, three are under construction and one has received approval. Brazil, Colombia, Chile and Mexico account for 45 projects, or 75% of the regional total.
Brazil leads with 13 projects, including nine operational installations and four planned developments. Colombia follows with 12 projects, comprising seven operational installations and five in the planning stage.
Research and demonstration projects dominate in both countries, although some commercial developments have also been identified. In Brazil, projects combine solar panels with horticultural crops and sugarcane cultivation. In Colombia, installations include melon and watermelon cultivation beneath PV structures, as well as projects incorporating livestock farming.
Chile ranks third with 11 projects, including eight operational installations, one under construction and two planned developments. These include experimental agrivoltaic systems installed over cherry orchards and the 9 MW Ayla Solar PV project, which includes a 22-hectare agrivoltaic area.
Mexico has nine projects, including four operational installations and five planned developments. They include the Tonatiuh project in Puebla and experimental installations developed by the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM).
Elsewhere in the region, Peru has five projects, including three operational installations and two planned developments. Bolivia has three projects, two operational and one under construction.
Costa Rica and the Dominican Republic each have two projects. Costa Rica has one operational and one planned installation, while the Dominican Republic has one operational project and one approved development.
Argentina, Panama and Uruguay each have one project, respectively under construction, planned and operational.
The combined reported PV capacity of Latin America’s agrivoltaic projects stands at approximately 239 MW, although capacity data are available for only 25 of the 60 identified projects.
Colombia accounts for the largest reported capacity, with 136.5 MW across seven projects, followed by the Dominican Republic with 50 MW, Brazil with 31.7 MW and Chile with 15.1 MW.
The figures include projects at various stages of development and therefore do not represent exclusively operational PV capacity.
The data suggest that agrivoltaic development in Latin America remains concentrated in pilot installations, university research projects and demonstration facilities.
Some projects classified as agrivoltaic involve solar-powered irrigation systems or PV installations where livestock grazing is used for vegetation management, without documented evidence of simultaneous agricultural production.
An open-access platform
AgRadiance cautions that the atlas’s project records and summaries are compiled from publicly available sources with the assistance of artificial intelligence and may contain errors, omissions or outdated information.
The atlas is designed as a reference tool for the early stages of project development. Users can identify existing and proposed projects in a given area, including canceled or stalled developments, and review applicable regulatory requirements before conducting site visits.
The platform is free to access and does not require registration. Users can also view historical map data dating back to 2009 to track how projects have progressed through different stages of development.
AgRadiance plans to integrate the atlas with its web-based design tool, allowing users to move from reviewing existing projects and regulatory conditions to mapping individual land parcels and assessing potential PV system configurations.

title: Efficient heating is not enough: Why the timing of electricity use matters for heat pumps - pv magazine Global
content:
When discussing the cost-effectiveness of heat pumps, the focus is usually on the seasonal performance factor (SPF), flow temperature and building insulation. While these factors remain crucial, the debate around dynamic electricity tariffs is too narrow if it focuses solely on how long a heat pump can be switched off. What matters is the overall flexibility of a household’s electricity consumption.
Flexibility does not require switching off the heat pump
On very cold winter days, well-designed heat pumps often need to run almost continuously, leaving little scope for shifting heat production. At milder temperatures, however, there is some flexibility: Buildings and hot water storage tanks can retain heat for several hours. For example, a home can be preheated overnight for the morning or during the day for the evening. Similarly, hot water production can be scheduled for periods when electricity prices are lower. How long this flexibility lasts depends on the building’s insulation, heating system and storage capacity, although it is generally insufficient to bridge entire days.
Even when a heat pump runs continuously, the electricity it consumes does not necessarily have to be drawn from the grid at the same time. A suitable battery storage system can charge from the grid when electricity prices are low and supply power later. In this case, it is not heat production that is shifted, but the timing of electricity drawn from the grid. This distinction is particularly relevant for households with photovoltaic systems and existing battery storage.
Winter creates new opportunities
In summer, PV systems cover a larger share of household electricity demand with self-generated solar power. In winter, heating demand increases while solar power generation declines, making households more dependent on grid electricity. An existing battery storage system, provided it supports grid charging and can be controlled in response to electricity prices, can therefore do more than store solar power. It can also take advantage of periods of low wholesale electricity prices.
An analysis by Ostrom of average hourly wholesale electricity prices during the winter months of 2025 illustrates the importance of timing. At 2 p.m., the average price was €0.0832 ($0.0965)/kWh compared with €0.1462/kWh at 7 p.m. – a difference of €0.063. However, such a price difference alone is unlikely to justify investing in a battery storage system solely to optimize electricity costs. In addition to the initial investment, storage losses and the achievable utilization rate must also be taken into account.
For households that already have battery storage, the economics are different. The key question is whether the potential savings from price differences outweigh additional storage losses, battery degradation and any costs associated with technical modifications. Even then, profitable operation is far from guaranteed. Average hourly prices also do not reflect the price differences that can actually be exploited on individual days. While the figures illustrate the importance of when electricity is drawn from the grid, they do not demonstrate actual savings.
Other flexible loads also play a role. Households charging electric vehicles, particularly in winter, often cannot rely solely on electricity generated by their own PV systems. Coordinated energy management can help shift charging to periods when grid electricity is cheaper. Even when solar generation is low, strong wind power output can drive down wholesale electricity prices.
The goal is not the cheapest hour, but the lowest operating cost
For heat pumps, electricity prices are not the only factor affecting operating costs. With air-to-water heat pumps, outdoor temperatures also matter. If temperatures are higher around midday than in the early morning, the system can operate more efficiently. An intelligent control system should therefore consider electricity prices, outdoor temperatures and actual heating demand simultaneously. Producing additional heat simply because electricity is cheap makes little sense if that heat is ultimately wasted.
Good insulation and efficient hot water storage can help minimize these losses. Automated controls can make better use of periods with low electricity prices than fixed schedules. What matters is whether the different system components can communicate with one another and whether the resulting savings outweigh any additional costs.
Assessing the cost-effectiveness of heat pumps therefore requires looking beyond the efficiency of the individual unit. Particularly in winter, when heat pumps may need to operate almost continuously, it is worth considering the entire energy system, including thermal storage, battery storage, PV installations and other electricity-consuming devices. The key question is not how often a heat pump can be switched off, but how intelligently a household can source the electricity it needs.
Matthias Martensen
is CEO and co-founder of
Berlin-based green electricity provider Ostrom
. The company offers digital electricity tariffs and solutions for the intelligent management of distributed energy systems.

title: India adds record 8.4 GW of open-access solar in first nine months of 2026 - pv magazine Global
content:
India added a record 8.4 GW of open-access solar capacity in the first nine months of 2026, up 29% from the same period in 2025, according to Mercom India’s Q3 and 9M 2026 Solar Open Access Market Report.
Open-access solar allows commercial and industrial (C&I) consumers to procure electricity from off-site solar projects through the grid, rather than relying solely on local distribution companies.
Growth was driven by increased adoption of captive ownership models and long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs), according to the report. A temporary exemption from Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) List-II requirements for eligible open-access projects also improved access to lower-cost solar modules, supporting project economics.
India added 2.3 GW of open-access solar capacity in the third quarter of 2026, down 32% from 3.4 GW in the preceding quarter and 8% from 2.5 GW in the third quarter of 2025.
“India’s record solar open access installations in the first nine months of 2026 reflect the strong demand from commercial and industrial consumers. However, the slowdown in Q3 highlights the growing impact of rising module prices, supply constraints, grid connectivity delays, and regulatory uncertainty,” said Priya Sanjay, managing director of Mercom India. “The economics of open access remain compelling, but inconsistent policies and execution bottlenecks are preventing the market from reaching its full potential.”
Rajasthan led quarterly capacity additions, accounting for 29% of installations, followed by Tamil Nadu and Gujarat. The five leading states accounted for 83% of India’s open-access solar installations in the third quarter.
Cumulative installed open-access solar capacity reached 39.3 GW by the end of September 2026. Karnataka led with a 21% share, followed by Rajasthan at 16% and Maharashtra at 15%.

title: Inox Solar Americas advances 3 GW U.S. solar cell facility to equipment installation phase - pv magazine Global
content:
Inox Solar Americas LLC has moved its 3 GW solar cell manufacturing plant in Greenville, North Carolina, into the equipment installation phase, keeping the facility on schedule to begin commercial production in the second quarter of 2027.
Spanning 515,460 square feet, the factory serves as the manufacturing base for Inox Solar Americas. Once operational, the plant will supply domestic monocrystalline cells directly to company module assembly operations, producing Galaxion cell architecture alongside Gamma Series monofacial and Vega Series bifacial panels.
The Greenville project builds on Inox Clean Energy acquisition of Boviet Solar U.S. manufacturing assets, which included an established 3 GW module footprint paired with a planned cell expansion. By utilizing existing infrastructure rather than starting from scratch, the company is avoiding greenfield timelines that have delayed domestic manufacturing efforts.
This expansion addresses a structural mismatch in the U.S. solar supply chain. While cumulative domestic module assembly capacity has surged past 75 GWdc to 80 GWdc, operational cell manufacturing capacity sits lower at roughly 20 GWdc. Upstream wafer and polysilicon capacities lag further behind at approximately 3 GWdc and 10 GWdc, meaning domestic cell makers will continue relying on qualified non-Foreign Entity of Concern wafer imports in the near term.
Bringing 3.0 GW of cell capacity online is designed to help utility-scale developers navigate federal procurement rules. Under updated Section 45X tax credit guidelines and trade provisions, project developers face pressure to prove non-restricted component origins to capture domestic-content bonus credits.
To meet requirements, the Greenville plant integrates automated inline testing, precision processing, and production-record traceability. Industry analysts emphasize that transitioning a domestic cell fab from equipment installation to commercial output remains an operational test, requiring cleanroom discipline and process engineering.
“By bringing cell technology, module manufacturing, and quality control together within our manufacturing platform, we are strengthening our ability to support customers with supply and bankability required for project pipelines,” said Ashok Nair, President and CEO of Inox Solar Americas.

title: Longi presents 25.2%-efficient solar module with triple-protection design, larger light-receiving area - pv magazine Global
content:
Chinese PV manufacturer
launched its Hi-MO X10 Full-Screen Triple-Protection PV module on Nov. 17 at an industry event in Qingdao, China. The module features a front-side light-receiving area ratio of 98.58%, the highest the company has achieved in a commercial product.
The module retains the standard 2,382 mm × 1,134 mm dimensions of Longi’s existing Hi-MO X10 lineup for distributed PV applications, while increasing the light-receiving area by 759.3 cm² through four structural modifications.
Longi said it eliminated 20 white gaps between cells using a low-temperature film-welding process that bonds the cells at ambient temperature before a low-heat lamination step. The process reportedly limits the resulting height difference to 130 micrometers and recovers 178 cm² of light-receiving area.
The company also relocated three front-side busbars to the rear of the module, adding another 294 cm². According to Longi, thinner busbar profiles and staggered positioning help mitigate the risk of microcracks associated with rear-side busbar stacking. The remaining modifications include reducing inter-string spacing from 1.48 mm to 1 mm and cutting the cell-to-frame creepage distance from 12.9 mm to less than 9 mm through the use of upgraded insulation materials.
The module delivers a maximum front-side power output of 680 W and a conversion efficiency of 25.2%. Its standard power rating for volume production is 670 W, which Longi claims is 20 W higher than that of mainstream TOPCon modules of the same size.
To address additional rear-side shading caused by the relocation of the busbars, Longi replaced flat ribbons with round-wire ribbons, introduced precision-insulated sub-busbar break points, and developed an alloy frame profile designed to prevent the frame’s C-shaped section from shading the cells. The company said these changes increase the rear-side light-receiving area by 2.5% and enable a maximum bifaciality of 85%.
The module’s triple-protection design targets three reliability challenges that Longi identifies as particularly significant for commercial and industrial (C&I) rooftop installations: hotspots, electrical arcing, and microcracks.
For hotspot protection, the company integrated additional structures equivalent to bypass diodes within each
hybrid passivated back contact
(HPBC) 2.0 cell, which it claims can limit hotspot temperatures to below 100 C. To mitigate electrical arcing, Longi uses laser fusion welding in the junction box to eliminate metal-to-metal interface gaps that can contribute to DC arc formation.
Microcrack resistance is addressed through the same low-temperature welding process used in the full-screen design, combined with thinner busbars to reduce mechanical stress during transportation and installation.
The module has received TÜV SÜD and TÜV Rheinland certifications under IEC 61215 and IEC 61730. Longi also reported double-stress potential-induced degradation (PID), light-induced degradation (LID), and light- and elevated-temperature-induced degradation (LeTID) testing, along with level-six salt-mist, ammonia, and dust testing, and hail-impact qualification using 25 mm and 35 mm hailstones.
The product comes with a 15-year materials warranty and a 30-year linear power-output warranty. Longi specifies maximum first-year degradation of 1% and annual linear degradation of no more than 0.35%.
Longi said shipments of its Hi-MO X10 Triple-Protection modules reached 1.5 GW in China’s C&I market in August 2026. The company added that triple-protection variants accounted for more than half of its distributed PV shipments in the first nine months of 2026.
Speaking at the launch, Longi Chairman Zhong Baoshen cited internal laboratory results showing that the company’s
hybrid interdigitated back-contact
(HIBC) solar cell had achieved a conversion efficiency of 28.29%, approaching the theoretical crystalline silicon efficiency limit of 29.4% cited by the company. He positioned the full-screen module design as a complementary approach to improving power output through structural optimization, alongside further gains in cell conversion efficiency.

title: Remote control and cybersecurity: Protecting renewable energy plants’ digital infrastructure - pv magazine Global
content:
Modern solar and wind farms are highly interconnected industrial facilities. Their operation depends on SCADA systems, plant controllers, weather stations, grid protection equipment, communication gateways and, in some cases, cloud platforms provided by equipment manufacturers or plant operators.
Remote control capabilities are essential to the operation of Spain’s electricity system. Red Eléctrica’s Renewable Energy Control Center (CECRE) monitors more than 4,500 renewable energy generation facilities in real time. Facilities, or groups of facilities, with an installed capacity exceeding 1 MW are monitored through telemetry data. The system operator can also transmit setpoints to regulate their output and maintain the balance between electricity generation and demand.
pv magazine Week Europe 2026
Do you want to strengthen and enhance the cybersecurity of your solar energy assets to safeguard them against emerging threats?
Join us on Dec. 3 for
pv magazine Week Europe
Cyber winter: Is Europe’s solar sector ready for the stress test?
Industry experts will explore real-world cyberattack scenarios, highlight potential vulnerabilities in solar and storage systems, and share practical, actionable strategies to protect your energy assets. Attendees will gain valuable knowledge on how to anticipate, prevent, and respond to cyber threats in the rapidly evolving solar energy sector.
The regulatory framework is primarily based on Royal Decree 413/2014, electricity system operating procedures and European grid connection requirements. Operating Procedure P.O. 9.2 governs the exchange of real-time information with the system operator and establishes communication requirements between generation facilities, control centers and the system operator.
Following amendments introduced by a resolution dated June 19, 2026, failure to comply with real-time data transmission requirements may also result in financial penalties. On cybersecurity, Article 4, Section 9.2, explicitly states:
“Both the SO’s control centers and the control centers authorized to exchange real-time information with the SO shall be responsible for ensuring protection against cyberattacks originating from their respective control centers.”
Remote control vs. remote access
Remote control and remote access serve different purposes at renewable energy facilities.
Remote control is associated with electricity system operations. The system operator can transmit setpoints or other operational instructions to a generation facility through an authorized control center. Red Eléctrica publishes a list of authorized control centers that have passed setpoint-following tests and are qualified to manage the integration of renewable energy generation facilities into the grid.
Remote access, by contrast, is used for operation and maintenance activities. Inverter manufacturers, engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractors, operation and maintenance (O&M) providers and plant operators may remotely connect to inverters, plant controllers or SCADA systems to monitor equipment, diagnose faults, update software, adjust configurations or provide technical support.
The ability to control a facility remotely does not mean that every inverter or wind turbine needs to be directly accessible from external networks. A more secure architecture can route setpoints through a protected control center or plant controller, which then distributes instructions to individual devices within a properly segmented operational technology (OT) network.
Inverters as critical access points
A cybersecurity breach affecting an inverter or plant controller can have consequences beyond the availability of individual equipment. It could result in unauthorized power curtailment, changes to reactive power or voltage settings, manipulated status data or coordinated failures across multiple devices sharing the same configuration.
The concentration of risk is particularly significant. Many installations rely on the same inverter models, firmware versions, communication protocols, manufacturer portals or centralized cloud platforms. A vulnerability in a shared remote maintenance system could therefore have more serious consequences than an isolated equipment failure.
Mitigating these risks requires a controlled technical and organizational architecture. Guidelines from Spain’s National Cybersecurity Institute (INCIBE) on secure remote access recommend measures including secure virtual private network (VPN) connections, controlled authentication and authorization, and protection of both access servers and endpoint devices.
Spain’s security framework for solar and wind power
Spain’s national security framework (ENS –
Esquema Nacional de Seguridad
) establishes security requirements for electronic systems and services used in the public sector. It is governed by Royal Decree 311/2022 of May 3 and aims to protect information systems, data, communications and electronic services through common principles, minimum requirements and security measures.
The ENS does not automatically apply to all private operators of solar and wind power plants. Its requirements become directly relevant when a private company provides information systems or electronic services to a Spanish public-sector entity, or when compliance is required under public contracts, concessions, subsidy conditions or tender specifications.
In the solar and wind sectors, this may include control and monitoring platforms operated on behalf of public-sector entities, IT and operational technology (OT) services supporting publicly owned energy facilities, or digital systems used to deliver services under public contracts.
The applicability of ENS requirements must therefore be assessed on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the company, project and contractual obligations involved.
Relationship between the ENS and the NIS2 Directive
The EU’s NIS2 Directive explicitly includes the electricity sector among its highly critical sectors, including activities carried out by private companies. Depending on their size, activities and classification, operators and service providers in Spain’s solar and wind energy sectors may fall within the scope of the directive as “essential” or “important” entities.
NIS2 requires entities within its scope to implement cybersecurity risk management measures covering incident response, business continuity, supply chain security, vulnerability management, access control, cryptography and multi-factor authentication.
Management bodies must approve these measures and oversee their implementation. Although the ENS and NIS2 are separate regulatory frameworks, they share substantial requirements.
In March 2026, Spain’s National Cryptologic Center (CCN) stated that ENS certificates of conformity could be used to demonstrate compliance with requirements arising from NIS2, pending the directive’s transposition into Spanish law.
For solar and wind farm operators, adopting an ENS-based approach can therefore offer practical advantages. In addition to implementing technical safeguards, companies can document, categorize and review their security measures systematically, making it easier to demonstrate their implementation and effectiveness to customers, regulators and business partners.
However, ENS certification should not be considered automatic or comprehensive proof of NIS2 compliance. Operators must also assess the directive’s applicability to their activities, sector-specific obligations, incident reporting requirements and management body responsibilities.
Conclusion
The growing digital interconnection of solar and wind farms in Spain is increasing their exposure to cybersecurity threats.
For inverters in particular, it is important to distinguish between the remote control capabilities required for grid operations and remote access granted to manufacturers or maintenance providers for commercial and operational purposes.
Spain’s ENS provides a structured, certifiable cybersecurity framework. Although its requirements do not automatically apply to all private solar and wind farm operators, the framework may become relevant through public contracts, other contractual obligations or its potential role in demonstrating compliance with the NIS2 Directive.

title: Sirius PV unveils 525 W perovskite tandem residential solar modules - pv magazine Global
content:
Texas-based module maker Sirius PV has introduced new partnerships with Caelux and IronRidge at the RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas, leading to new and refreshed products across its lineup.
The partnership with Caleux has resulted in the Sirius PV’s new HybridTandem residential solar module, made with Caelux’s Energy Producing Glass and rated to produce 525 W DC under standard test conditions in the same footprint as the company’s existing 450 W residential modules.
Sirius PV says that power rating is expected to increase over time as the Caelux technology continues to develop. In recent remarks to
pv magazine USA
, Caelux CEO Scott Graybeal
outlined his company’s roadmap
to increasing the power output of its perovskite thin-film glass by more than 26% by 2030.
Sirius PV says it is currently working through the remaining testing and certification processes and look forward to bringing this next-generation product to customers in the near future.
The partnership with IronRidge will see Sirius PV integrating module frames compatible with the racking maker’s new EPIC Aire universal mid-and-end clamps. The new system is designed to allow solar modules to hinge and lock into place, saving workers time on residential rooftops.
Sirius PV says the new approach to module clamping has the potential to make installations up to 30% faster, significantly reducing labor costs and improving productivity for installers.
Modules featuring EPIC-compatible frames are expected to be available from Sirius PV in limited quantities during the first half of 2027, with widespread availability across the company’s product portfolio in the second half of the year.
The company’s first two HybridTandem modules featuring the EPIC-compatible frame will be on display at the BayWa r.e. booth on the RE+ show floor.
Minnesota-based module maker
Heliene introduced a utility-scale module with Caelux glass

title: Solar panel cleaner combines electrostatic force with ionic wind - pv magazine Global
content:
A research team in Algeria has developed a hybrid dust-removal system for PV panels that combines an electrostatic plate with a corona-induced ionic wind. The researchers built a prototype and filed a
patent application
“The primary novel contribution lies in this two-stage approach: The electrostatic field of the leading plate is intended to oppose particle adhesion and pre-lift the dust, which is then transported away by the electrohydrodynamic drag force of the ionic wind,” the researchers said. “By combining particle detachment and transport, this dual-action strategy overcomes the limitations of standalone electrohydrodynamic methods.”
The researchers built a 60 cm-wide cleaning head mounted on a wheeled platform that moves along a horizontal PV panel, covering its full width in a single pass. At the front, a metal plate inclined at 45 degrees generates an electric field that helps lift sand grains from the glass surface. Behind the plate, a high-voltage sawtooth electrode produces a strong electric field at its tips, ionizing the surrounding air and generating a localized electrical discharge known as a corona. As the ions move toward two grounded copper tubes, they propel surrounding air molecules, creating an ionic wind that sweeps away the loosened sand grains.
To test the system, the researchers evenly distributed sieved, dry sand collected from the Algerian Sahara over a roughly 0.1 m² section of PV glass, with initial dust loadings ranging from 30 g/m² to 130 g/m². They weighed the sand before and after a single cleaning pass to calculate the percentage removed by mass. They also varied the applied voltage, travel speed, plate-to-glass distance, dust loading, and grain size, while measuring the discharge current and outlet airspeed.
The researchers conducted each test twice at a temperature of around 25 C and a relative humidity of approximately 45%. They compared the hybrid system with a standalone ionic-wind system under identical operating conditions.
In laboratory tests, the hybrid system removed more than 95% of deposited dust by mass at initial loadings of up to 90 g/m². The system achieved this performance at an applied voltage of 20 kV, a travel speed of 3.3 cm/s, and a plate-to-glass distance of 2 cm. At a dust loading of 130 g/m², removal efficiency dropped to approximately 55%. The researchers suggested that the upper dust layers may have shielded underlying particles from the electric field or airflow.
“While this work establishes the core proof-of-concept at a fixed panel inclination of 0°, future research will expand upon these findings to evaluate performance under broader field parameters,” the researchers said. “Subsequent investigations will examine the combined impact of variable panel tilt angles and gravitational assistance, assess the influence of environmental factors such as relative humidity and moisture-induced particle adhesion, and evaluate long-term operational durability for automated field integration.”
The researchers presented their findings in “
Hybrid electrostatic–ionic wind system for efficient dust removal from photovoltaic panels
,” published in the
Journal of Electrostatics
. The research team included scientists from Algeria’s
Djillali Liabes University of Sidi Bel-Abbes
, Ibn Khaldoun University of Tiaret, Mustapha Stambouli University of Mascara, and the University of Blida.

title: Anthropic Is Pushing New Products, and Big Discounts, to Justify Its Huge Valuation
content: To justify its enormous new valuation as a public company, Anthropic needs to show that it can expand quickly in other areas of business the way it did with coding. Its early efforts are showing signs of promise—and highlighting the steep challenges it faces. Anthropic is gaining traction with Claude Cowork, an AI tool for nontechnical business users, and persuading some customers to spend in new areas such as cybersecurity. The company is also hoping to embed itself deeper in companies’ core operations with Claude Managed Agents, a set of tools that developers can use to build and run agents without having to manage the underlying servers and other infrastructure. At the same time, intensifying competition has prompted Anthropic to offer deep discounts to customers willing to devote a certain percentage of their AI budgets to the startup—and show documents to prove it, according to managers at the customers and software licensing experts. And in many new product areas, Anthropic faces more entrenched competition than it did when its Claude Code product took the business world by storm starting late last year. OpenAI is also targeting cybersecurity as a major growth area, for example, and Anthropic’s push this month into office productivity apps such as spreadsheets and brainstorming tools puts it in direct competition with Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace, products from two tech giants that are also major financial backers of Anthropic. Vertice, a software procurement firm, said that Anthropic has begun offering some credits worth up to $100,000 for its products as companies in recent months have started expanding their usage beyond engineering teams running Claude Code to Claude Cowork for sales, finance, human resources and marketing teams. The credits are offered in exchange for customers signing higher yearlong spending commitments or agreeing to sign those contracts by a certain date, said Vertice CEO Eldar Tuvey. But customers are also wary about the prospect of a surge in spending on Anthropic’s products and are looking for ways to monitor and in some cases pare back high spending as they adopt Claude Cowork, Tuvey said. Investors appear optimistic. Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 a share late Wednesday, well above its marketed range of $70 to $78 last week. That makes it the biggest IPO ever , gives Anthropic a fully diluted valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion, and will rank the five-year-old AI developer among the biggest publicly traded U.S. companies. Many analysts and investors ahead of Anthropic’s first day of trading Thursday were expecting the share price to jump further. Beyond Claude Code Anthropic was well behind OpenAI in revenue before Claude Code caught fire. Anthropic’s revenue surged to $4.7 billion in the first quarter of this year—more than all of last year—then grew 144% from that level in the second quarter. That pace has slowed, with third-quarter revenue rising 47% from the second quarter to $17 billion. Anthropic doesn’t break out sales by products or industries, but most customer spending is still geared toward Claude Code, according to customers and consultants. Anthropic’s IPO prospectus says that the top 5% of enterprise customers that use Claude Code spend about 20 times as much per month as those that don’t use the coding tool. The company has told investors that its efforts to diversify revenue are going well. Adoption of Claude Cowork—which debuted in preview in January and launched widely in April—has outpaced that of Claude Code in the nine months after the coding tool debuted in February 2025, it said, without providing figures. Anthropic has launched tailored Claude-powered tools and features for seven sectors—financial services, financial advisers, healthcare, life sciences, legal, education and government—and for broader business functions: Claude Security, Claude Design and Claude Science. Its next big use case is arguably cybersecurity. Eric Foster, CEO of TENEX.AI, an Anthropic consulting partner, said his large enterprise clients in recent months have shifted 10% to 20% of their Anthropic spending toward scanning and patching vulnerabilities in their code repositories to defend against potential hacks. They previously spent their Anthropic budget entirely on coding. Still, those customers are generally using the models with their own harnesses—software tools to manage the underlying model—rather than using Claude Security directly, indicating Anthropic may have to fight for customers to use its applications. Claude Managed Agents, another major new product, is still in public beta, but some Anthropic partners have already set it up for customers. Jamie Shepard, president of Enabuild, a consultancy that works with Anthropic customers in regulated industries like healthcare, said Claude Managed Agents has been a primary driver of a roughly 65% increase in sales prospects his firm has seen over the past few months. This adoption could benefit Anthropic. Claude Managed Agents comes with its own harness that controls how Claude agents access external data, remember previous conversations and navigate the series of steps involved in completing tasks. Agents require a high degree of customization, and once customers adopt Anthropic’s harness, it becomes more difficult for them to switch to a different provider, Shepard said. Discounts With Strings Attached While Claude Code’s runaway success largely caught rivals off guard, big competitors are already vying for many of the same new opportunities that Anthropic is pursuing. OpenAI President Greg Brockman, for example, told The Information this month that there is “no question” that cybersecurity will become a bigger business for OpenAI than coding. And the leap in spending on Anthropic and other pricey AI products this year has prompted many companies to look to lower-cost alternatives. Customers including FedEx, Robinhood, Coinbase and Shopify have developed their own software for coding that allows them to easily switch between Anthropic, OpenAI and open-source models. And OpenAI’s efforts to undercut Anthropic’s prices have swayed some firms to use OpenAI’s coding tool, Codex. Robust competition, customer cost concerns and the relative ease of switching AI models have prompted Anthropic to employ various tactics to woo new customers and keep others in the fold. Anthropic gave clients credits of up to $2,000 per user to test Claude Cowork, Claude Design and Claude Security when they were introduced, according to a partner of the AI firm that works with about 1,000 of its large enterprise customers. Anthropic also appears more open about giving large customers bigger discounts than it has in the past, according to managers from two customers. In at least two instances, the discounts it offered were larger than 30%, said the managers. One said that level of discount was more than double what Anthropic had given his firm in its prior agreement. OpenAI, meanwhile, has offered discounts higher than the 20% to 30% that some founders said they received on listed prices for its models—in at least one case, 40% to get a company to switch from competing AI coding tools to Codex. Anthropic is trying to ensure that its discounts lead to lasting business. To get them, some customers have to agree to earmark a certain percentage of overall AI spending for Anthropic, under what is known as a “share-of-wallet” clause, said the managers from the two customers. More recently, Anthropic has started asking some customers to show their invoices and other documents to prove they are meeting these terms, said Madisyn Ellsworth, an analyst at NPI Financial, a firm that helps companies negotiate contracts with Anthropic and other software providers. NPI first noticed this language in Anthropic’s agreements in early November, said Ellsworth. While OpenAI also includes share-of-wallet clauses in some of its contracts, NPI hasn’t seen any instances where the ChatGPT maker is asking customers to produce documentation, she added. One software firm said Anthropic has moved from a discount of around 15% on listed token prices for a $1 million spending commitment in the first quarter to nearly 30% after the firm agreed to spend $3 million over the summer. Most of the increased spending came from human resources, finance and sales teams using Claude Cowork to perform tasks such as generating financial forecasts and preparing market research reports. While the company spent more than 90% of its Anthropic budget on engineering tasks earlier this year, 60% now goes to coding and around 40% to Claude Cowork as well as tools like Claude Design and Claude Security for niche projects. Anthropic told the software firm it would offer a discount higher than 30% if the company committed to spending more than $5 million annually.

title: Anthropic’s Public Debut Looms
content: We all need a break from the Nvidia soap opera, so we’re switching things up today and talking about that other drama percolating in the background—Anthropic’s public debut. The company behind Claude priced its initial public offering on Wednesday night at $83 a share, several dollars above its preliminary pricing range, and at a level that values the whole company at around $1.5 trillion. Seeing as this is the first top AI model developer to go public, not to mention the biggest, we’d bet the stock reaches $150 when it opens on Thursday, as everyone and their dog vies for a piece of the action. Of course, if they were smart, they’d hold back. The stock is more than likely to settle lower in the next few days, as the initial burst of exuberance dissipates. As for where the stock will trade in six months, I can’t guess. The crystal ball I ordered online got stolen en route to my apartment— thanks for nothing, FedEx. (The Information on Thursday will livestream a two-hour video discussion on Anthropic’s valuation, tech, cybersecurity strategy, drug discovery ambitions, as well as market movements: Check it out , starting at 11:30 a.m. PT / 2:30 p.m. ET.) We shouldn’t assume Anthropic’s first year as a public company will be like that of another groundbreaking tech firm, Google, whose shares steadily rallied in the months after its 2004 IPO and a year later were trading more than 200% higher than its IPO price. For one thing, Google was a cash machine from its early days. In 2004, the year it went public, its free cash flow rocketed 200% from 2003 and just grew from there. Anthropic could be the opposite. It generated $5.6 billion in free cash flow in the first nine months of this year, but its business model is about to shift to one where it will generate minimal, if any, cash. That’s because Anthropic is investing in leasing chips and running them itself in its own data centers, rather than relying entirely on outside cloud firms to run its AI. That move will change “the cash flow profile of our business,” it coyly says in its IPO prospectus. It’s a smart move in the long run, giving Anthropic more control over the infrastructure that its services run on, which should help it keep costs under control. “Investors generally agree with the logic that a company this dependent on compute should be more vertically integrated,” according to research firm William Blair in a note Wednesday. But in the medium term, Anthropic has to make sure it can pay the bills. The company is also spending a fortune paying other cloud firms for computing capacity. All up, including money being spent on leasing its own chips, the company has $452 billion in purchase commitments and lease agreements due before the end of 2030. That translates to a significant annual nut for Anthropic to cover. Remember, its revenue in the first nine months of this year was $33 billion, although its annualized run rate reached $81 billion at the end of October, the company said in its IPO filings. Still, given Anthropic’s hefty commitments, it can’t afford any kind of slowdown. And yet, given the intensifying competition from other AI models—including open-source models that businesses are trying more and more as a way of improving the bang for the buck they get on AI spending—its future growth rate is anything but assured. Anthropic is truly the first of its kind—but whether it will prove a profitable business in the long run is still up in the air. For that reason, investors may do well to be careful at what price they buy the stock. Palo Alto Networks’ Latest Purchase Cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks has been on a shopping spree lately , snapping up Datadog rival Chronosphere for $3.35 billion at the start of the year and Israeli login-software firm CyberArk for $25 billion a short time later, not to mention the smaller purchases of Koi Security, Portkey and Embrace since then. But on Wednesday Palo Alto struck a different kind of deal—the purchase of Applied Compute for $4.5 billion in stock. Applied Compute isn’t a cybersecurity firm but a young startup that helps companies customize AI models with their own data. That’s a hot field, as more businesses decide they don’t want to use the leading AI models from companies like Anthropic for anything that deals with sensitive internal data, given questions about the security of that data. Meanwhile, cybersecurity is becoming a massive issue for businesses, given AI’s ability to spot holes in software. Palo Alto presumably sees Applied Compute as a way to pitch businesses on combining its skills in cybersecurity with Applied’s more secure customized models. As my colleague Aaron Holmes puts it, AI security will be increasingly handled by customized small models—which is a future that Palo Alto is now well positioned for. No wonder Palo Alto stock jumped 9% in after-hours trading on Wednesday. In Other News • Nvidia held its first employee all-hands meeting without CEO Jensen Huang on Wednesday morning, with one notable executive on stage: former sales chief Jay Puri .  More on the meeting here. • U.S. banks including JPMorgan and Citigroup have sought protection against violations of semiconductor export bans in a loan they are considering for Bridge Data Centres, a Singapore-based data center operator that once hosted Megaspeed, the firm at the center of the widening Jensen Huang scandal, according to Bloomberg. • Tencent President Martin Lau said Wednesday that Washington’s new rule barring Chinese companies from accessing Nvidia’s advanced AI chips through overseas data centers “sets everyone back in China.” • Meta Platforms is delaying distributing a new class of shares while a lawsuit filed by investors opposed to the plan plays out, Bloomberg reported. title: Bret Taylor’s Sierra in Talks to Raise at $30 Billion Valuation
content: Sierra, the AI customer support startup founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, has been in talks to raise new funding at around a $30 billion valuation, according to two people with knowledge of the fundraise. That price would nearly double the $15 billion-plus valuation it received in its last round announced in May. The three-year old startup is discussing raising around $1.5 billion in new funding, one of the people said.  Lightspeed Venture Partners, Greenoaks and Benchmark are in talks to invest, the person said. The talks are still early and terms could change. The potential fundraising highlights continued investor interest in startups that are building AI applications and that are seeing rapid revenue growth and pulling ahead of competitors. San Francisco-based Sierra said last month that it had surpassed $400 million in annualized revenue, doubling its revenue pace from just five months prior. A spokesperson didn’t respond to requests for comment. Meanwhile, Decagon, a top rival to Sierra, was generating around $100 million in annualized revenue at the end of the second quarter and projecting between $175 million and $200 million in annualized revenue by year’s end, said a separate person who has spoken with Decagon executives. Decagon has recently been speaking with investors about raising hundreds of millions in new funding, the person said, though its valuation target couldn’t be learned. Sierra and Decagon have historically differentiated from each other by going after different types of customers. While Sierra serves larger companies such as JP Morgan Chase, Cigna and Liberty Global, Decagon has targeted startups and smaller businesses like Perplexity, Notion and Duolingo. More recently, Decagon has added larger customers like Delta, American Airlines, Hertz, Avis and Deutsche Telekom, according to a person with knowledge of the business. AI applications like Sierra and Decagon have seen rapid revenue growth during the AI boom, as businesses rush to try new tools. However, many of these startups have not seen the 70%-plus gross margins that traditional software businesses have enjoyed. Their margins are hit by the high costs of frontier models, though AI model developers such as OpenAI have been aggressively slashing prices in recent months. Additionally, many AI app startups like Sierra also hire technical consultants, sometimes called forward deployed engineers, that work closely with businesses  to help them customize Sierra’s tech for their specific applications. Such employees can also be costly and negatively affect gross margins depending on how a startup categorizes such costs. (Sierra’s gross margins couldn’t be learned.) Sierra has previously raised more than $1.5 billion in funding from investors including Tiger Global Management, GV, Greenoaks, Sequoia Capital and Benchmark.

title: China’s Moonshot AI Scraps $150 Million Deal to Access Nvidia Chips in Indonesia
content: Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based developer of the Kimi models, has scrapped a $150 million deal to access Nvidia Blackwell chips through a data center in Indonesia, after the U.S. this week announced a rule to restrict Chinese companies from accessing advanced chips remotely, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. Moonshot signed the contract with a Southeast Asian neocloud to rent access to a sizable cluster of Blackwell Ultra B300 chips, starting from as early as next year, the people said. The B300 is one of Nvidia’s most powerful AI chips, and is barred by the U.S. government from sale to China. Chinese companies were able to access restricted Nvidia chips from data centers outside of the country, a loophole that was plugged by the rule released by the U.S. Commerce Department this week. To use the loophole, Chinese companies in the past several years signed large deals to rent data centers equipped with the state-of-the-art Nvidia chips in other countries, with Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand among the most popular locations. Under the new rule, data centers already serving Chinese customers above a certain computing threshold have 90 days to obtain a U.S. license. Moonshot’s scrapped deal in Indonesia could be a harbinger of more cancellations, particularly for projects still being built. Moonshot rose to global prominence in July after its K3 model displayed capabilities rivaling U.S. frontier models. The access to Nvidia Blackwell chips from outside of China was crucial to Moonshot’s development of the model, and the startup had been seeking more Blackwell chips for its next model, Kimi K4, The Information reported in July. Shortly after K3’s release, the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, an agency under the Department of Commerce, said it was formally investigating Moonshot’s access to advanced AI chips. In a mark of its hunger for compute, Moonshot agreed to a roughly 50% upfront payment for the $150 million deal in Indonesia, one of the people with direct knowledge said. Typical contract terms require an upfront payment of around 15%. Moonshot has also paused discussions for other new deals, as it reviews the impact from the new regulations, said the other person with direct knowledge. Moonshot declined to comment. Under the new rule, data centers outside the U.S. equipped with AI chips up to certain threshold are required to perform strict checks on customers for any ownership links to China. The U.S. also requires a license for the export of advanced chips to companies headquartered in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, countries with a high risk of diversion of chips. The computing threshold that triggers the  license requirement is exceedingly low: equivalent to roughly 300 of the most advanced AI chips on the market, according to law firm Sidley Austin . The deals that Chinese AI firms look for usually involve at least a couple thousand chips. The U.S. move formally restricts a critical compute source on which Chinese labs have long relied, throwing their AI development plans into disarray. The restriction is likely to raise the cost of training models, according to a note this week by Bernstein analysts led by Qingyuan Lin. Fears of running afoul of the new rules have also prompted bankers to reconsider lending to Chinese-linked projects. Executives at five lenders have discussed abandoning or passing on a $480 million deal for Singapore-based neocloud Aolani, meant to fund the purchase of advanced Nvidia chips for ByteDance ’s use, Bloomberg reported . The chips are slated to be housed in a data center in Malaysia.

title: How to Diagnose a Recurring Technical Problem with Google Gemini
content: Persistent IT problems can drain employee productivity and strain help desk teams. And while a  one-off technology problem often amounts to little more than a nuisance, recurring problems often have a real impact on the business. Imagine, for instance, that you run IT support for your company, and employees keep reporting that their VPN connections are dropping, locking remote workers out of company systems. Even with your IT team helping one user after another, the tickets keep piling up, and the underlying issue remains unaddressed. Google Gemini can help IT teams sort through this information, spot patterns, and identify the root of the problem to help the organization get back to business. Step 1: Define the Problem First, you’ll want to use Gemini to cut through the chaos of helpdesk logs to better understand the frequency of the issue and create a consolidated dataset for further analysis. Take a screenshot of the error message that your users are getting, and export data from recent support tickets into a Google Sheet. Then, ask Gemini to compare the ticket data against the error message. Try this prompt: You are a Level 2 debugging specialist. Analyze the attached error screenshot to identify the exact error code or message. Using this key, review the attached support tickets from the last 60 days and find all tickets that contain the identical error message. Output the results as a table. Step 2: Hunt for Root Cause From a dataset of 500 help tickets, Gemini might identify two dozen or so dropped VPN connections, providing a table that identifies the ticket number, date, and location of each. This narrower dataset will make it easier to find out what the tickets have in common (and, therefore, what might be causing the problem). Your ticket export should already include each employee’s operating system, VPN client version, and location. To see what the affected employees have in common, prompt Gemini again: You are a technical data analyst. Analyze the consolidated ticket data to identify statistically significant correlations between the ‘VPN connection dropping’ issue and the following attributes: operating system, VPN client version, and user geolocation. Format the findings as a ranked list, stating the calculated confidence level for each correlation. The results of this step can be extremely revealing. For example, Gemini might note that only macOS users running a particular client version are experiencing the problem. Step 3: Identify the Solution The good news is that your helpdesk team has already solved users’ VPN problem multiple times. However, it’s likely this is the first time anyone has looked at all of these tickets together, since they were previously scattered among tickets for various one-off problems. Therefore, it’s highly possible no one in the organization knows the most common fix, even if your helpdesk has already applied that solution over and over again. In your Gemini chat, type: From the ‘Resolution Notes’ field of all closed tickets in the consolidated data, extract and rank the top 5 most successful, non-escalated troubleshooting actions that resolved the ‘VPN connection dropping’ issue. Output the steps as a numbered list, including the calculated frequency/success rate for each step. Gemini will identify which fixes have been tried and list their success rates. For example, Gemini might note that every resolved ticket required the user to install a new client version and clear the macOS DNS cache. Step 4: Create a Playbook Now that you know how often VPN connections are dropping, what is causing the problem, and how it has been fixed in the past, you can give your frontline technicians a clear, repeatable playbook for handling the issue. This will ensure that the problem gets fixed quickly, without unnecessary escalation to senior engineers. Gemini can quickly draft a playbook with desired content, length, and tone. Try this prompt: You are a Level 2 technical writer. Draft an updated, internal-facing knowledge base article titled ‘Resolving recurring VPN drops: root cause analysis and Tier 1 triage.’ Structure the article with two main sections: ‘Summary of root cause’ and ‘Tier 1 troubleshooting steps.’ The tone must be concise and instructional, explicitly targeting Level 1 helpdesk technicians. The playbook will give your technicians exactly the information they’ll need when the issue pops up again in the future. And a problem that previously robbed teams of hours of productive time each month will instead be resolved in minutes.

title: U.S. Commerce Department Rushed to Clear Nvidia H200 Exports to China
content: In recent months, Jeffrey Kessler, the official overseeing the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, has pressured staff to expedite the approval of sales of Nvidia ’s H200 graphics processing units to China, according to three people with knowledge of the matter. In some cases, Kessler directed staff at BIS —an agency under the Commerce Department—to approve the exports over objections from other U.S. government departments, two of those people said. The H200, launched in 2023, is an older generation of Nvidia chips that developers can use to train and run AI models. In December 2025, President Donald Trump approved the chip, which is a generation behind Nvidia’s mainstay Blackwell product, for sale to China, after intense lobbying from former CEO Jensen Huang. As part of the approval, Nvidia agreed to give the U.S. government a 25% cut of H200 sales to China. The pressure on BIS staff to speed up the H200 approvals, which hasn’t previously been reported, could add further scrutiny to a crisis that has engulfed Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. He resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive last week after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence suspect spied for China, who also built a network of companies that move billions of dollars of restricted Nvidia chips to China. Lawmakers have since opened probes into how Commerce approved Nvidia chip sales to China, and want Huang, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and BIS chief Kessler to testify. Meanwhile, as the furor intensified, Nvidia’s current leaders this week said they pulled the plug on some chip sales to China. During the company’s Tuesday evening earnings call, interim CEO Colette Kress said the chipmaker had stopped shipping a class of export-compliant chips, which includes the H200, to China. Kress didn’t explain the reason for the decision. When it was still selling such chips in China, there was a lot of red tape Nvidia had to go through to complete such sales. Under the U.S. export rules, four departments—Commerce, State, Energy and Defense—had to rubber-stamp each export sale of H200s to Chinese buyers. Under a rule Commerce issued in January, the exporter had to certify that the chips wouldn’t go to China’s military or to blacklisted entities. Separately, U.S. export regulations required BIS to weigh the reliability of each party to a sale, such as if they can be trusted in their intended use of the chips and not passing the chips to other companies or the Chinese military. The procedure is designed to also prevent the chips from ending up in smuggling channels. Yet, Kessler, the Commerce under secretary who runs BIS, regularly pressured staff to expedite the approval without having ample opportunity to conduct due diligence on Chinese companies that submitted the export requests, the three people said. BIS issued some licenses even after reviewers’ checks turned up red flags from other departments, two of the people said. As a result, BIS granted approvals to at least two companies that have ties to the Chinese military or state-owned enterprises, or were involved in the smuggling of Nvidia Blackwell chips into China, according to people with direct knowledge and a review of these companies’ registration records. The Commerce Department expedited H200 licensing because processing the licenses was a priority for the Trump administration, said a separate person familiar with the matter, who added that the recipients of the licenses were still subject to the same national security conditions and due diligence process. Nvidia, for its part, said its H200 sales to customers in China went through the appropriate government approval process. “The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China,” said an Nvidia spokesperson. For at least some H200 licenses, Kessler took the position that the usual interagency review wasn’t needed, according to the two people with knowledge of the matter. That review dates to an executive order signed by President Bill Clinton in 1995. It lets the State, Defense and Energy departments weigh in on export license applications alongside Commerce, and sets up a formal appeals process for when they disagree. In some cases, BIS stepped in to approve export licenses for customers seeking Nvidia H200s even when other agencies refused to sign off on those applications, one of the two people said. Questionable Approvals One of the companies that received an H200 license is Zhejiang Yindun Cloud Technology, which is tied to Range Intelligent Computing Technology Group, a Shenzhen-listed data center operator, according to one of the two people and two separate people familiar with the matter. Range buys powerful Nvidia chips from companies involved in the smuggling network and rents them to local tech firms, two of the three people said. Yindun was controlled by the family members of an executive at Range until June 2026, when the ownership was transferred to companies controlled by the Tibetan government, according to corporate registration records and two people close to the company. Another licensee, Shanghai LinkWise, operates in a data center built by a company tied to the Chinese navy. LinkWise became a partner in an undersea data center in Shanghai in 2025, according to a Shanghai government announcement , and has since moved in. The data center developer’s largest shareholder is Beijing Highlander Digital Technology, which has been a supplier to China’s navy since 2004— according to the company’s website —and which was put on a U.S. trade blacklist in 2022. LinkWise’s website says it has developed specialized shipping containers that each can host 16 Nvidia Blackwell servers, though it is unclear whether the company has any of the servers. The push to approve chip sales to China didn’t extend to Nvidia’s main rival. Leaders at BIS didn’t rush staffers to approve sales of Advanced Micro Devices’ MI325X, which has performance comparable to the H200’s and which was also cleared by Trump for exports to China, according to one person with knowledge of the situation. “Export controls should evolve with changes in technology, while protecting national security,” Kessler said in a statement when the rule was issued in January. “Permitting the sale of the H200 to China under controlled conditions will strengthen the American technology ecosystem.” A U.S. export license only clears part of the hurdle for Chinese companies to access the H200. Beijing has been resisting the H200 flooding into China to wean the country off American technology. The Chinese government in January told some tech companies it would approve H200 purchases only in special circumstances, such as for university research labs, The Information reported. Beijing later cracked the door open, approving a small batch of H200s to companies including ByteDance and Alibaba. In the meantime, Kress, Nvidia’s interim CEO, sought to downplay the financial impact that discontinuing sales of H200 and other chips to China would have on the company. On Tuesday, she told analysts that Nvidia sold $2.4 billion of licensed data center products to China from its Hopper family of chips—which includes the H200—during the fiscal third quarter. That represented only 2% of the company’s $115.8 billion in revenue during that period.

title: Will Anthropic’s IPO Lead To An Exodus of Anthropic Employees?
content: Today is a major milestone for Anthropic . The five-year-old maker of Claude beat its archrival OpenAI to the public markets, and many of its employees are going to become millionaires, if not billionaires, when the company starts to trade later today. The big question is what today means for Anthropic’s future. Before we get to that, let’s set the scene. Anthropic priced the offering at $83 a share , well  above its preliminary pricing range, valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion. Chances are the stock will trade significantly higher when it opens later Thursday. For employees looking to cash in, they’ll need the stock to stay higher for a while. While they can sell up to 10% of their shares on the first day of trading, they can’t sell more until the company reports its full-year 2026 earnings early next year. Assuming the stock doesn’t tank, the sudden influx of money will help Anthropic employees buy houses and donate a big chunk of their newfound wealth to causes like shrimp welfare . Counterintuitively, though, it may also lead them to leave the very company that brought them the wealth in the first place. You may think that employees at a company as philosophically driven as Anthropic are as bought in as the cofounders and in it for the long haul. That’s not necessarily true. At the end of the day, many of the employees, especially those who have joined more recently from big tech companies, might not be drinking the Kool-Aid as much as just trying to make a quick buck. Take Jacob Coxon , a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher who made headlines in September when he quit his job over concerns that AI “could kill us all.” When asked by Stanford political science professor Robert Reich earlier this month why he wouldn’t give up his OpenAI equity if he was so concerned about the potentially dangerous actions of AI labs, he responded, “I like money, bro. I agree it's blood money.” (After the interview, Coxon seemed to walk back his statements and pledged in a post on X to give away his OpenAI equity to charity when it goes public.) That’s an extreme example, but I’m sure a not-insignificant number of Anthropic employees wouldn’t mind taking their newfound wealth and taking a nice, long vacation on a beach somewhere! Another option for these staffers is joining another AI lab. I’ve heard of multiple instances of employees leaving one AI developer for another so they can diversify their own personal holding of equity in these companies. That way, if it’s not Anthropic that wins the AI race, but OpenAI, they’ll still be fine. Losing a significant number of researchers would not bode well for Anthropic. One of the reasons why the company has been so successful thus far is because of its low turnover. (The company said in its S-1 that it had experienced only 1% “regrettable attrition” of its employees in the last 12 months—an impressive figure!) And, if these researchers were to go to rival labs, they could bring their proprietary knowledge with them. Anthropic’s ability to retain staff is one of the many issues that investors will be watching once Anthropic is public. Even assuming Anthropic easily replaces anyone who leaves, by hiring (as it has already done) from other tech firms, there will be an impact. Outsiders will likely bring new perspectives and cultures that could clash against Anthropic’s existing culture. Today is the first day of Anthropic’s new life: let’s see how it goes. Here’s what else is going on… Overheard In Nvidia’s all-hands meeting Wednesday, interim CEO Colette Kress tried to soothe employees and prevent a potential talent exodus, The Information reported. She told employees that they can expect pay raises and more equity at the end of this year. Kress’ remarks come after more than 10,000 people who said they were Nvidia employees signed an unofficial petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. Tencent President Martin Lau said Wednesday that Washington’s new rule barring Chinese companies from accessing Nvidia ’s advanced AI chips through overseas data centers “sets everyone back in China”. The new rule, Lau said, could slow the development of new models. Wall Street executives and the National Security Agency told Congress that tech outages this week stemmed from attempts to patch security vulnerabilities identified with AI, not from cyberattacks, according to the Washington Sun. Meta Platforms has paused plans to issue a new class of shares that could help it raise more capital for AI spending as it contends with pending shareholder lawsuits. The company will not issue the new Class C shares while the legal battle plays out, it said in a court filing on Wednesday. Policy Watch The Trump administration is weighing requiring U.S. companies to disclose their use of Chinese AI models, possibly as a way to discourage the increasing use of open-weight Chinese models which can be cheaper than their closed U.S. counterparts, Reuters reported. California Governor Gavin Newsom released a proposal that would give California broad powers to impose safety measures on an AI company, Politico reported. The measure would allow state officials to intervene if they judge AI models at risk of escaping human control, require independent evaluators inside labs, and shut down AI models in emergencies. Deals and Debuts See The Information’s Generative AI Database for an exclusive list of private companies and their investors. Anthropic on Wednesday said it raised $81 billion in its initial public offering after pricing the IPO at $83 a share, above its marketed range of $70 to $78 a share, the largest in history. Anthropic sold 956.4 million shares and the seven co-founders sold 23.6 million shares for $83 each. This gives the company a fully diluted valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion. Palo Alto Networks plans to acquire Applied Compute , an AI startup founded by three former OpenAI researchers, for $4.5 billion in stock, the companies announced Wednesday. It's the latest in a string of deals by the cybersecurity giant as it aims to serve as an all-in-one provider for companies seeking to use AI safely. Sierra , which makes AI customer service agents, is in talks to raise about $1.5 billion at a valuation of about $30 billion, The Information reported. Lightspeed Venture Partners , Greenoaks and Benchmark are in talks to invest. MegaRobo , which automates science labs with robots and AI, raised nearly $200 million in a funding round joined by the Oman Investment Authority. Moonshot AI , the Beijing-based developer of the Kimi models, has scrapped a $150 million deal to access Nvidia Blackwell chips through a data center in Indonesia, after the U.S. this week announced a rule to restrict Chinese companies from accessing advanced chips remotely, The Information reported on Wednesday. BrightAI , which uses AI to monitor utility and industrial equipment, raised $97 million in a funding round led by Smith Point Capital. Linq , which builds messaging tools for AI agents, raised $90 million in a funding round led by Andreessen Horowitz. Pulley , a San Francisco-based AI construction startup, announced $64 million in new funding, including a $41 million Series B round and a $23 million Series A round from investors like Jump Capital , Catalyst Investors , CRV and Susa Ventures . Arva AI , a New York City- and London-based startup that develops agents for banking operations, raised $20 million in Series A funding led by Arthur Ventures Vero Security , which secures companies’ A.I tools and agents, raised $11 million in a seed funding round led by TLV Partners. Voyage Labs , a Menlo Park, Calif.-based startup building a personal AI agent that plans and books trips and local outings, raised $12 million in seed funding led by Kleiner Perkins . Botsync , which makes robots for factories and warehouses, raised $11 million in a funding round led by IvyCap Ventures. Google released Gemini 4 Neon , a model designed to be faster than its most powerful public model Gemini 4 Carbon and with deeper reasoning than Gemini 4 Hydrogen . The model is built for efficient cyber defense, Google said, with improved safety guardrails and behavior from Carbon. OpenAI on Wednesday published new results highlighting the growing capabilities of its AI models in chip design , reporting significant improvements to both its in-house Jalapeño chip and Advanced Micro Devices ’ flagship graphics processing unit designs. U.S. banks including JPMorgan and Citigroup have sought protection against violations of semiconductor export bans in a loan they are considering for Bridge Data Centres , a Singapore-based data center operator that once hosted Megaspeed , the firm at the center of the widening Jensen Huang scandal, according to Bloomberg. The AI Futures Project , a nonprofit that forecasts how AI may impact the future, released a proposal for how AI companies could limit and disclose how much computing power they allocate to research, slowing the pace of AI development to prioritize safety.
